title:
Tunable Aza-BODIPY
Photocatalysts for Near-Infrared
Metallaphotoredox Atom Transfer Radical Polymerization
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The merger of photoredox and transition-metal catalysis has significantly advanced radical and redox transformations, yet its reliance on UV or visible light continues to limit applications in optically complex and spatially confined environments. Herein, we introduce a modular family of tetraaryl aza-boron-dipyrromethene (aza-BODIPY) organic photocatalysts (PCs) for near-infrared (NIR) metallaphotoredox atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP). We systematically modulated peripheral electronics and core bromination, evaluating the dyes through quantum-chemical, electrochemical, and spectroscopic methods. This approach identified the key parameters governing catalytic performance: a delicate interplay between triplet-state accessibility, redox properties, and photostability. The optimized aza-BODIPY dye enables well-controlled ATRP of diverse acrylates and methacrylates at ultralow catalyst loadings, down to 5 ppm PC and 50 ppm copper complex. The system is further translated to open-air aqueous conditions, enabling rapid, high-throughput synthesis of water-soluble polymers in a 96-well plate format. Taking advantage of the enhanced penetration of NIR light, we demonstrate controlled polymerization through challenging physical barriers, including ex vivo tissue. Overall, this work defines design principles for far-red/NIR-absorbing aza-BODIPY PCs and expands the scope of NIR-mediated polymer synthesis to optically turbid, spatially restricted, and aqueous environments.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
An Embedded Plasticization
Strategy for Flexible Thermally
Activated Delayed Fluorescence Polymers with High Luminance
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) polymers offer the theoretical advantage of achieving 100% internal quantum efficiency. Together with their solution processability, TADF polymers are promising candidates for flexible display technologies. However, emissive polymers that simultaneously combine efficient TADF emission with mechanical flexibility remain rare. Here, we report an embedded plasticized linker strategy for mechanically compliant TADF polymers. Polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based flexible segments are covalently incorporated into acridine–benzophenone–carbazole polymer backbones. This “TADF unit + plasticized linker” design preserves the donor–acceptor electronic structure required for delayed fluorescence while introducing flexibility into the emissive polymer framework. The resulting polymers exhibit small singlet–triplet energy gaps, clear delayed fluorescence, and favorable film deformability. The deformation behavior of the neat polymer films was evaluated on PDMS substrates under an applied substrate strain of 75%. Notably, the optimized rigid organic light-emitting diode (OLED) based on PIDC(2,7)-EO achieves a maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 20.1% and a high luminance of 85 988 cd m–2. This luminance value is among the highest reported for polymer-based TADF OLEDs. Flexible OLEDs fabricated on flexible substrates further deliver a maximum EQE of 14.7%. These results demonstrate efficient electroluminescence from flexible device architectures. This work establishes embedded plasticized linkers as an effective molecular design strategy for high-performance mechanically flexible TADF polymers. This strategy provides a promising route toward next-generation flexible OLED technologies.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
A Mixed
Conducting Polymer with pH-Dependent Selectivity
for the Oxygen Reduction Reaction
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Achieving 4-electron oxygen reduction with metal-free electrodes has remained a longstanding challenge. Here, we show that poly(benzimidazobenzophenanthroline) (BBL), an n-type ladder polymer, breaks this barrier through an electrocatalytic inner-sphere 2 + 2 series mechanism─a mode of reactivity unprecedented among organic mixed ionic-electronic conductors (OMIECs). Using pH-dependent rotating ring-disk voltammetry, we find that this series mechanism occurs over separate potential windows on BBL. At more positive potentials, an initial reduction wave correlated with electron polaron formation in BBL produces exclusively hydro(gen) peroxide across all pH values, followed by a second, pH-dependent wave for hydro(gen) peroxide reduction at more negative potentials. At pH 14.0, this second wave enables complete four-electron reduction of O2 (n ≈ 4) to OH–, driven by formation of a bipolaronic state in BBL. Decreasing the pH instead stabilizes a hydrogenated state in BBL incapable of O–O bond cleavage, reverting selectivity to n ≈ 2. These insights reveal that the coupling between ion selectivity during electrochemical ion-insertion and product selectivity during ORR catalysis shapes active-site structure and poisoning, establishing a new design principle in the emerging field of OMIEC electrocatalysis.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
On-Resin P(V) Polyphosphorylation
of Serine, Threonine,
and Tyrosine
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Protein phosphorylation is the most abundant post-translational modification (PTM) and plays a central role in regulating biological processes. Attaining discretely polyphosphorylated peptides is an open challenge. Their chemical synthesis relies on coupling of phosphorylated amino acid building blocks, which suffer from base-mediated elimination and incomplete couplings, or postsynthesis functionalization via a global phosphoramidite approach, which is prone to side reactions during oxidation. Herein, we developed an on-resin phosphorylation that utilizes a protected and activated phosphorus(V) species. This method gave ≥95% conversion for monophosphorylation of serine, threonine, and tyrosine and tolerated oxidation-sensitive methionine, cysteine, and tryptophan residues. Up to five phosphorylations were installed site-selectively, with superior performance to building block approaches, and it remained effective on sequences up to 83 residues. With an efficient method for site-selective polyphosphorylation established, the specificity of antibodies directed against phosphorylated variants of the oncoprotein MYC was evaluated. These antibodies are often used for evaluating the role of phosphorylation sites (phosphosites) in regulating MYC in cancer. Although all antibodies maintained selectivity for their specific phosphosite, binding varied upon additional phosphorylation sites around the epitope, underscoring the need for careful validation of antibodies to prevent misinterpretation. Overall, this strategy enables efficient access to complex, defined polyphosphorylated peptides for future investigations into the biological roles of phosphorylation sites on MYC, and provides a broadly applicable method for the synthesis of precisely (poly)phosphorylated peptides and proteins.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Ion-Pair Receptors
Couple Cation Binding with Molecular
Electron Storage for Room-Temperature Birch-Type Reduction
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Birch reduction provides a powerful route to partially dearomatized products from aromatic precursors, but classical protocols rely on highly reactive solvated electrons generated from alkali metals in cryogenic liquid ammonia, offering limited molecular control over reducing equivalents. Here we show that ion-pair receptors couple Na+ binding with molecular electron storage within electron-deficient diimide-based π-frameworks. Reduction with sodium generates persistent sodium-associated radical-anion ion pairs in which the unpaired electron is delocalized predominantly over the π-accepting framework. Time-dependent UV–vis and EPR measurements establish persistence of the representative Na+·IP-4•– state in THF at room temperature under an inert atmosphere. Control experiments show that covalent integration of the Na+-binding and electron-accepting domains markedly enhances reduced-state persistence and productive electron transfer relative to the isolated components or their noncovalent combination. The resulting molecularly stored reducing equivalents enable room-temperature Birch-type reductions of polycyclic aromatic substrates in high yields using unprecedented catalytic receptor loadings. These results establish coupled cation binding and molecular electron storage as a supramolecular strategy for regulating highly reducing equivalents in solution-phase dearomatization chemistry.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Cationic Ionomer Coatings
Promote Anion Electroreduction:
Nitrate Reduction as a Model Reaction
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrolysis technologies represent a promising pathway to valorize abundant feedstocks using renewable electricity. While ionomers serve critical roles as ion conductors and catalyst binders in electrolyzers, their impact on electrochemical transformations of ionic species remains poorly understood compared to extensively studied neutral-molecule conversions like water splitting and CO2 reduction. Herein, we use the electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction as a model transformation to investigate the influence of ionomer coatings in anion electroreduction reactions, which face fundamental challenges from electrostatic anion depletion near negatively polarized cathodes and premature desorption of anionic intermediates. We demonstrate that cationic ionomer coatings increase local nitrate concentration up to 10-fold compared to bulk electrolyte due to the interfacial Donnan potential. While prior studies have shown that ionomers can influence the local reaction microenvironment, this work provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first quantitative measurement of nitrate concentration within ionomer coatings as a function of charge density and its impact on catalysis. A 5-fold enhancement in ammonium partial current density was achieved with the ionomer bearing the highest charge density. Using in situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS), we quantified enhanced local nitrate concentration (up to 1.1 M versus 0.1 M in bulk electrolyte), conversion, and supply with increasing charge density. This study establishes guiding principles for tuning ionomer charge identity and density to control interfacial ion concentrations in electrochemical transformations of dilute charged substrates.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
X-Shaped Multichannel
Conjugation Enabled by
Excited-State Aromaticity
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Molecular topology governs the photophysical properties of polycyclic π-conjugated systems by defining their effective conjugation pathways. Conventionally, linear π-extension is considered more effective than angular extension in increasing the effective conjugation length and narrowing the optical bandgap. Here we uncover an inverse topology–property relationship in π-extended dihydrophenazines (DHPs): linear extension unexpectedly blueshifts fluorescence, whereas angular extension produces pronounced redshifts. Transient spectroscopy, theoretical calculations and aromaticity analyses reveal that Baird aromaticity–driven planarization of the DHP core redistributes π-delocalization in the S1 state, causing linear fusion to disrupt global π-delocalization and shorten the effective conjugation length, while angular fusion promotes cooperative delocalization across the fused framework and extends it. Successive angular fusion progressively activates four structurally distinct π-extension branches through the shared Baird-aromatic DHP core, generating an X-shaped multichannel conjugation network. These findings reveal how excited-state aromaticity reprograms conjugation topology, offering new insights for controlling π-delocalization and emission.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Catalytic Interphases
Enable Sulfur Redox Catalysis
in All-Solid-State Lithium–Sulfur Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Weak solid–solid contact with limited chemical and transport continuity is a common bottleneck in solid-state batteries, particularly in all-solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries (ASSLSBs), where Li2S/S8 conversion requires catalytic acceleration but lacks a continuous solid-state catalytic pathway. Here, we propose an interphase catalysis strategy for solid–solid sulfur conversion by transforming discrete catalyst/reactant interfaces into a chemically integrated reaction interphase. WO3 is identified as a suitable oxide to construct such a metastable mixed-anion S–W–O catalytic interphase on Li2S based on the work-function difference between the metal oxide catalyst and Li2S/S8, which serves as a practical screening rationale for evaluating the relative tendency toward sulfur–oxygen coordination exchange. The interphase contains unsaturated W centers and a polarized electronic environment, enabling coupled electron/Li+ transport and dynamically regulating sulfur redox through coupled sulfur-species exchange. This integrated interphase further stabilizes cathode interfaces during repeated Li2S/S8 conversion. As a result, the optimized cathode sustains stable cycling over 15000 cycles at 10 C and a temperature of 60 °C. A record-high Li2S loading of 30 mg cm–2 with an areal capacity of 21.2 mAh cm–2 is also achieved, demonstrating interphase catalysis as an effective route to overcome solid-state sulfur-conversion limitations in practical ASSLSBs.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Stiffness
Directs Intracellular Fate and Intercellular
Transport of Nanoparticles
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nanoparticles have been developed as delivery vehicles to achieve uniform distribution of drugs in the tumor, but they are still not optimal for deep tumor penetration due to the hindrance by the dense extracellular matrix. Enabling active transport via tumor cells has been explored as a solution, which has been achieved by tuning the size and surface chemistry of nanoparticles. Here, we show that particle stiffness is another key determinant. Using positively charged polyglycerol nanogels with matched size, charge, and composition, we found that stiff nanogels preferentially enter cells via clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME), undergo lysosomal processing, and are efficiently exocytosed, enabling transcellular transport. In contrast, soft nanogels are taken up mainly by macropinocytosis, accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, and exhibit prolonged intracellular retention. Finally, the efficient CME and subsequent exocytosis of stiff nanoparticles contribute to the enhanced transcytosis efficiency, allowing them to penetrate 3D tumor spheroids. This stiffness-dependent cellular itinerary operates without additional surface modifications, revealing a general design principle whereby intrinsic mechanical properties can control intracellular and intercellular transport behavior of nanoparticles.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Modulation of MOF
Catalytic Activity to Exploit Cystine
Dependency for Immunometabolic Therapy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Tumor immunometabolism plays an important role in tumor progression and immune cell activity and is therefore critical to the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy. Modulation of immunometabolism to boost cancer immunotherapy is mostly based on targeting tumor cell metabolism, which often fails to address the tumor-promoting functions maintained by stromal cells. In contrast, targeting a metabolic checkpoint shared by tumor cells and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) can potentially overcome this limitation but has been relatively underexplored. Herein, a locally delivered, ultrasound activatable nanocatalytic platform is reported for immunometabolic cancer therapy. The platform is composed of sulfasalazine and a gallium-modified Fe-TCPP metal–organic framework nanozyme codelivered in an oxidized sodium alginate-based hydrogel. Ultrasound-activated gallium-modified Fe-TCPP boosts electron transfer, peroxide activation, and reactive oxygen species production while disrupting iron balance. Simultaneously, sulfasalazine inhibits SLC7A11-mediated cystine uptake in CAFs and tumor cells, reducing matrix remodeling and weakening the tumor’s antioxidant defense. This dual approach increases oxidative stress, reshapes the tumor microenvironment, induces immunogenic tumor cell death with ferroptotic traits, matures dendritic cells, and strengthens CD8+ T-cell responses. Consequently, it suppresses tumor growth in an immunocompetent osteosarcoma model and remains effective in a patient-derived OSCC xenograft model. Together, these findings demonstrate that targeting shared SLC7A11-mediated cystine dependence integrates stromal remodeling, tumor redox disruption, and antitumor immune activation.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Kinetic
Control of Symmetry-Broken Spin Architectures
of Azafullerene on [10]Cycloparaphenylene Templates: From Frustrated
2D Lattices to Quasi-1D Chains
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Supramolecular host–guest complexation provides a powerful strategy for stabilizing organic radicals and organizing them into functional spin architectures. Here, we investigate the kinetic pathways for on-surface complexation of spin-1/2 azafullerene radicals (C59N•) within templated [10]cycloparaphenylene ([10]CPP) nanohoop monolayers on Au(111), revealing a strongly anisotropic energy landscape that governs radical migration and encapsulation. Migration of isolated C59N• along the [10]CPP rims proceeds via relatively low energy barriers (∼0.45 eV), leading to preferential confinement at the nanohoop periphery prior to azafullerene encapsulation. C59N• relocation to the global energy minimum at the [10]CPP center requires overcoming substantially higher barriers of at least ∼0.8 eV, with interfullerene interactions raising these barriers further. High C59N• mobility and relaxed lateral confinement at [10]CPP template edges also activate an alternative assembly pathway in which azafullerene intercalation induces in-plane exfoliation of [10]CPP lines from the 2D [10]CPP array, creating a reconstructed two-dimensional superlattice composed of alternating zigzag chains of azafullerenes and linear rows of encapsulated C59N•⊂[10]CPP complexes. This edge-driven reorganization gives rise to anisotropic lattices of encapsulated radicals with one-dimensional structural motifs. The control over the rich energy landscape of C59N•⊂[10]CPP complexation thus enables access not only to geometrically frustrated two-dimensional lattices but also to quasi-one-dimensional chain motifs of spin-1/2 carrying radicals within a single supramolecular platform.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
A
Flexible Complementary Memristive Synapse for Convolutional
Neural Network Applications
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The memristive artificial synapse, which typically operates on the basis of various filamentary conductance-update mechanisms, has been extensively utilized to implement hardware neural networks for brain-inspired computing. However, the stochastic conductance-switching characteristics that arise from uncontrollable filamentary evolution within the two-terminal device have long hindered hardware neural networks from achieving training and recognition performance comparable to their software neural network. Here, we propose a flexible complementary memristive synapse that achieves highly linear conductance-update behavior while preserving a large dynamic range. This synapse consists of a homogeneous bilayer of two amorphous indium–gallium-tin oxide (a-IGTO) films deposited under different oxygen partial pressures: an oxygen-deficient, VO-rich layer formed without O2 supply and an oxygen-supplied, VO-poor layer formed with O2 supply, exhibiting incremental and decremental conductance-update behaviors, respectively. The distinct oxygen-vacancy-related states and filament-evolution characteristics of the two layers suggest vacancy-mediated layer-to-layer redistribution, which can mutually compensate the nonideal conductive filament evolution of the two different layers, thereby facilitating more gradual modulation of the net conductance. The proposed flexible synapse exhibits robust mechanical stability and durability after 12,000 bending–release cycles, as confirmed by electrical characterization while maintained in the bent state at a bending radius of 2 mm. Finally, the applicability of the proposed flexible synapses to HW-NNs is evaluated through a VGG-8-based CIFAR-10 image recognition simulation using experimentally measured synaptic characteristics for weight updates in the two fully connected layers.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Nanoarchitecture
of Cobalt Phthalocyanine for Enhanced
Chloramphenicol Hydrodechlorination through Direct Electron-Transfer
Mechanism
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrocatalytic hydrodechlorination (ECHD) provides a sustainable method for treating water polluted with chlorinated organic compounds under ambient conditions. Cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc) represents a molecular catalyst with economic benefits and high selectivity, although its performance is limited by significant molecular stacking. To this end, we constructed ordered CoPc nanotubes (CoTs) for ECHD studies, alongside conventional CoPc single molecules and disordered aggregates as reference systems. All materials catalyzed ECHD via a direct electron transfer (DET) route on the CoPc active state under turnover conditions. The ordered CoT architecture accelerated interfacial and internal electron transfer, boosting the intrinsic activity. Degradation involves simultaneous reduction of terminal nitro and chloro groups, and the latter is suggested to follow an energetically favorable remote attack pathway. At full chloramphenicol (CAP) conversion, CoTs delivered an ECHD ratio of 83.9%, which is superior to recent benchmarks. For practical use, a flow-cell system achieved a treatment flux of 6.79 L h–1 g–1, which is 5 times that of a standard H-cell. This work underscores the pivotal role of molecular ordering in enhancing ECHD and offers design guidelines for non-noble metal heterogeneous electrocatalysts.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Machine-Learning
Dynamics of Redox-Active Materials:
Polaron Diffusion on the TiO2(110) Surface
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In redox-active materials, atoms dynamically change their oxidation states in response to excess charge and electronic transport, with the potential for novel technologies spanning electronics, catalysis, and energy storage and conversion. Despite the remarkable progress of modern artificial intelligence methods in accelerating atomistic simulations, capturing the quantum-mechanical nature of charge transport and dynamically varying oxidation states remains a fundamental challenge, limiting scientific and technological progress. In this work, we introduce a machine-learning-based molecular dynamics framework capable of explicitly tracking the oxidation state dynamics arising from small-polaron hopping (excess charges trapped on single lattice sites that diffuse upon thermal activation). Our model uses descriptors augmented with charge localization information at each time step and is trained on density functional theory data to capture signatures of polaronic diffusion. We apply our method to the rutile TiO2(110) surface, which is a prototypical reducible oxide. Our simulations reveal that charge-carrier diffusion is highly sensitive to the local surface environment: polarons preferentially localize near oxygen vacancies, whereas their interaction with hydroxyl groups is weaker. These results provide a microscopic interpretation of experimental observations, highlight strategies to tune charge-carrier mobility through surface engineering, and demonstrate the applicability of our approach to investigating charge transport in complex materials.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Charge-Induced Formation
and Field-Driven Directional
Motion of Vacancies in a Two-Dimensional Halide
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Controlling defect evolution in two-dimensional (2D) materials is essential for reliable nanoelectronic functionalities, yet selectively inducing defect formation and externally driven migration remains a key challenge. Here, we demonstrate two distinct mechanisms governing halogen vacancy formation and migration in a PbBr2 monolayer on highly ordered pyrolytic graphite using low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy combined with density functional theory calculations. We show that halogen vacancies reshape the local density of states and electrostatic potential beyond the immediate defect site. Crucially, electric fields and charge injection mediate distinct atomic-scale responses: tip-induced electric fields drive directional vacancy migration and coalescence, whereas charge injection from the tunneling current induces vacancy formation, with enhanced efficiency when coupling to shallow defect states. These results demonstrate that direct electrical stimuli can drive both vacancy motion and creation in a two-dimensional, predominantly ionic material system. Our findings establish a framework linking defect-induced electronic structure, local electrostatics, and externally driven atomic rearrangement under conditions relevant to device operation.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title: Addition–Migration Cascade for Ortho‐Selective Carbon Functionalization of Phenols
content:
A nucleophilic addition–migration–rearomatization cascade enables selective ortho‐carbon functionalization of phenols using diverse organometallic reagents. The strategy accommodates Csp3‐, Csp2‐, and Csp‐centered nucleophiles, providing access to densely substituted phenols and enabling a concise total synthesis of honokiol.








ABSTRACT
Ortho‐ and para‐carbon‐disubstituted phenols are prevalent in natural products and pharmaceuticals, yet their selective synthesis remains challenging. The strong resonance‐donating effect of the hydroxyl group renders phenols electron‐rich, activates both ortho and para positions, and limits their direct functionalization with external nucleophiles. Herein, we report an addition–migration–rearomatization strategy for the ortho‐selective carbon functionalization of phenols using readily accessible para‐quinol carbonates and diverse organometallic nucleophiles. The transformation proceeds through nucleophilic 1,2‐addition to the dienone carbonyl, followed by C1‐to‐C2 group migration and rearomatization, thereby enabling the formal installation of carbon nucleophilic substituents at the enone α‐position. A broad range of sp3‐, sp2‐, and sp‐hybridized nucleophiles, including alkyl, vinyl, aryl, heteroaryl, polyaromatic, and alkynyl reagents, participate efficiently under mild conditions. DFT calculations identify syn‐methyl facial attack as kinetically preferred over syn‐Boc facial attack by 24.72 kcal mol−1, establish that both SN2′ manifolds are noncompetitive, and show that aromatization proceeds via a Mg‐assisted decarboxylation/deprotonation pathway rather than an unassisted route. Synthetic utility is demonstrated through a concise five step synthesis of the bioactive natural product honokiol from commercially available allyl anisole.

title: A Homoleptic Biradicaloid‐Ligated Analogue of Ferrocene
content:
A biradicaloid‐ligated ferrocene complex is reported. This was synthesised via an isolated Fe(I) intermediate which circumvents redox‐induced ligand dimerisation observed when Fe(II) precursors were used. Both complexes were analysed by ab initio calculations to provide an insight into their electronic structures.








ABSTRACT
In this communication, we report the synthesis, characterisation and electronic structure of a ferrocene analogue containing two biradicaloid ligands, representing the first homoleptic sandwich complex in this ligand class. In this quest, we found that the target compound was unattainable via routes involving Fe(0) or Fe(II) intermediates, and counterintuitively that the rare and much less‐explored +1 oxidation state was crucial for the synthesis.

title: Single‐Step Orientational Self‐Assembly of Pd Metallacycles and Heterometallic Pd–Pt Helical Cages From Heteroditopic Ligands
content:
Donor inequivalence combined with coordination mode adaptability in heteroditopic tetrazole–pyridine ligands enables orientational self‐assembly of metallacycles and helical cages with selective Pd(II)/Pt(II) partitioning in a single step, despite their closely matched coordination preferences. This strategy provides single‐step access to heterometallic helical cages with guest‐induced chiroptical properties.








ABSTRACT
Controlling the self‐assembly of heterometallic supramolecular architectures without generating statistical mixtures remains a major challenge. Here, we show that adaptable coordination modes of tetrazole units in heterodipotic tetrazole–pyridine ligands direct both orientational self‐sorting and selective metal organization. Reaction with cis‐protected Pd(II) acceptors afforded Pd6(L)4 metallacycles (L = L1–L3), in which tetrazolate coordination through an unusual (2,3) binding mode is exploited in the orientational self‐sorting. In contrast, ligand L4 employed its (1,3) coordination mode together with the pyridyl donors to generate a Pd9(L4)6 helical cage and the heterometallic Pd9Ag(L4)6, and Pd3Pt6(L4)6 cages in single‐step self‐assembly processes. Remarkably, despite the closely matched coordination preferences of Pd(II) and Pt(II), the synergistic effects of donor inequivalence and the flexible coordination behavior selectively partitions the two congeneric d8 ions into distinct coordination sites within the Pd3Pt6(L4)6 cage. The uncommon (1,2,3) tetrazolate binding mode additionally enables formation of the Pd9Ag(L4)6 cage. Encapsulation of enantiopure guests by the helical cages induces host chirality and corresponding chiroptical responses. These results demonstrate that coordination mode flexibility of the tetrazole moiety combined with the pyridyl unit can direct the formation of metallacycles and helical cages and enable selective partitioning of closely related metal ions in a single‐step assembly.

title: A Single‐COF Photocatalytic System for One‐Pot Oxygen Reduction Coupled Ammoximation of Cyclic Ketones
content:
Porphyrin–polyimide COFs enable one‐pot oxygen reduction coupled ammoximation of cyclic ketones. Photoinduced electron transfer activates O2 at imide carbonyl sites, generating *OOH that directly oxidizes NH4+ to NH2OH, which then condenses with ketones. IMCOF‐1 delivers cyclohexanone oxime at 18.55 mmol g−1 h−1, avoiding H2O2 accumulation and enabling a single‐COF cascade.








ABSTRACT
Photocatalytic oxygen reduction over covalent organic frameworks (COFs) has been extensively studied for H2O2 production, but the in situ utilization of oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) intermediates in chemical synthesis remains underexplored. Herein, two porphyrin‐based polyimide COFs, IMCOF‐1 and IMCOF‐2, are reported as photocatalysts for the one‐pot ORR‐coupled ammoximation of cyclic ketones using O2 and NH4OAc. Under light irradiation, IMCOF‐1 achieves a cyclohexanone oxime formation rate of 18.55 mmol g−1 h−1 and is effective for several other cyclic ketones. Mechanistic investigations reveal that photoinduced electron transfer from the porphyrin units to the electron‐deficient imide moieties promotes charge separation and activates O2 at the carbonyl sites. The resulting surface‐bound *OOH intermediates are proposed to participate in ammonia oxidation and subsequent NH2OH formation, which then condenses with cyclic ketones to yield the corresponding oximes. In contrast to stepwise systems that first accumulate H2O2 before ammoximation, the present one‐pot strategy enables the in situ utilization of oxygen‐derived reactive intermediates without requiring substantial bulk H2O2 pre‐accumulation, eliminating the need for H2O2 isolation, storage, and transport, thereby improving safety and atom economy while maintaining high selectivity. This work demonstrates the potential of directly harnessing ORR‐derived intermediates for the light‐driven synthesis of value‐added nitrogen‐containing chemicals.

title: Distinct PXR Inverse Agonism Mechanisms Rely on Differential Ligand‐induced Co‐Regulator Recruitment
content:
Pregnane X receptor (PXR) antagonism is ligand‐encoded: SPA70 recruits corepressors NCoR1 (nuclear receptor corepressor 1)/SMRT (silencing mediator for retinoid and thyroid‐hormone receptors) while binding coactivators, and is modulated by retinoid X receptor alpha (RXRα); MI891 causes cytoplasmic retention and corepressor‐dependent repression, independent of RXRα. These insights expand the inhibitory spectrum beyond on/off switch models.








ABSTRACT
The pregnane X receptor (PXR) displays exceptional ligand promiscuity, yet the molecular basis of its antagonism remains poorly defined. PXR inhibition has traditionally been attributed to the displacement of coactivators from the activation function‐2 (AF‐2) surface. Here, we show that PXR antagonism is mechanistically heterogeneous, with distinct inhibitory mechanisms determined by ligand structure. Comparative analysis of imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine, MI891, and SPA70 antagonists reveals multiple non‐canonical inhibitory mechanisms that decouple coregulator recruitment from transcriptional output. Notably, SPA70 preserves compatibility with coactivator recruitment while remaining transcriptionally inactive, consistent with concurrent corepressor engagement and a distinct coactivator‐compatible antagonist state. In contrast, MI891 stabilizes a PXR conformation that favors NCoR1 and SMRT binding and impairs nuclear translocation. MD simulations and mutagenesis reveal ligand‐specific perturbations of α12 and the α10/α11 region that underlie these effects. Together, these findings establish a ligand‐encoded framework for PXR antagonism that extends beyond the classical on/off switch model.

title: Spin‐Correlated Wavelength–Intensity Dual Modulation in Organic Diradicals via Excited‐State Channel Engineering
content:
A carboline‐appended luminescent diradical featuring coexisting through‐bond and through‐space charge‐transfer (TSCT) emissive channels was designed. Magnetic‐field‐ and temperature‐induced spin‐population redistribution modulates the relative contributions of these electronically distinct channels, enabling correlated changes in emission intensity and wavelength.








ABSTRACT
Luminescent diradicals translate open‐shell spin dynamics into optical readouts, yet their spin‐dependent responses have largely been confined to emission‐intensity changes, while concurrent wavelength modulation remains rare. Here, we introduce a through‐space charge‐transfer (TSCT) strategy in which appending a δ‐carboline donor to a carbazole‐bridged diradical preserves the native through‐bond charge‐transfer (TBCT) pathway while introducing a higher‐energy TSCT‐related emissive channel. At low temperature, δCbCz(TTM)2 exhibits pronounced magnetoluminescence (MagLum) enhancement together with an approximately 31 nm field‐induced blue shift, while zero‐field warming from 4.5 to 20 K produces an approximately 25 nm blue shift. Temperature‐dependent MagLum measurements show that the additional spectral and intensity changes induced by the magnetic field are rapidly attenuated upon warming, supporting a common spin‐dependent mechanism. The structural analogue αCbCz(TTM)2 exhibits a similar dual response with a smaller wavelength shift, highlighting the sensitivity of the response to donor topology. Time‐resolved spectroscopy, variable‐temperature EPR, and quantum–chemical calculations support a spin‐correlated photophysical model in which magnetic and thermal perturbations regulate spin‐dependent population redistribution, thereby modulating the relative contributions of TBCT‐ and TSCT‐related emissive channels and producing correlated changes in emission intensity and wavelength. This work establishes through‐space excited‐state channel engineering as a route for extending spin‐correlated luminescence beyond intensity‐only modulation.

title: The Elusive Fluoropolysulfates [FS2O6]– and [FS3O9]–, a New Class of Weakly Coordinating Anions
content:
The isolation and structural elucidation of the first fluoropolysulfates [FSnO3n]– (n  =  2, 3) is presented. The novel compounds Pb[FSO3][FS2O6] as well as the fluorotrisulfates K[FS3O9] and [Se4][FS3O9]2 show markedly different solid–state structures compared to their (hydrogen–)di–/trisulfate analogues. The electrostatic potentials of the anions, the bonding situations and frontier molecular orbitals for the [FS3O9]– anion and the non–covalent interactions in [Se4][FS3O9]2 were additionally studied using quantum chemical calculations.








ABSTRACT
The isolation and structural characterization of the fluorodi‐ and fluorotrisulfate anions, [FS2O6]– and [FS3O9]– are reported. The [FS2O6]– anion has been obtained from reactions of SO3 with XeF2 in the presence of PbF2 as the salt Pb[FSO3][FS2O6] (triclinic, P1¯$\bar{1}$, Z = 2, a  =  508.65(3), b  =  909.67(5),  c  =  969.67(5) pm, α  =  89.494(2)°, β = 77.373(2)°, γ  =  76.466(2)° and V  =  424.99(4) Å3). The [FS3O9]– ion forms in the reaction of K[FSO3] with SO3 at room temperature as the potassium salt K[FS3O9] (monoclinic, P21/c, Z = 4, a = 1048.69(8), b  =  786.39(6), c =  969.58(7) pm, β = 90.431(2)° and V  =  799.6(1) Å3). The use of the [FS3O9]– ion as a weakly coordinating anion was demonstrated with the isolation of [Se4][FS3O9]2 (monoclinic, P21/n, Z = 2, a = 719.2(1), b  =  1576.0(2), c =  897.7(1) pm, β = 113.015(5)° and V  =  936.5(2) Å3), obtained from the reaction of selenium, SO3 and XeF2 at 80°C. We investigated the anions quantum chemically concerning their molecular electrostatic potentials and the electronic energies of formation. The non–covalent interactions in [Se4][FS3O9]2 were analysed using Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM) and Natural Bond Orbital Analysis (NBO).

title: Electrostatic Cation Intercalation Into Polymeric Self‐Assembled Monolayers Enables Ambient‐Air Fabrication of 32.73% Efficient Monolithic Perovskite/Silicon Tandem Solar Cells
content:
Cation intercalation reconstructs the polymeric SAM to coordinate wettability, interfacial energetics, and buried‐interface formation. This molecular‐level regulation translates scalable ambient‐air processing into efficient charge transfer and a certified 32.73% monolithic perovskite/silicon tandem.








ABSTRACT
Polymeric self‐assembled monolayers (SAMs) enable stable, efficient, and scalable perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells (TSCs) based on silicon heterojunction (HJT) bottom cells. However, severe steric hindrance within the polymer matrix disrupts the directional anchoring of phosphonate groups, thereby limiting macroscopic work‐function regulation and sustaining a persistent hole‐extraction barrier. Herein, we report a targeted molecular reconstruction of the buried interface via the electrostatic intercalation of phenethylammonium iodide (PEAI). Templated by the polymer backbone, the intercalated PEA+ cations adopt a highly directional vertical arrangement. This oriented molecular scaffold provides a strong intrinsic dipole while driving the electronegative iodide (I−) counterions to enrich at the uppermost interface. This synergistic spatial decoupling maximizes the net upward dipole, triggering a favorable energy level realignment that effectively overcomes the hole extraction barrier. Concurrently, the halide‐enriched SAM dictates crystallization kinetics during ambient‐air slot‐die coating, inducing rapid “burst nucleation” to minimize solvate intermediates and suppress basal voids. Consequently, our 1 cm2 TSC achieves an independently certified power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 32.73%. Benefiting from monolithic crystallographic integrity, the unencapsulated device maintains an enhanced T80 lifetime of 2182 h under continuous maximum power point tracking.

title: Evolution‐Inspired Multi‐Objective Bayesian Optimization for Protein Engineering
content:
Evolution‐inspired multi‐objective Bayesian optimization (EvoMOBO) integrates protein language models with Bayesian optimization for multi‐objective protein sequence optimization. Inspired by natural evolution, it efficiently navigates sequence‐objective landscapes and identifies combinatorial variants with improved performance.








ABSTRACT
Protein engineering requires efficient navigation of vast sequence spaces under limited evaluation budgets, especially when multiple properties must be optimized simultaneously. We developed evolution‐inspired multi‐objective Bayesian optimization (EvoMOBO), an active‐learning framework that integrates path‐dependent sequence generation, global candidate competition, and explicit multi‐objective optimization, enabling efficient prioritization of high‐value variants without exhaustive library enumeration. Compared with state‐of‐the‐art methods on complete steroid receptor DNA‐binding domain (DBD) and ParD3 antitoxin landscapes, EvoMOBO achieved greater target‐region enrichment while maintaining sequence diversity across two‐ and three‐objective tasks. In the DBD landscape, optimization guided by simulation‐derived geometric descriptors enriched variants with satisfactory experimental performance without experimental labels. Building on this validation, we applied EvoMOBO to two enzyme‐engineering tasks using mechanistic descriptors, with experiments reserved for final validation. For an old yellow enzyme from Geobacillus kaustophilus, probabilities of substrate binding and reaction preorganization guided optimization of a non‐native oxidative dehydrogenation, yielding a variant that increased substrate conversion from 17.5% to 95%. For a formate oxidase from Aspergillus oryzae, stability‐related descriptors identified aggregation‐resistant variants that nearly doubled diethyl phthalate degradation in a photoenzymatic cascade. Together, these results demonstrate robust multi‐objective optimization by EvoMOBO and show that mechanism‐derived descriptors can effectively guide protein engineering toward experimentally improved functions.

title: Each Atom and Electron Matters: A Continuous Gold Nanocluster Series
content:
A continuously growing gold nanocluster series (Au41, Au42, Au43, and Au44) is controllably synthesized, providing an unprecedented platform to directly visualize and elucidate how individual atoms dictate nanocluster behavior with respect to geometric and electronic structures.








ABSTRACT
Achieving continuous atom‐by‐atom structural evolution and elucidating the associated quantum size effects in metal nanoclusters remain highly challenging, primarily due to the intrinsic thermodynamic preference for discrete magic‐number configurations. In this study, we present a synergistic ligand‐engineering strategy that combines dynamic ligand coordination with fluorine chemistry to break this preference. The use of weakly coordinating phosphine ligands facilitates adaptive ligand rearrangement during progressive core expansion, while fluorine‐induced noncovalent interactions establish a robust molecular and supramolecular spatial lock, thereby stabilizing cluster molecules and enhancing crystallization. Through this approach, we successfully isolated and structurally characterized an unprecedented continuous series of gold nanoclusters: Au41–Au44. Comprehensive experimental and computational structural and photophysical analyses reveal non‐monotonic geometric evolution and atom‐specific modulation of electronic structure, thereby providing direct evidence for the principle that “each atom and electron matters” in dictating cluster geometry and electronic structures. Collectively, this work fills the structural gap in medium‐sized, phosphine‐protected gold nanoclusters and provides a continuous cluster series that serves as an ideal model for probing quantum size effects at the atomic level.

title: Real‐Time Discrimination of Parallel Single‐Cell Exocytotic and Exosome Catecholamine Signaling by Multichannel Hollow Nanoelectrodes
content:
Multichannel hollow carbon nanoelectrodes enable real‐time discrimination of classical exocytosis and exosome‐mediated catecholamine release in single cells. This platform directly links release‐pathway identity to chemical output, revealing parallel but non‐compensatory regulation and selective loss of catecholamine oxidation from the exosome pathway under cargo‐loading disruption.








ABSTRACT
Chemical communication in single cells often involves multiple vesicle release pathways that can carry overlapping messenger molecules. However, existing methods cannot discriminate between these pathways simultaneously under matched conditions, making their intrinsic relationship difficult to resolve. Here we establish a multichannel hollow carbon nanoelectrode‐based strategy for real‐time discrimination of classical exocytosis and exosome‐associated release. Distinct electrochemical signatures generated within the hollow geometry enable pathway resolution, while the multichannel architecture expands effective sampling coverage over the cell surface and improves event capture efficiency. Using this approach, we show that the two catecholamine signaling routes remain active under environmental perturbation but exhibit non‐compensatory changes in release activity. Under cargo‐loading disruption, classical exocytosis retains reduced catecholamine output, whereas exosome‐associated release persists but becomes largely chemically silent. These findings uncover a previously inaccessible chemically silent state of exosome‐associated release and reveal that cells can preserve a release pathway while selectively reshaping its chemical consequence. More broadly, this work shows that parallel release routes can convey fundamentally different chemical information under the same cellular conditions and establishes a general strategy for studying pathway‐specific chemical regulation in other secretory systems.

title: Radical C─N Coupling at Electrified Carbon Nanotube Interfaces
content:
An applied electric field at a conductive carbon nanotube (CNT) interface promotes catalyst‐free radical C─N coupling through interfacial electron transfer. Real‐time mass spectrometric monitoring and mechanistic studies indicate that the confined interfacial environment facilitates efficient C─N bond formation under ambient conditions.








ABSTRACT
Nitrogen‐containing motifs are central to pharmaceuticals, materials, and bioactive molecules, yet controlling radical C─N bond formation under mild and catalyst‐free conditions remains challenging. Here, we report an electrified carbon nanotube (CNT) interface that promotes radical C─N coupling of aniline derivatives and N‐containing heterocyclic compounds under ambient conditions. Mechanistic experiments show that the enhanced reactivity arises from the coupling of the applied electric field with interfacial charge transfer through the CNT network. Radical trapping, redox probing, and density functional theory calculations support a field‐assisted electron‐transfer pathway involving nitrogen‐centered radical intermediates. Our results indicate that the applied field lowers the barrier to radical generation, underscoring its critical role in enabling the reaction. This work demonstrates that conductive nanointerfaces can enable localized radical bond‐forming chemistry under an externally applied electric field.

title: Dynamic Metal Encapsulation in a Pt/TiO x system Regulated by Pt-Assisted TiO2 Amorphization
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Strong metal–support interaction (SMSI) plays an important role in heterogeneous catalysis, but remains poorly understood, particularly on the origin of SMSI under an oxidative atmosphere. Hereby grand canonical structure exploration of over 4 million bulk PtTi alloys and Pt or PtTi-supported Ti oxide (TiOx) surface structure candidates, we resolve the Pt/TiOx system, a text-book example of SMSI, under both reductive and oxidative conditions: it experiences an encapsulation─deep encapsulation─decapsulation dynamic reconstruction under a sequence of H2 reduction─O2 oxidation─H2 plus O2 redox thermal treatment. The whole process was kinetically simulated by long-time (69 ns) molecular dynamics simulations, revealing in detail how a 3 nm Pt nanoparticle undergoes nonclassical SMSI under an oxidative and redox atmosphere. We find that Pt-assisted TiO2 amorphization is the key to the transition of various SMSI states at different conditions, which elevates Ti chemical potential via amorphization toward low-coordinated [TiO4]. Finally, explainable machine learning models were developed to predict nonclassical SMSI cases and clarify their rarity in nature.</jats:p>

title:
Unlocking Intrinsic
Chirality in Luminescent Copper
Clusters via Intramolecular Spatial Confinement
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Most luminescent clusters that exhibit pronounced chiral signals typically rely on predesigned chiral ligands; however, stimulating the intrinsic chirality of clusters in the absence of exogenous asymmetric ligands remains a significant challenge. In this study, based on a series of structure-correlated Cu2 clusters, we demonstrate that intramolecular spatial confinement effectively induces distortions in flexible ligands, thereby imparting asymmetry to the cluster framework. This molecular asymmetry further determines the orientation of cluster entities during supramolecular assembly, thus enabling the modulation of chirality across this cluster series between inactive (“off”) and active (“on”) states. In addition, these structure-correlated Cu2 clusters display bright and tunable luminescence, allowing for the fabrication of uniform thin films that function as practical scintillation materials for high-resolution X-ray imaging. Collectively, this work provides a novel perspective for regulating the chiroptical properties of metal clusters through the activation of intramolecular spatial confinement and offers valuable insights into the fabrication of cluster-based nanomaterials with tailored photophysical performances.</jats:p>

title:
Dye-Sensitization Enables
Visible-Light-Driven N–N
Bond Cleavage in a Dinuclear Rhenium Dinitrogen Complex
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Conversion of μ-N2 complexes into nitrogenous compounds is one of the most important and challenging chemical transformations in N2 fixation. Although photochemical N2 splitting has been demonstrated, existing approaches predominantly rely on high-energy ultraviolet light that generally affords low efficiency and poor selectivity. Herein, we establish a visible-light-driven molecular photosensitization strategy that enables efficient and selective N–N bond cleavage in a dinuclear rhenium dinitrogen complex. Blue light excitation of the organic photosensitizer 4DPAIPN (2,4,5,6-tetrakis(diphenylamino)isophthalonitrile) is shown to initiate N–N scission to afford the corresponding rhenium nitride in 96% yield. Kinetic analysis of nanosecond transient absorption data through the Balzani-Scandola model indicates energy transfer from the photosensitizer to an acceptor state that lies approximately 2.31 eV above the ground state of the μ-N2-bridged dirhenium complex. This photosensitization strategy decouples light harvesting from N–N bond activation, eliminates the need for UV light, and shows broad applicability across different visible-light absorbing photosensitizers, including transition metal complexes and organic chromophores with long-lived, high-energy triplet excited-states. These findings establish dye-sensitization as a powerful strategy for visible-light-driven N–N bond cleavage for mechanistic study and the future realization of a photochemical pathway for nitrogen fixation.</jats:p>

title:
Programming Oxygen
Reduction Selectivity via Peroxo
Basicity: Acid-Controlled 2e–/4e– Reduction Switching at a Dicobalt Platform
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Achieving switchable 2e–/4e– oxygen reduction selectivity within a single molecular catalyst remains an unmet challenge because the key metal–oxygen intermediate typically commits to one pathway. Herein, we demonstrate that this limitation can be overcome by elevating the basicity of the peroxo intermediate to a level where both proton-transfer (PT) and proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) manifolds become accessible, with the dominant pathway dictated solely by the external acid strength. A dicobalt μ-1,2-peroxo complex supported by an electron-rich macrocyclic poly-NHC ligand exhibits a computed pKa1 of ∼8.8, placing it in a unique thermodynamic window. Stoichiometric protonation bifurcates cleanly: strong acids (HClO4) trigger rapid diprotonation to release H2O2, whereas weak acids (Et3NHOTf) promote O–O bond cleavage to afford a μ-hydroxo complex. Under catalytic conditions, this dichotomy translates into complete selectivity switching─100% H2O2 with HClO4 versus 90% H2O with Et3NHOTf, accompanied by a switch in the rate-determining step from O2 binding to PCET (KIE = 1.60). Crucially, a structurally analogous but less basic peroxo complex predictably inverts the selectivity to H2O under identical conditions, providing a closed-loop validation of the basicity-selectivity relationship. These results establish intermediate basicity as a general, tunable design parameter for programming product selectivity in multielectron catalysis.</jats:p>

title:
Synthesis and Crystal
Structure of Bulk Methanetetrol
C(OH)4
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Methanetetrol, C(OH)4 (orthocarbonic acid), is an elusive tethrahydroxymethane that, due to its rapid dissociation under ambient conditions, has never been synthesized in bulk. A recent study detected the formation of C(OH)4 molecules in the gas phase. Here, we show that C(OH)4 can be synthesized in a diamond anvil cell through the reaction between H2O and CO2 at 45(3) GPa and 50(3) GPa and temperatures &lt;1200(200) K. The crystal structure of C(OH)4 was determined by single-crystal X-ray diffraction and corroborated by density-functional theory calculations together with Raman spectroscopy. It is composed of isolated [C(OH)4]-molecules linked by strong hydrogen bonds. Under high-pressure conditions, orthocarbonic and carbonic acids are denser than coexisting water ice phases, allowing them to segregate gravitationally and form stable reservoirs of oxidized carbon. These phases incorporate large amounts of carbon into their crystal structures as part of [CO4]4–- or [CO3]2–-building blocks. Because the amount of carbon that can be stored as CO2 in clathrates or filled-ices is significantly smaller, orthocarbonic and carbonic acids may provide a host mechanism for sequestering large carbon inventories in the icy mantles of water-rich exoplanets.</jats:p>

title:
Dynamic
Acidic Adsorbates Govern Fast Oxygen Incorporation
in Ceria through Interfacial Electrostatics
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) is a key heterogeneous process underpinning energy conversion, catalytic, and sensing technologies. However, reported ORR kinetics at oxide surfaces often vary widely because surface chemistry evolves under operating conditions. Ceria-based fluorites have been proposed as protective layers to stabilize perovskite electrodes, but ORR kinetics are typically considered sluggish and reported values have large variability. Herein, we demonstrate that cathodic polarization triggers an unexpected activation in Gd-doped ceria (CGO) dense thin films at 500 °C, enabling oxygen incorporation rates that surpass state-of-the-art materials such as La0.5Sr0.5FeO3−δ and approach the performance of La0.6Sr0.4CoO3−δ. Operando near-ambient-pressure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (NAP-XPS), supported by ex situ surface-sensitive tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS), reveals that CGO surface activation coincides with a reversible, overpotential-dependent modulation of sulfate adsorbates. Integration of these measurements with nondilute space-charge modeling suggests that charged adsorbates dynamically tune the near-surface electrostatic potential and electron concentration, thereby controlling oxygen incorporation kinetics. These results support adsorbate-induced electrostatic effects as a key mechanism in ceria and show that ORR kinetics are dynamically set by surface chemistry under operation, rather than by intrinsic bulk defect chemistry alone.</jats:p>

title: Porphyrin-Driven Redox Tuning in Structurally Defined De Novo Heme Proteins
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Designing redox proteins with predictable and tunable electron transfer properties is a major goal in de novo bioenergetics. Here we show that replacing heme B with a series of structurally conservative non-natural metalloporphyrins enables broad modulation of redox potentials over 400 mV in the de novo designed monoheme m4D2 and diheme 4D2 T19D. The non-natural porphyrins bind with high affinity and do not compromise either the heme binding site or global protein structure, as evidenced by X-ray crystallography and NMR spectroscopy. We also report the native-like NMR structure of m4D2 loaded with the non-natural and symmetric iron 2,4-dimethyldeuteroporphyrin IX, confirming our modular approach to tetrahelical redox protein design. This work establishes a versatile platform for constructing tunable electron carriers for engineered bioenergetic pathways and bioelectronic applications.</jats:p>

title:
Multiphase
Inorganic-Rich Interphases with Integrated
Li-Ion Capture-Transport Ability for High-Rate Lithium Metal Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Lithium metal batteries promise high-energy-density storage but are limited by unstable solid–electrolyte interphases, which couple poor passivation, sluggish Li+ transport, dendritic deposition, and safety risks. Herein, we report a multiphase inorganic-rich solid–electrolyte interphase (m-SEI) containing P- and Al-derived species including Li3P, LiAl5O8, Li3PO4, and Li2Al, which is formed from the in situ reaction between a flame-retardant aluminum diethyl hypophosphite (ADP) interlayer and lithium metal. This multicomponent inorganic SEI enables an integrated capture-transport mechanism by combining high Li+ affinity, facilitated desolvation, and low-barrier Li+ migration pathways in individual inorganic phases and their heterophase interfaces, thereby facilitating rapid Li+ interfacial migration. Its chemical inertness and high Young’s modulus of 17.14 GPa further suppress electrolyte decomposition and Li dendrite growth. As a result, the Li-metal batteries with m-SEI deliver an extended lifespan of 1000 h at a high current density of 4 mA cm–2. Li||NCM811 full cells with a high cathode loading (20 mg cm–2) and ultrathin Li foil (50 μm) retain 80% capacity after 250 cycles, while Li||NCM811 pouch cells retain 90% capacity after 500 cycles. This work establishes the capture-transport mechanism as an effective design principle for regulating Li+ interfacial dynamics and offers a practical interphase-engineering strategy for constructing ion-conductive and chemically protective interphases in durable lithium metal batteries.</jats:p>

title:
Hydration-Dependent
Working-Surface Chemistry in Photocatalytic
Methane Coupling
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Selective photocatalytic methane coupling requires directing methane-derived intermediates toward C–C bond formation while limiting their oxidation to CO2, yet how the reaction environment controls this competition through surface chemistry remains unclear. Water is ubiquitous in photocatalytic methane conversion, but its influence is commonly interpreted through specific chemical functions rather than through its broader effects on working-surface chemistry. Here, Au/ZnO is used as a compositionally defined, coupling-competent model catalyst to reveal how hydration regulates carbon transformation pathways by reshaping the working-surface chemistry. Systematic variation of water availability reveals three hydration-dependent catalytic regimes with markedly different product distributions. Moderate hydration increases the ethane production rate from 1590 to 8407 μmol g–1 h–1 and enables ethylene formation, whereas excessive hydration increases CO2 production and lowers C2 selectivity. In situ spectroscopies show that these catalytic regimes are accompanied by hydration-dependent changes in methane adsorption, methane-derived and coupling-related surface intermediates, and oxygen-deficient surface states within a reaction network involving both carbon- and oxygen-centered radical chemistry. Moderate hydration establishes surface conditions that favor C–C coupling and C2 hydrocarbon accumulation, whereas excessive hydration favors oxidized surface species and carbonate formation. These results identify hydration as a key determinant of the steady-state surface chemistry governing carbon partitioning between C–C coupling and oxidation during photocatalytic methane conversion.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of
the American Chemical Society

title:
Tailoring Solid-State
Reaction Pathways for Bulk Fluorination
of Mn-Rich Rock-Salt Cathodes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Manganese-based cation-disordered rock-salt (DRX) cathodes offer high capacities without relying on cobalt and nickel, but maintaining that capacity over extended cycling often requires bulk fluorination. The challenge is that incorporating fluorine into Mn-rich DRX host structures is hindered by unfavorable thermodynamics and the stability of LiF, often necessitating elevated synthesis temperatures that promote severe lithium and fluorine volatilization. This study overcomes that limitation by manipulating the solid-state reaction pathway using unconventional Li6MnO4 and MnF2 precursors in a challenging Mn-rich model system (Li1.2Mn0.6Ti0.2O2–xFx). This precursor engineering strategy reshapes the thermodynamic landscape. Computational modeling and in situ X-ray diffraction reveal that by using reactive starting materials, we suppress the crystallization of less reactive intermediates, enabling bulk fluorination at a lower temperature. The resulting DRX retains both a high fluorine content and the lithium excess required for three-dimensional percolation, delivering improved electrochemical performance relative to material synthesized from conventional precursors.</jats:p>

Journal of

title: Photoresponsive Mechanically Interlocked [ a n]Daisy Chain Network
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Muscle integrates molecular-machine motion with hierarchical structural organization, enabling it to sustain large deformations under physiological loads. Mechanically interlocked molecules offer a versatile platform to mimic such molecular-level motion, but efficiently translating it into macroscopic material performance, akin to muscle, remains challenging. Herein, we report a mechanically interlocked network (MIN) with [an]daisy chain backbone which can efficiently scale up the photoresponsive behavior of mechanical bonds, exhibiting intelligently tunable mechanical properties. In specific, photoresponsive unit of arylazopyrazole (AAP) is embedded onto the axis of each mechanical bond in the [an]daisy chain backbone. Ultraviolet light triggers the trans-to-cis (E/Z) isomerization of the AAP moieties, and when amplified through the [an]daisy chain backbone, it brings about significant changes in the material’s properties. On one hand, the E/Z isomerization significantly shortens the dimension of the [an]daisy chain framework, resulting in a notable increase in the material modulus (from 1.6 to 4.0 MPa). On the other hand, the cis configuration of AAP formed after the isomerization restricts the mobility of the mechanical bonds, resulting in a shorter elongation at break (from 343% to 272%). Our work presents an efficient method for amplifying mechanical bond responsiveness, providing a fresh perspective for the development of intelligent materials.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of
the American Chemical Society

title:
Efficient Long-Wavelength
Through-Space Charge-Transfer
Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence in Conformationally Adaptive
Emitters without Conformational Locking
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Through-space charge-transfer thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TSCT-TADF) emitters often employ conformationally constrained donor–acceptor architectures to control through-space electronic coupling, particularly for long-wavelength emission. Here, we report conformationally adaptive orange-to-red TSCT-TADF emitters based on an S-shaped donor−π–acceptor−π–donor framework composed of phenoxazine donors, xanthene linkers, and a dibenzo[a,j]phenazine acceptor. Structural and NMR analyses reveal substantial conformational mobility, while systematic conformational searches and excited-state calculations identify thermally accessible conformers with distinct donor–acceptor geometries and excited-state characteristics. Comparative studies with reference compounds and fragment-resolved transition-density analysis show that the xanthene linker primarily acts as a conformational regulator and that the low-energy CT states have predominant TSCT character with only minor linker involvement. Temperature-dependent early-time photoluminescence measurements reveal continuous spectral relaxation in fluid toluene that slows upon cooling and is absent in rigid Zeonex and mCBP hosts, providing strong evidence for structural relaxation following photoexcitation within a pre-existing conformational ensemble. The emitters exhibit orange-to-red TADF with reverse intersystem crossing rates on the order of 105–106 s–1. Organic light-emitting diodes employing these emitters show electroluminescence at 598–624 nm, external quantum efficiencies up to 14.9%, and limited efficiency roll-off over a broad luminance range. These results demonstrate that efficient long-wavelength TSCT-TADF can be realized without permanent conformational locking and establish a framework for understanding the interplay between ground-state conformational heterogeneity and excited-state structural relaxation.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of
the American Chemical Society

title:
Design and Evolution
of an Orthogonal HaloTag for
Multiplexed Labeling in Cells
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The self-labeling protein HaloTag is used to install a wide variety of functional small molecules in cells and living organisms with exquisite specificity with respect to cell type and subcellular localization. HaloTag is a core part of many biotechnology-based tools for sensing, tracking, and manipulating biological systems with a high degree of spatial and temporal control. Due to the limitations of fluorescent proteins and other self-labeling proteins, most of these tools have historically been restricted to a single channel. In this work, we used structure-guided rational design and directed evolution to produce an orthogonal HaloTag protein called OrthoTag which reacts selectively with a modified chloroalkane substrate. OrthoTag retains many of HaloTag’s superior properties, and reaction rate measurements with purified proteins show OrthoTag and its substrate have 109-fold mutual orthogonality to HaloTag with respect to substrate concentration. We demonstrate the application of OrthoTag for multiplexed labeling experiments in mammalian cells with minimal optimization. Going forward, OrthoTag should be straightforward to incorporate into HaloTag-based systems to allow simultaneous measurement or manipulation of two biological targets or processes. The availability of multiple high-performance self-labeling proteins will enable the continued development of new multiplexed biotechnology methods.</jats:p>

title:
Zeolite-Confined
Triatomic Cu Oxides at Silanol Nests
as Hydrogen Transport Channels for H2 Production from Methanol
Steam Reforming
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cu-based catalysts offer high methanol steam reforming (MSR) activity but are limited by unstable Cu+–Cu0 interconversions due to the redox and sintering labilities of Cu. Herein, we developed a universal amino-functionalized “gripper” strategy for firmly and precisely anchoring atomically dispersed metals (e.g., Cu, Co, Ni) within Beta-zeolite. Triatomic Cu oxide (Cu3Ox) sites lower the methanol dehydrogenation activation barrier, and the synergistic interplay with adjacent OH groups from silanol nests accelerates H2 evolution and the MSR reaction. Spatially decoupling Cu-mediated methanol activation from silanol-driven H2 evolution at silanol nests as proton transport channels within the confining zeolite framework also effectively protected Cu from sintering, achieving a high specific activity of 951 molH2·molCu–1·h–1 and over 600 h of stability under continuous regeneration. This work provides a universal strategy for synthesizing atomically dispersed metal catalysts and a new design principle for maintaining the Cu structure during MSR.</jats:p>

Journal of
