title: Diffusion Models for Small-Molecule Design
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Diffusion models (DMs) have emerged as a class of generative models for controllable small-molecule design in drug discovery capable of progressively transforming noisy or partially specified molecular states into candidate structures under structural, geometric, and property constraints. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of the methodological foundations and representative applications of diffusion-based molecular generation, emphasizing the alignment among molecular representations, generative dynamics, controllable design, and evaluation and validation. Particular attention is given to recent advances in property- and structure-guided generation, target-aware and fragment-based design, multiobjective optimization, and synthesis-aware generation. We also discuss the roles of data sets, computational evaluation, and prospective experiments in assessing the chemical and biological relevance of generated molecules. By organizing these developments within a unified conceptual framework, we provide computational chemists and drug discovery researchers with a structured roadmap that balances the mathematical rigor with chemical intuition. Throughout, we highlight current methodological limitations and unresolved challenges and conclude with future directions toward chemically credible and experimentally grounded molecular design. To facilitate navigation of this rapidly evolving field, we introduce an interactive companion platform (https://diffsmd.scbdd.com) that provides a curated, continuously updated repository of model architectures and visualizations.</jats:p>
journal: Chemical Reviews

title: Dual-Solvent Screening for Nondestructive In-Situ Optical Patterning of CsPbX3 QDs/PMMA
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Perovskite quantum dot (PQD)-polymer composites are widely pursued for display devices due to their excellent film-forming capacity, low cost, and favorable process compatibility. However, interfacial incompatibility between PQDs and polymers from mismatched surface chemistry triggers PQD aggregation and severe photoluminescence quenching, hindering microdisplay applications. Herein, a dual-solvent screening strategy is demonstrated for I-184-initiated crosslinked PQD-PMMA photoresists to balance solubility and lead-ion coordination strength. Undesired lead-solvent intermediate formation and residual solvent accumulation are suppressed to homogenize PQD dispersion and preserve optical performance. The 20 μm green patterned film retains 93% of the initial photoluminescence quantum yield with no photoluminescence peak shift and a narrow full width at half-maximum of 16.6 nm. The PQD pattern presents sharp pixel edges, 7.10% critical dimension deviation, 97.1% replication rate, and intersection over union of 0.92. This solvent engineering enables the revitalization of conventional polymers and addresses bottlenecks in photolithographic patterning of PQD-polymer composites.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Rational Selection of Hole Contacts with an Organic Light-Emitting Diode Industry p-Dopant for Fully Vacuum-Processed Perovskite/Silicon Tandems
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Translating perovskite/silicon tandems to fully vacuum-based manufacturing requires vacuum-compatible p-doped hole contacts, yet clear selection criteria for doped hole-transport materials (HTMs) remain underdeveloped compared with C60-based electron contacts. Here, we report a fully vacuum-processed perovskite/silicon tandem reaching 29.1% power conversion efficiency, among the highest reported for tandems with fully vacuum-deposited perovskite top cells, enabled by transferring the organic light-emitting diode (OLED)-industry p-dopant NDP-9 and an evaporable arylamine HTM into the perovskite stack. Comparing TaTm, Spiro-TTB, and TAPC shows that contact selection does not follow apparent host–dopant interaction strength derived from theoretical calculations or conventional optical, vibrational, and photoemission spectroscopies. Instead, device-level charge extraction and recombination metrics identify NDP-9-doped TaTm as the most effective contact, also yielding 20.0% in a single-junction 1.70 eV wide-bandgap cell. These results point to transport-based screening as a practical route to selecting vacuum-compatible doped hole contacts.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Operando Time-of-Flight Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry Reveals Iodine-Mediated Redox Chemistry in Solid-State Li–S Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Understanding dynamic reaction pathways in all-solid-state batteries remains challenging because electrochemical processes occur at buried solid–solid interfaces and transient intermediates are difficult to detect with conventional analytical techniques. While operando techniques typically probe structural or macroscopic changes, direct detection of reactive species during operation remains experimentally demanding. Here, we introduce a dynamic operando time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry platform that enables continuous chemical analysis of processes in a solid-state battery under electrochemical bias. Using this approach, we directly observe a pronounced increase of the I2– signal during charging of a Li–S composite cathode containing LiI, indicating the formation of elemental iodine. Concurrent changes in the sulfur-containing ion signals suggest the involvement of iodine species in the ongoing redox processes. These results reveal transient, low-concentration species at buried interfaces undetectable by other operando techniques, offering a pathway for identifying reactive intermediates in conversion-type solid-state batteries and related electrochemical systems.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: A Self-Driving Laboratory for Accelerated Electrolyte Discovery
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The development of electrochemical materials is constrained by extensive formulation spaces and the low throughput of manual screening. Here, we report a self-driving electrochemical laboratory integrating liquid-handling robotics, online electroanalysis, and Bayesian optimization to accelerate electrolyte discovery. Operating in a 96-well microtiter format, the platform automatically formulates candidate electrolytes, performs temperature-controlled electrochemical measurements, and iteratively updates surrogate models to explore high-dimensional chemical spaces. This framework was applied to the development of high-entropy aqueous electrolytes for low-temperature zinc metal batteries. The system screened hundreds of formulations, and multiobjective optimization yielded an electrolyte with a conductivity of 134.1 mS cm–1 and an electrochemical stability window of 2.50 V, with ∼2019 h of cycling stability in symmetric cells at –20 °C. This approach significantly reduces experimental labor while accelerating the development of electrochemical materials.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Mesoscale Chiroptical Order in Achiral Metal-Halide Nanoplatelet Assemblies
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This viewpoint presents the circular dichroism emerging directly from the self-assembly of achiral metal-halide perovskite nanoplatelets such as Cs3Cd2Cl7, Rb3Cd2Cl7, and CsPbBr3. Specifically, even when they form only short-range, polydisperse assemblies rather than the long-range helical superlattices reported in prior works, these short assemblies also exhibit chiral optical properties. The effect persists across emissive and nonemissive systems; with diverse stacking morphologies, and both in solution and film forms. Thus, this viewpoint establishes mesoscale chirality as a general principle of nanoplatelet self-assemblies.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title:
Ultrafast Imaging
of Dynamic Disorder in Superionic
Chalcocite
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The optimal functionalities of matter often appear at emergent structural orders involving entangled changes in the lattice structures and the underlying atomic degree of freedom. Here, we report laser-induced, thermally driven dynamic structural orders evolving in the low- to high-chalcocite transition of copper(I) sulfide using time-resolved electron diffractometry in ultrafast electron microscopy. We filmed the complete phase trajectory of the transient atomic motions and the hierarchical decoupling of structural orders that unfold over time. Moreover, a transient, disordered state is unveiled. The disordered state emerges during the superionic diffusion of copper ions along a few-nanometer-thick lattice channels. Temporal gating of the various combinations of structure could expand the range of accessible functional states in matter.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Attempts
to Understand and Manipulate the Orientation
and Retention of Peptides Inside Nanopores Expand the Toolbox for
Nanopore-Based Proteomics
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nanopore techniques have emerged as promising tools for deciphering complex proteomics from the single-molecule level by profiling individual peptides. The entry orientation of a peptide and its subsequent retention inside the nanopore are crucial for the analytical results but remain challenging to be properly defined, which limits the sensing capability of nanopore-based proteomics technology. Here, we propose that electrically driving peptide entry into α-hemolysin nanopores against opposing electroosmotic flows is a promising platform to guide the polypeptide with a preferential orientation. α-Hemolysin mutants with opposite ion selectivity have been engineered and employed to measure peptides at pH 3.8 and at alkaline pH exceeding 10.0. The impact of peptide charge distribution on the orientation has been investigated by simulating the peptide dipole moment and electrophysiology measurements. In addition, the retention position of the peptide has been altered by introducing tryptophan residues at position 125 within the β-barrel region of α-hemolysin, which increases the sensitivity for specific peptide region and enables the detection of initially inaccessible monomethylation modifications. Thus, we present a rational framework to investigate and manipulate the orientation and dwelling position of peptides inside the α-hemolysin nanopore, which can enhance our capability to profile polypeptides by using nanopore techniques.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Self-Assembly of
Two-Dimensional Open Structures with
Adjustable Square Voids
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Self-assembly of anisotropic particles offers a powerful route to design materials with tailored microstructures. Here we investigate two-dimensional systems of patchy hard rectangles using Monte Carlo simulations and free volume theory, mapping their phase diagram across packing fractions and interaction strengths. Low attraction recovers excluded-volume phase behavior (isotropic–tetratic–smectic), while intermediate attraction strengths feature a broad isotropic–smectic coexistence region. For high interaction strengths our theory predicts, and simulations confirm, a highly ordered “weaver” phase characterized by a four-rectangle unit cell that forms a regular grid of square voids. Although the pure weaver phase forms only in a narrow window of packing fractions, it coexists with either the isotropic gas or smectic solid over a wide range of packing fractions. Patchy rectangles demonstrate how shape together with tunable interactions can be utilized to self-assemble porous materials with precisely adjustable void sizes and geometries and could be realized using DNA origami structures.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Truly Asynchronous
and One-Hot Constraint Probabilistic
Potts Computing with Floating-Body Metal–Oxide–Semiconductor
Field-Effect Transistors
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This work presents a truly asynchronous physical Potts node (TAPPN) using floating-body metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistors (FB-MOSFETs) to overcome the scalability and encoding overhead limitations of binary Ising-based probabilistic computing. The TAPPN enables native multistate representation without external random-number generators (RNGs) or complex digital arbitration by the intrinsic stochastic single-transistor latch (STL) effect and a drain-sharing configuration. The stochastic source and the one-hot constraint are realized by three transistors, and the node requires 25 transistors and 220 nW including the readout, compared with 2160 transistors and 52 μW for a self-contained digital node evaluated at the same boundary. Its truly asynchronous operation allows efficient exploration of the problem space in large-scale graph-coloring benchmarks. In simulations of the update rule, the Potts-based system achieves a higher success probability than simulated annealing (SA) and parallel tempering (PT) on graph-coloring benchmarks. For an integrated array assumed to operate at 5 MHz, the architecture is projected to reach a time-to-solution (TTS) of 3.4 μs and an energy-to-solution (ETS) of 504 nJ. This platform establishes a complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS)-compatible pathway toward large-scale, multistate combinatorial optimization.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Breaking the Capacity–Stability
Trade-Off in
High-Voltage LiCoO2 via Opposite Co/O Redox Activity
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>LiCoO2 (LCO) suffers from daunting capacity–stability trade-off due to deeper Co oxidation and ensuing O oxidation (O2– → Co4+ electron transfer) at high-voltage (≥4.5 V). Aggressive Co4+ and O2/On– (0 &lt; n &lt; 2) species result in pronounced mechanical/chemical failure and fast capacity decay. Most of the state-of-the-art solutions partially resolve these problems yet sacrificing capacity. Herein, facilitated Co3+/4+ redox and effectively restrained O redox are simultaneously achieved by amplifying Co t2g electron density of states (DOS) near the Fermi level while reducing O 2p electron DOS. Consequently, the engineered cathode harvests a remarkable initial capacity of 212.1 mAh g–1 at 4.6 V (vs 212.9 mAh g–1 of bare LCO). Moreover, advanced multiscale X-ray/electron spectroscopy and imaging techniques reveal that mitigated O redox prevents irreversible phase transitions, lattice O loss, and undesirable surface parasitic reactions. As a result, the cathode has reinforced electrochemical (capacity retention of 88.4% within 330 cycles at 5C) and thermal stability thanks to fatigue-free (de)lithiation channels, less new-generated Co3O4 layer, and inorganic-rich cathode/electrolyte interphase (CEI) film. This work provides a valuable inspiration for the electronic structure engineer of robust LCO cathode toward high operation voltages.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
An Optoelectronic
SnP2S6 Memristive
Neuron for Biologically Inspired Multimodal Neuromorphic Information
Processing
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Neuromorphic systems capable of integrating multiple sensory modalities offer a promising route toward energy-efficient information processing that more closely emulates biological neural networks. Here, we demonstrate a multifunctional ITO/SnP2S6/Ti memristive neuron that combines reproducible volatile resistive switching and integrate-and-fire dynamics under electrical-pulse stimulation with wavelength-selective photoresponses and short-term optoelectronic synaptic plasticity. Leveraging these experimentally measured device characteristics, we construct a multimodal neuromorphic recognition framework that integrates volatile memristive neurons with programmable memristive synapses. Inspired by the parallel processing of visual features in the primate visual system, structural and color information are independently encoded and processed through separate electrical and optical pathways before being integrated for classification. Importantly, inference is implemented using experimentally measured neuronal firing statistics and programmed synaptic conductance states, rather than idealized device models, thereby establishing a direct link between device characteristics and system-level functionality. As a proof-of-concept, the framework is evaluated on a fruit-recognition task using a subset of the Fruits-360 image data set, achieving a classification accuracy of 94.9% through multimodal fusion and substantially outperforming recognition based on either modality alone. These results establish SnP2S6 memristive devices as a versatile platform for integrating electrical and optical neuronal functionalities and highlight their potential for hardware-realistic multimodal in-sensor neuromorphic computing.</jats:p>

title:
Bright
Alkyl Quantum Defects Govern Early Carbon Nanotube
Pharmacokinetics in Mice
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Fluorescent quantum defects in single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) are a major advance in nanocarbon research, owing to their bright, single-photon emission at telecom wavelengths and versatile conjugation chemistries for biomedical sensing and disease targeting. Here, we introduce an efficient, oxygen-free sonochemical route that generates long-chain alkyl defects, simultaneously shortening nanotubes and producing a bright, homogeneously emissive (6,5) SWCNT ensemble. Among 15 screened reactants, the branched-chain NiaproofⓇ 4, which molecular dynamics simulations show packs more densely and uniformly than linear surfactants, yields a 3.4-fold brightness enhancement and a sharp emission peak near 1108 nm. Single-particle spectroscopy reveals J-aggregate emission redshifts at high defect densities, and fibrinogen titration shows defect chemistry governs protein-driven coating displacement. Using a home-built short-wave infrared imaging system (25 mW cm–2, 989 nm excitation, 1150 nm long-pass collection), we show that these sparse defects (∼9–16 μm–1) drive different pharmacokinetics between NiaproofⓇ 4– and lipid-PEG–functionalized (6,5) at early time points, converging as protein-corona formation masks the underlying chemistry. Histology localizes the nanotubes within macrophages of mononuclear phagocyte system–associated organs. Intravenous administration (∼41 μg kg–1) causes no acute toxicity and a short ∼2-day retention. The NiaproofⓇ 4 group exhibits a reduced circulating myeloid-cell fraction following corona formation, which may reflect organ recruitment and sequestration, while the accompanying increase in CD3+ T cells may partly reflect a proportional shift in leukocyte composition.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Ultrafast High-Photogain
UV–Vis-NIR Broadband
Photodetection in Parallelly Overlapped Stacking Type-I GaSe/MoTe2 Heterostructure
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Broadband photodetectors are important for next-generation optoelectronic applications, ranging from fundamental science, environmental monitoring, industrial detection to artificial-intelligence-enabled Internet of Things systems, where both high responsivity and fast response are critically demanded. Typically, a trade-off exists between the two in the photogating effect, making it challenging to achieve both simultaneously. This study reports a parallelly overlapped stacking GaSe/MoTe2 heterostructure with type-I band alignment (PSH-GM), which simultaneously realizes an ultrafast photoresponse of 523 ns and a high responsivity of 8.95 × 103 A·W–1, together with a noise equivalent power of ∼0.38 × 10–14 W·Hz–1/2 and a specific detectivity of 8.01 × 1011 Jones. Furthermore, PSH-GM exhibits a responsivity of up to 103 A·W–1 over a broad spectral range of 355–1100 nm, covering the ultraviolet (UV), visible (Vis), and near-infrared (NIR) regions. The underlying photodetection mechanism of the parallelly overlapped stacking type-I heterostructure is clarified using photocurrent mapping, and the origin of the dark current shift at different operation frequencies is elucidated, both of which offer insights into the design principles of two-dimensional heterostructures optimized to simultaneously achieve high responsivity and high response bandwidth. Imaging demonstrations are conducted at 355, 520, and 850 nm, and free-space optical communication is demonstrated at 115.2 kbit·s–1, which highlights the potential of PSH-GM for broadband UV–Vis–NIR photodetection, ultrafast data communication, high-speed imaging, and integration into advanced optoelectronic systems.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Overcoming
Oral Environmental Barriers: Nanoengineering
Strategies for Antimicrobial Peptides in Biofilm-Associated Oral Diseases
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Biofilm-associated oral diseases impose a substantial global health burden and are closely linked to systemic inflammation. Although antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics, their therapeutic efficacy in the oral cavity is limited by barriers in the oral environment. Free AMPs are rapidly removed by salivary flow, destabilized by local proteases, and impeded by substantial diffusion barriers within mature biofilms. Nanoengineering provides a systematic approach to address these limitations. In this review, we present a barrier-oriented framework for AMP delivery and examine how nanomaterial design addresses the specific constraints of the oral environment. Interfacial engineering prolongs local retention, spatial protection preserves AMP stability, and microenvironment-responsive systems provide on-demand activation for effective biofilm disruption. Alongside these approaches, multifunctional nanosystems combining antimicrobial, immunomodulatory, and regenerative activities are discussed. Finally, key translational challenges, including biosafety, microbiome homeostasis, manufacturing, and regulatory barriers, are critically examined. This review traces the development of AMP nanoengineering from passive delivery vehicles toward precision therapeutic platforms that respond dynamically to the oral microenvironment.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Biomimetic Nanozyme-Decoys
Reprogram Immune Niches
to Intercept Colitis-Carcinoma Transition
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CAC) arises from chronic inflammatory niches characterized by persistent oxidative stress and dysregulated immune cell recruitment. Current anti-inflammatory therapies provide only transient symptom relief and fail to prevent malignant progression due to their inability to simultaneously mitigate oxidative injury and immune chemotaxis. Our analysis of clinical samples revealed markedly elevated C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (CXCL2) in intestinal tissues from patients with inflammatory bowel disease and CAC, implicating the CXCL2-CXCR2 (C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 2) axis in driving excessive neutrophil and macrophage infiltration and fostering tumorigenesis. Herein, we report a biomimetic nanozyme (PB@ECM) that reprograms inflammatory immune niches to intercept CAC progression. PB@ECM integrates a Prussian blue nanozyme core with genetically engineered macrophage membranes, enabling concurrent scavenging of reactive oxygen species through superoxide dismutase- and catalase-like activities and sequestration of CXCL2 via membrane-displayed CXCR2 receptors. In murine models of colitis and CAC, PB@ECM significantly alleviated intestinal inflammation, suppressed neutrophil and macrophage infiltration, and effectively inhibited colitis-carcinoma transition. Notably, treatment with PB@ECM significantly prolonged survival compared with other groups. By disrupting the pathological crosstalk between oxidative stress and immune chemotaxis, this work establishes a biomimetic nanozyme strategy for preventing inflammation-driven carcinogenesis.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Data-Driven
Atomic Interplay Modulation Enables Dual-Functional
High-Entropy Alloy Mediator for Li–S Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have emerged as appealing candidates to achieve performance regulation in Li–S batteries. Nevertheless, the design principles and working mechanisms of HEAs for dual electrodes remain elusive because of their structural disorder and chemical complexity. Herein, we propose a data-driven maneuver to enable rapid and precise screening of a customized HEA nanocatalyst (FeCoNiCuVMn, 6E-HEAs) via a performance-oriented theoretical criterion in the realm of Li–S electrochemistry. The delicate modulation of atomic interplay in 6E-HEAs simultaneously accelerates sulfur redox kinetics and stabilizes lithium metal deposition. Consequently, Li–S batteries sustain favorable cycling performance at 1.0 C over 1000 cycles while affording a capacity decay rate of merely 0.067% per cycle. The pouch cell harvests a specific capacity of 884.8 mAh g–1 at 0.5 C with steady cyclic operation. Our study elucidates crucial roles of effective compositional gain in boosting bidirectional Li–S electrocatalysis, offering atomic-level insights into HEA design for electrocatalytic reactions.</jats:p>

title:
Addressable
Control of Hybrid Spin Qubit in Single-Atom
Copper-Modified Fullerene
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Developing high-dimensional solid-state quantum technologies requires overcoming the trade-off between spin dimensionality and quantum coherence. Hybrid spin architectures offer a promising solution to expand the quantum state space bottom-up by combining rapid electronic manipulation with robust nuclear phase memory. However, solid-state hybrid spin materials capable of simultaneously supporting both electron and nuclear spin manipulations remain exceedingly rare. Here, we report a Cu2+ (S = 1/2, I = 3/2) hybrid spin system dispersed in a magnetically silent C60 matrix, in which we not only demonstrate comprehensive coherent control over both electron and nuclear spin degrees of freedom but also strike a balance between spin dimensionality and coherence time. The pristine carbon environment suppresses surrounding magnetic noise, acting in tandem with dynamical decoupling to prolong the electron spin coherence time to 16.16 μs. Simultaneously, the nuclear quadrupole interaction of Cu2+ breaks the degeneracy of the nuclear spin manifold, enabling precise addressability of an eight-dimensional Hilbert space. Furthermore, strong electron–nuclear hyperfine coupling acts as a powerful lever, accelerating the nuclear spin Rabi frequency by a factor of 17. By achieving the coexistence of a large manifold of addressable levels and long-lived quantum coherence, Cu/C60 provides a high-dimensional hybrid spin node and a compelling bottom-up approach to expanding the quantum state space.</jats:p>

title: Understanding Charge Acceptance Limitations During Extreme Fast‐Charging of Li‐ion Batteries
content:
Overpotential component analysis successfully decouples ohmic, kinetic, and transport voltage losses during extreme fast charging of lithium‐ion batteries. These measurements reveal that severe concentration gradients primarily dictate charge acceptance limits. Introducing an acetonitrile co‐solvent accelerates solvation‐shell exchange and bulk ion mobility, effectively minimizing transport overpotentials to improve fast‐charging performance across porous electrode architectures.








ABSTRACT
Extreme fast charging in lithium‐ion batteries is limited by their poor charge acceptance at high C‐rates. We use overpotential component analysis to decouple ohmic, kinetic and transport voltage losses during fast charging. The concentration gradients are identified as the primary culprit in poor charge acceptance, so we study carbonate electrolytes that utilize acetonitrile, a low viscosity, high dielectric liquid, as a co‐solvent to improve ion transport. Our results indicate acetonitrile co‐solvent successfully reduces fast charging concentration gradients and therefore improves charge acceptance at high C‐rates, particularly when used in combination with interface‐stabilizing additives. Molecular dynamics simulations show that ACN enhances Li+ transport through a combination of reduced bulk viscosity and increased solvation‐shell lability, with shorter solvent residence times and faster coordination exchange producing transport gains beyond those expected from viscosity reduction alone. Finally, we use three‐electrode cells to deconvolute overpotential at each electrode, and the specific LiNi0.8Mn0.1Co0.1O2 (NMC811) electrode architecture and loading used in our study is found to have much higher overpotentials than our graphite electrode. In particular, the significant differences in NMC811 concentration gradients between electrolytes with or without acetonitrile indicate that the design of electrode architecture is crucial for extreme fast charging applications.

title: Data‐Driven Host Microstructure Design Toward Efficient and Durable Room‐Temperature Sodium–Sulfur Batteries
content:
During the early cycles of room‐temperature Na–S batteries, stepwise sulfur conversion and distinct electrolyte decomposition pathways construct the cathode–electrolyte interphase (CEI). We use machine learning to identify key carbon‐host parameters governing CEI formation and electrochemical performance. A balanced pore network synchronizes sulfur‐species evolution, electron transfer, and electrolyte reactions, promoting uniform CEI formation and high durability of room‐temperature Na–S batteries.








ABSTRACT
Porous carbon materials are critical hosts for chalcogen‐ and halogen‐based conversion‐type cathodes, as they govern the activity and durability of electrochemical reactions. Understanding how their microstructures regulate electrolyte‐electrode interactions remains challenging given multiple coupling factors and dynamic changes during electrochemical cycling. Herein, machine learning was first used to screen three pore structure parameter windows relevant to electrochemical features from a large experimental dataset (23 carbon hosts and 1055 specific‐capacity data points). Based on these screened windows, three representative carbon hosts, namely micropore‐rich carbon, balanced carbon, and meso/macropore‐rich carbon, were synthesized as model systems. We reveal that pore structure governs sulfur species evolution, thereby dictating the competition between polysulfide‐mediated reactions and solvent self‐decomposition. The resulting spatial‐compositional differences of the cathode–electrolyte interphase (CEI) were found to profoundly impact energy efficiency, reversibility, and rate performance. The balanced carbon cathode with optimized inorganic‐organic distribution delivers an initial capacity of 1249.4 mAh g−1 and retains a capacity of 784.8 mAh g−1 after 500 cycles. This work not only proposes a data‐driven strategy for identifying CEI‐relevant pore structure windows, but also provides mechanistic insight into how physical metrics of porous carbon modulate multi‐step complex reactions and ultimately influence electrochemical performance.

title: Renewable Intermittency Redistributes Catalyst Recovery and Membrane Degradation in Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis
content:
Solar‐mimicking intermittency is shown to redistribute degradation and recovery in AEM water electrolysis. Operando XAS reveals reversible oxidation‐state and coordination changes in reconstructed NiFe (oxy)hydroxide layers during zero‐load intervals, while complementary membrane analyses identify concurrent chemical and morphological deterioration. Intermittency thus emerges as a driver of competing catalyst recovery and membrane degradation.








ABSTRACT
Renewable intermittency is widely regarded as a durability stressor in water electrolysis, yet its impact on competing degradation and recovery processes within the cell remains unclear. Here, we show that realistic intermittent operation redistributes catalyst recovery and membrane degradation in anion exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE). A Ni–Fe‐based AEMWE single‐cell was operated under high‐resolution, solar‐mimicking load profiles that reproduce day–night intermittency without external buffering. Electrochemical diagnostics reveal reversible changes in activation, Ohmic, and mass‐transport losses, indicating partial performance recovery during zero‐current intervals. In situ X‐ray absorption spectroscopy attributes this behavior to reversible oxidation‐state and coordination changes of Ni and Fe, associated with the reversible formation and relaxation of amorphous (oxy)hydroxide surface layers. In contrast, hydrogen crossover measurements reveal increased crossover under low‐current operation, while post‐mortem membrane analyses provide independent evidence of membrane deterioration, identifying a critical system‐level limitation. These results show that intermittency does not uniformly mitigate degradation but redistributes it across cell components, enabling catalyst self‐restoration while exacerbating membrane vulnerability. This work establishes intermittency as a double‐edged operational parameter and provides a framework for designing materials and operating strategies for durable, battery‐free AEM water electrolysis.

title: Skunk Cabbage‐Inspired AIEgen Photoactuators With Multiwavelength Response, Ultrafast Actuation, and Multicolor Fluorescence
content:
Bioinspired NIR‐responsive actuators are developed using AIEgens integrated into Janus polyimides at ultra‐low doping (0.25 wt%). These actuators overcome the 980 nm absorption barrier, achieving 900°/s bending speed while preserving >90 MPa strength. Multiwavelength response and multicolor fluorescence enable programmable motions for advanced soft robotics.








ABSTRACT
Near‐infrared (NIR)‐responsive polymer actuators doped with inorganic photothermal agents face trade‐offs between photothermal performance and mechanical properties due to limited compatibility. Besides, most systems remain confined to 808 nm operation, as extending to 980 nm is hindered by poor absorption. Inspired by skunk cabbage thermogenesis, we develop ultra‐fast, multicolor fluorescent NIR‐responsive actuators by integrating aggregation‐induced emission luminogens (AIEgens) with excellent compatibility and photothermal properties into Janus‐structured polyimides (PIs) at ultra‐low doping (0.25 wt%). The multi‐donor‐π structure of AIEgen achieves redshifted NIR absorption extending to 980 nm and enhanced photothermal abilities through boosted intramolecular donor–acceptor interactions and molecular motion‐facilitated nonradiative decay (MMFND). Mirroring the mitochondrial working mode, AIEgens are uniformly embedded within PIs without compromising structural integrity, preserving mechanical properties above 100 MPa. Under NIR illumination, PI actuators achieve deformation with a bending speed of 900°/s, which facilitates crawling, gripping, and rapid continuous bidirectional flipping. The combination of multiwavelength photoresponse and multicolor fluorescence endows materials with dynamic information encoding. Programmable motions are implemented under different wavelengths through sequential, penetrative, and heat‐transfer actuation. This work provides guidelines for smart materials requiring precise 980 nm actuation with maintained mechanical robustness.

title: Defined Matrices Reveal Epithelial‐ and Mesenchymal‐Specific Responses to Stiffness and Adhesion in Human iPSC‐Derived Intestinal Organoids
content:
Defined PEG hydrogels enable human iPSC‐derived intestinal organoid culture without Matrigel. PEG‐ and Matrigel‐cultured organoids both support duodenal‐like epithelial identity, but direct comparison reveals subtle epithelial differentiation‐marker shifts and stronger mesenchymal ECM‐remodeling/integrin programs in PEG. Stiffness modulation shows modest epithelial sensitivity, including MUC2‐associated changes, with limited mesenchymal response.








ABSTRACT
Human intestinal organoids (hIOs) are powerful models for studying development and disease, yet dissecting how physical and matrix cues shape epithelial and mesenchymal responses remains challenging due to reliance on ill‐defined matrices. Here, a fully defined hIO workflow was developed in which Matrigel was replaced by recombinant human substrates during pluripotent stem cell differentiation and by polyethylene glycol (PEG) hydrogels during 3D culture, while maintaining organoid viability and epithelial cytodifferentiation. Transcriptomic analyses show that both PEG‐ and Matrigel‐cultured hIO epithelial cells are most similar to human duodenal reference populations, and have greater transcriptional similarity to fetal than adult duodenal references. Despite this overall similarity, PEG culture is associated with subtle shifts in epithelial differentiation‐associated gene expression, together with altered mesenchymal ECM‐remodelling and integrin‐associated programs. Increasing matrix stiffness produces modest effects in epithelial cells, including increased MUC2‐positive cells, whereas mesenchymal transcriptional responses to stiffness are limited. Together, these findings establish a fully defined hIO platform that retains responsiveness to inflammatory stimulation while enabling controlled investigation of how matrix composition and stiffness shape epithelial and mesenchymal cell states in models of intestinal development and fibrosis.

title: A Dual‐Locked and H2S‐NO Tandem‐Activatable NIR‐II Nanoagent for Colon Cancer Theranostics
content:
We report a dual‐locked and H2S‐NO tandem‐activatable NIR‐II nanoagent CTBNN‐NPs for colon cancer theranostics. CTBNN‐NPs can be tandemly activated by the overexpressed H2S and the in situ released NO, thus turning on NIR‐II emission. The activated CTBNN‐NPs also demonstrate robust type‐I PDT and PTT performance, achieving NIR‐II fluorescence imaging‐guided elimination of colon cancer together with NO gas therapy.








ABSTRACT
Dual‐locked activatable theranostics have been emerging as a promising cancer therapy platform. However, most of the reported dual‐locked systems only restricted to enzyme‐responsive probes, new molecular tools with other biomarker‐responsiveness still remain challenging. Moreover, optical manipulation in the second near‐infrared (NIR‐II) window can potentially boost the theranostic efficacy, but having rarely been explored. In this study, we report a dual‐locked and gas tandem‐activatable NIR‐II nanoagent for colon cancer theranostics. Water‐dispersible nanoparticles containing a nitrated organic small molecule (CTBN) and an acid‐responsive NO donor (NONOate; CTBNN‐NPs) are fabricated, displaying negligible emission in visible‐NIR region. Upon uptake by colon cancer cells, CTBNN‐NPs can be tandemly activated by the overexpressed H2S and the in situ released NO, thus turning on NIR‐II emission extending to 1200 nm. Moreover, the activated CTBNN‐NPs also demonstrate augmented NIR absorption as well as robust photothermal and type‐I photodynamic performance, achieving NIR‐II fluorescence imaging‐guided efficient photo‐elimination of colon cancer together with NO gas therapy, while exhibiting limited efficacy in the tested cervical and breast cancer models. This work provides a new molecular design approach to dual‐locked and H2S‐NO tandem‐activatable nanoagents with gas‐responsive and NIR‐II active capabilities, highlighting the exciting potential for cancer theranostics.

title: Sensitive, Broadband, and Stable Short‐Wave Infrared Photodetection and Imaging in Mixed‐Dimensional Organic/Inorganic Heterostructures
content:
Schottky barrier engineering in mixed‐dimensional organic/inorganic type‐II PTF/WSe2 heterostructures enables highly sensitive and stable short‐wave infrared photodetection across the 1060–1470 nm broadband range. Combining organic light absorption with efficient charge transport and optimized contact barriers yields a responsivity of 2894 A/W and a shot‐noise‐limited specific detectivity of 1.0 × 1012 Jones at 1310 nm.








ABSTRACT
Conventional short‐wave infrared (SWIR) photodetectors confront cost disadvantages and fabrication complexity, whereas two‐dimensional (2D) van der Waals devices exhibit inherent performance limitations. Mixed‐dimensional organic/inorganic heterostructures offer a promising strategy for SWIR photodetection, synergizing strong optical absorption and tunability of organic semiconductors with high charge mobility and stability of inorganics. However, critical challenges remain in architecture design, including optimal carrier‐collection geometry, material selection, and interface engineering for boosting devices’ performance. Herein, a type‐II band‐aligned PTF/WSe2 mixed‐dimensional heterostructure is reported for high‐performance broadband SWIR photodetection via heterostructure synergy and rational Schottky barrier engineering. The Cr/p‐WSe2/PTF configuration (∼ 0.28 eV barrier) achieves superior performance, while Cr/n‐WSe2/PTF suffers from a higher barrier (∼ 1.18 eV). The optimized device achieves broad spectral photoresponsivity (∼ 103 A/W, 1060–1470 nm) and exceptional performance at 1310 nm: ultrahigh photoresponsivity (R = 2894 A/W), robust specific detectivity (D* = 1.0×1012 Jones), and excellent long‐term ambient stability. Versus standalone PTF, it delivers 17‐fold higher photoresponsivity and 96% lower bias voltage. High‐resolution SWIR image‐pattern reconstruction, together with concurrent performance improvements after six months of controlled storage, validates this PTF/WSe2 mixed‐dimensional heterostructure's potential for advancing next‐generation high‐performance SWIR detectors.

title: Designing a Thermochemically Active Hydrogel With In Situ‐Formed Ceramic–Carbon Hybrid Barrier for Suppressing Thermal Runaway Propagation
content:
A thermochemically active boric acid (BA) cross‐linker within a poly(AMPS) hydrogel is introduced to suppress thermal runaway propagation (TRP). This strategy enables dual‐mode protection: synergistic massive heat absorption and in situ formation of an insulating ceramic–carbon barrier. Consequently, the peak temperature of an adjacent cell is reduced by over 500°C, presenting a novel design principle for next‐generation battery safety materials.








ABSTRACT
Preventing thermal runaway propagation (TRP) is critical for the safety of lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs). While hydrogel interlayers actively cool through water evaporation, their mechanical reinforcement with conventional fillers dilutes the water‐rich matrix and reduces enthalpy. Here, we propose a paradigm‐shifting strategy by using boric acid (BA) as a thermochemically active cross‐linker in a poly(AMPS) hydrogel. BA reconstructs the hydrogel network through dual N─H⋯O hydrogen bonding and B⋯O═C coordination, simultaneously enhancing compressive strength by 567%. Upon thermal runaway, the composite provides dual‐mode protection: (1) synergistic heat absorption (volumetric enthalpy > 2000 J cm−3) via water evaporation and BA stepwise dehydration, accompanied by flame‐inhibiting SO2 release. (2) In situ formation of a highly insulating ceramic–carbon hybrid barrier. Post‐test analysis reveals a critical BA content of 25 wt%, where tetrahedral boron coordination (63.3% BO4) maximizes covalent B─O─C bonds that chemically “weld” B2O3 to carbon. This trend in BO4 fraction with BA loading quantitatively explains the exceptional TRP suppression, reducing the adjacent cell's peak temperature by over 500°C. Beyond a high‐performance material, this work establishes a general design principle: employing reactive fillers that orchestrate both multi‐stage energy management and tailored barrier synthesis, paving the way for next‐generation battery safety materials.

title: Preserving Polymorphic Crystalline Structures in Bulk Heterojunctions for Efficient Organic Solar Cells
content:
Structural consistency of the BTP‐eC9 Form II polymorph is established across single‐crystal packing, powders, neat films, and bulk heterojunctions, directly bridging molecular packing with functional active‐layer structure. Preserving this polymorph promotes ordered donor–acceptor assembly, efficient charge transport, and suppressed recombination, yielding 20.61% efficient organic solar cells and 17.93% efficient large‐area flexible devices.








ABSTRACT
The crystal structure of a material profoundly influences its physical, optical, and electronic properties. However, precise control over polymorph formation of non‐fullerene acceptors (NFAs) in bulk heterojunction active layers remains challenging for optimizing organic solar cell (OSC) performance. Here, we employ a non‐halogenated mixed‐solvent system comprising carbon disulfide (CS2) and o‐xylene (OXY) to selectively regulate the crystallization of the high‐performance acceptor BTP‐eC9. A specific polymorph (Form II) is preferentially induced and consistently identified in powder, neat‐film, and bulk heterojunction samples by correlating wide‐angle x‐ray scattering (WAXS) and grazing‐incidence wide‐angle x‐ray scattering (GIWAXS) patterns with simulations derived from the corresponding single‐crystal structures. Compared with Form I, Form II exhibits improved optoelectronic properties, including extended exciton diffusion length, balanced charge mobility, and suppressed non‐radiative recombination. Consequently, Form II‐based devices achieve a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.61% with a fill factor of 82.85%, representing a 27.0% relative improvement over Form I devices (PCE = 16.23%). Moreover, this method enables scalable manufacturing, with flexible OSCs (1 cm2 active area) fabricated by slot‐die coating achieving a PCE of 17.93%. This work establishes a practical pathway for solution‐processed polymorph control and reveals the relationship among single‐crystal packing, acceptor molecular packing, and device performance.

title: Upcycling Piezoelectric Single‐Crystal Debris Into High‐Performance Flexible 0–3 Composites
content:
Industrial PMN–PT single‐crystal debris is upcycled into high‐performance flexible 0–3 piezoelectric composites through controlled particle refinement and dielectrophoresis (DEP)‐assisted curing. Vertically connected quasi‐1–3‐like particle networks embedded in a compliant PDMS matrix enable efficient stress transfer, high piezoelectric response, and mechanical flexibility. The optimized composite achieves d33 = 118.5 pC N−1, positioning it among the highest‐performing flexible 0–3 piezoelectric composites.








ABSTRACT
High‐value piezoelectric single‐crystal debris remains an untapped resource for flexible electromechanical materials. Although relaxor‐based ferroelectric single crystals offer exceptional piezoelectric properties, off‐cuts inevitably generated during precision processing are typically discarded because their irregular geometries prevent direct device integration. Here, we report a recycling‐to‐device upcycling strategy that converts industrial Pb(Mg1/3Nb2/3)O3–PbTiO3 (PMN–PT) single‐crystal debris into high‐performance flexible 0–3 piezoelectric composites and energy harvesters through material–structure–mechanics co‐design. A ball‐milling‐based particle refinement procedure converts the debris into dispersible particulate fillers, while dielectrophoresis (DEP)‐assisted curing reorganizes randomly dispersed particles in a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) matrix into vertically connected quasi‐1–3‐like networks. The polymer matrix provides mechanical tunability, allowing flexibility and dynamic stress transfer to the aligned single‐crystal network to be jointly optimized. The optimized composite achieves a d33 of 118.5 pC N−1 while retaining mechanical flexibility, placing it among the highest‐performing flexible 0–3 piezoelectric composites. Comparative experiments and finite‐element simulations reveal that single‐crystal‐derived fillers exhibit stronger DEP‐induced enhancement than polycrystalline counterparts owing to more coherent intraparticle electromechanical conversion. Integrated into flexible energy harvesters, the optimized composite delivers a peak areal power density of 284.2 µW cm−2. This work establishes a scalable upcycling pathway for reutilizing high‐value functional crystal waste in flexible self‐powered electromechanical systems.

title: pH‐Responsive Synthetic Cells for Programmable In Situ Protein Synthesis and Release
content:
A synthetic cell is engineered to convert environmental acidification into nucleic acid signaling that activates protein synthesis. By coupling proton‐channel sensing, pH‐responsive DNA transduction, and toehold‐regulated translation, the platform enables acid‐triggered protein production within hydrogel‐embedded synthetic cells. This strategy expands the repertoire of condition‐associated cues that synthetic cells can interpret for responsive biomaterials, biosensing, and controlled delivery.








ABSTRACT
Lipid membrane‐bound synthetic cells provide programmable, cell‐like compartments for on‐demand biomolecule production. However, most cell‐free gene expression systems in synthetic cells are regulated by user‐imposed cues rather than signals associated with environmental or physiological states. Here, we present an acidity‐transducing synthetic cell that converts external pH changes into nucleic acid information to drive in situ protein synthesis. The system integrates gramicidin A proton channels for pH sensing, triplex‐forming single‐stranded DNA (ssDNA) that releases a trigger ssDNA upon acidification, and a toehold switch RNA that activates translation in response to the released trigger ssDNA. This work further reveals that tuning the annealing length between the pH‐responsive and trigger ssDNAs controls the trigger‐release pH, which is critical for enabling acid‐triggered protein synthesis. The synthetic cells retain their pH‐responsive activity when embedded in alginate hydrogels, creating acidity‐responsive materials that synthesize proteins in situ rather than release preloaded cargo. Cell‐penetrating peptide tagging further enables selective protein release and target‐specific binding. This work establishes a molecular transduction strategy for programming synthetic cell materials to sense environmentally relevant acidity and generates functional biomolecules on demand.

title: Ultralow Loading Iridium Doped Hollandite Manganese Oxide Nanowires for Efficient Acidic Oxygen Evolution Reaction
content:
Ultralow iridium loading in hollandite MnO2 nanowires delivers an order of magnitude higher Ir mass activity than commercial IrOx for acidic water oxidation. Across pH and potential, Ir stays framework‐associated while Mn reconstructs, yet the most restructured catalyst is not the most dissolved, indicating that dissolution alone is an incomplete measure of degradation.








ABSTRACT
Efficient and durable catalysts for the acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) are critical for hydrogen production but remain limited by reliance on scarce iridium (Ir). We present an ultralow‐loading Ir catalyst (3 at%, <16 µgIr cm−2) integrated within a hollandite MnO2 framework, which lowers the overpotential at 10 mA cm−2 from 580 mV (undoped α‐MnO2) to 303 mV and delivers an Ir mass activity an order of magnitude higher than commercial IrOx. Varying pH and potential, we combine ICP‐MS dissolution measurements with x‐ray absorption spectroscopy, electron energy loss spectroscopy, and 4D scanning transmission electron microscopy. Dissolution is modest, with at least 79% of the Ir and 76% of the Mn remaining after 6 h under applied potential, and Ir remains oxidized and associated with the hollandite framework. Mn, in contrast, undergoes pH‐ and potential‐dependent reduction and local structural disorder. Notably, the strongest Mn reconstruction (pH 0, 1.65 V) coincides with moderate dissolution, whereas the greatest Ir and Mn loss (pH 0, 1.60 V) occurs where the residual material is less reconstructed. Net dissolution therefore does not report on local structural change, highlighting the need to evaluate dissolution, reconstruction, and oxidation state together when designing and assessing Ir‐efficient mixed‐metal oxide catalysts.

title: Fluoride‐Mediated Host‐Activator Engineering in Homogeneous Lithium Glass Scintillators for Thermal‐Neutron Detection and Imaging
content:
The study introduces fluoride‐mediated host‐activator engineering in homogeneous Ce3+‐activated lithium aluminosilicate thermal‐neutron glass scintillators. By modulating the glass host structure, mitigating defect‐related trapping, and redistributing Ce‐centered correlations, fluoride incorporation enables higher effective Ce loading and enhances scintillation efficiency. The optimized 6Li‐enriched glass delivers excellent light yield and energy resolution, while scalable two‐inch plates achieve thermal‐neutron imaging with 1.35‐mm spatial resolution.








ABSTRACT
Homogeneous lithium‐aluminosilicate‐glass scintillators offer transparency, scalable fabrication, and compositional flexibility, but their neutron response is limited by defect trapping and activator loading concentration. Here, fluoride‐mediated host‐activator engineering is introduced to overcome these coupled limitations in Ce3+‐activated lithium aluminosilicate glasses. F− preferentially coordinates with Li+ and Mg2+, preserving the primary Si/Al─O tetrahedral units while reorganizing inter‐tetrahedral linkages. The resulting host‐network reconfiguration suppresses electronic disorder and defect‐mediated trapping, modulates medium‐range Ce‐centered correlations, broadens the viable Ce‐concentration window, and enables efficient excitation capture at ∼9 wt% CeO2 (twice that of GS20). After 6Li enrichment, it delivers 8003 photons neutron−1, an energy resolution of 6.8%, a decay time of 85.06 ns, and a neutron peak‐to‐trough ratio of 77:1. To the best of our knowledge, these values represent the highest light yield and best energy resolution reported for a homogeneous transparent 6Li‐enriched glass scintillator, achieving single‐digit neutron energy resolution for the first time and approaching the performance of 3He proportional counters and high‐performance crystalline scintillators. A transparent plate exceeding 2 inches further enables proof‐of‐concept two‐dimensional thermal‐neutron imaging with a system‐level spatial resolution of 1.35 mm, demonstrating the scalability of the glass for position‐sensitive neutron imaging.

title: Sustainable Soft Electronic Devices by High‐Performance Recyclable Elastomers and Conductors
content:
System‑level closed‑loop recyclable soft electronics via a multifunctional poly(thioctic acid) elastomer and liquid metal conductors: A multifunctional poly(thioctic acid) elastomer integrates strong adhesion, high thermal conductivity, stretchability, self‐healing, and recyclability for sustainable soft electronics. Combined with printable and recyclable liquid‐metal conductors, the resulting devices maintain robust electrical interfaces, recover circuit functionality after mechanical rupture, and enable closed‐loop reprocessing, offering a system‐level route toward durable and environmentally responsible wearable electronics.








ABSTRACT
Soft electronics have driven emerging advancements, which are expected to have wide‐range and large‐scale applications in health management, electronic skins, soft robotics, and interactive human‐machine interfaces. However, existing strategies mainly focus on isolated components, and system‐level soft electronic devices combining sustainable fabrication, robust performance, and versatile integrated functions have rarely been explored. Herein, we develop a recyclable soft electronic system enabled with multifunctional poly thioctic acid (TA) elastomer and high‐performance elastic metallic conductors. The multifunctional TA elastomer exhibits an exceptional combination of stretchability (435% strain), fracture energy (5.5 kJ/m2), apparent adhesion energy on Cu (10.7 kJ/m2), and thermal conductivity (0.69 W/m·K). These properties enable robust mechanical and electronic interfacing with different electronic components for sustainable soft circuits, while also endowing the electronic systems with outstanding self‐healing and recycling capabilities. Furthermore, by integrating with printable and recyclable elastic conductors based on eutectic liquid metals, the sustainable soft electronic systems can fully restore circuit functionality after complete mechanical rupture with the selfhealing capability of the composite elastomer and the elastic conductor. The system can be reprocessed to achieve full functionality restoration. The materials strategy developed in this study renders a promising solution for the development of soft and sustainable electronic devices.

title: Ion–Electron Coupling Transport in Semiconductor Nanotubes for Retinomorphic Vision
content:
We develop an ion‐electron coupling strategy to construct a bio‐inspired retina that can generate two distinct ionic and electronic current signals from the same type of optical stimulus. By mimicking the parallel phototransduction pathways of biological retinas, the system enables diverse visual functions, including luminance adaptation, color discrimination, and traffic‐signal recognition and response.








ABSTRACT
A key limitation of current artificial visual systems lies in their single‐channel signal transduction, which fundamentally departs from the parallel processing architecture of the biological retinas enabled by rod and cone cells. To bridge this gap, we developed a retinomorphic vision device by ion‐electron coupling transport based on carbon nanotube (CNT)/zinc oxide (ZnO) heterostructured nanotubes. Upon optical stimuli, this device generates two distinct ionic and electronic current signals, effectively mimicking the parallel phototransduction pathways in biological vision. This dual‐channel property enables efficient machine vision perception, achieving luminance adaptation and color discrimination accuracies of 96.5% and 98.2%, respectively. Furthermore, traffic‐light‐guided closed‐loop navigation of a mobile vehicle in a real scene has verified its application potential in embodied intelligence. This “single device enabled, distinguishable dual‐channel readouts” principle opens a new avenue toward artificial vision systems.

title: Rate Capability of Lithium‐Rich Manganese‐Based Oxide Cathodes: Charge–Discharge Kinetics, Multiscale Bottlenecks, and Dynamic Rate‐Determining Steps
content:
The rate‐determining step in Lithium‐rich Manganese‐based oxide cathodes remains unresolved between two coupled bottlenecks: Li+ diffusion, described by the limiting current density, and interfacial electron transfer, described by the exchange current density. This review proposes a dynamic j0/jd framework showing how their balance shifts with cycling and rate, guiding the rational design of fast‐charging cathodes.








ABSTRACT
Lithium‐rich manganese‐based oxide (LRMO) cathode materials deliver a reversible specific capacity exceeding 250 mAh g−1 through synergistic anionic and cationic redox, promising for next‐generation high‐energy‐density batteries, yet their poor rate capability remains a critical barrier to practical deployment, particularly for fast‐charging applications. This review deconstructs rate‐limiting mechanisms at three levels, namely direct charge‐transport impediments, kinetic sluggishness of anionic redox, and degradation cascade of phase transformations, voltage decay, and microcracking that exacerbates kinetics. A central insight is that the rate‐determining step (RDS) shifts from electron‐transfer to ion‐diffusion dominance, governed by the exchange current density (j0) and the limiting current density (jd). Modification strategies are classified into two threads, kinetic enhancement by shortening diffusion paths and lowering migration barriers, and structural stabilization by reinforcing bonds and suppressing oxygen release. Importantly, the often‐overlooked charging kinetics are critically assessed, as the asymmetric nature of anionic redox imposes a more severe bottleneck for fast charging than for high‐rate discharging. Methodological limitations in cross‐study C‐rate comparisons, arising from variations in electrode loading and testing protocols, are also examined to enable more rigorous evaluation of reported performance. This review ultimately provides a theoretical foundation for rational design of high‐rate LRMO cathodes toward practical energy storage applications.

title: Liquid Luminescent Materials Based on 10H‐Pyrido[1,2‐a]‐5‐indolium Salts
content:
A kinetically stabilized ionic liquid glows with intense blue luminescence while remaining fluid and indestructible. The rigid N‐doped fluorene cations (10H‐pyrido[1,2‐a]‐5‐indolium, PIn+) and tethered anions lock the radiative pathways, resulting in exceptional emission efficiency and resilience when subjected to heat, vacuum, and chemical stress. This establishes a new molecular design principle for robust and flexible photonic materials.








ABSTRACT
Next‐generation flexible optoelectronics and soft robotics require adaptive luminescent materials that withstand extreme environments while remaining deformable. However, the photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) of current solvent‐free ionic liquids suffers from fundamental limitations arising from aggregation‐caused quenching and rapid nonradiative decay, and these liquids degrade under thermal and chemical stress. This study presents a supramolecular locking strategy that overcomes these limitations through kinetically stabilized anion–π+ interactions. Specifically, a rigid N‐doped fluorene (10H‐pyrido[1,2‐a]‐5‐indolium, PIn+) was paired with selected anions to maintain fluidity and suppress nonradiative molecular motion by locking radiative pathways in the liquid state. This ionic tethering approach yielded an unprecedented PLQY of 80% in the liquid state while preserving the solvent‐free liquid nature of the material. These highly emissive ionic liquids exhibited extreme physicochemical robustness, withstanding thermal decomposition up to 400°C, retaining intense emission without volatilization even under reduced pressure at 250°C, and resisting strongly acidic and basic environments. Derived from a versatile and readily synthesizable fluorene platform, this system also provides broad opportunities for structural customization. These findings establish a general molecular design principle for highly robust and emissive liquid fluorophores, providing a foundation for indestructible and flexible photonic technologies operating under extreme conditions.

title: Pd Single‐Atom Engineered Janus BiOCl/MXene Heterostructure for Printed Self‐Decoupled Temperature‐Humidity Dual‐Mode Sensors
content:
Pd single‐atom engineered Janus BiOCl/MXene heterostructure enables self‐decoupled temperature and humidity dual‐mode sensing by establishing orthogonal response mechanisms, in which quasi‐2D interfacial proton conduction governs hydrocapacitance transduction and delocalized carrier diffusion drives thermovoltage output. In combination with machine learning, this multi‐modal sensing platform powers the integrated closed‐loop therapeutic system capable of real time wound healing evaluation and on‐demand drug release.








ABSTRACT
The advancement of flexible sensing technologies is of paramount importance in biomedical engineering. However, achieving high‐fidelity multi‐modal temperature‐humidity sensing without inter‐channel cross‐talk and computational post‐processing remains a formidable challenge due to overlapping transduction mechanisms. In this study, an unprecedented electron‐ion synergistic functional material, featuring a unique inherent self‐decoupling capability, was developed based on the Janus hierarchical heterostructure. Through interfacial chemical engineering of Pd single‐atom anchoring and heterogeneous‐nucleation‐driven vertical growth of BiOCl on hollow MXene, the constructed material architecture successfully establishes fundamentally segregated electronic and ionic stimulus‐response pathways. Specifically, humidity fluctuations trigger ultra‐fast quasi‐2D proton conduction facilitated by localized potential wells and electronic redistribution generated around atomically dispersed Pd sites, while temperature gradients induce entropy‐driven carrier diffusion within the conductive MXene network. By suppressing signal cross‐talk through rigorous mechanistic orthogonality, the fabricated sensing array exhibits outstanding response characteristics (37.5/50 ms for humidity response/recovery and 25/62.5 ms for high/low‐temperature response), alongside superior oxidation resistance and robust functional durability (enduring 5000 cycles of testing). Ultimately, leveraging this multi‐modal sensing platform and machine learning algorithm, the integrated closed‐loop therapeutic system enables accurate evaluation of wound healing progression as well as on‐demand drug release, pioneering a new paradigm for next‐generation flexible electronics and adaptive healthcare modalities.

title: Dynamic, Wet‐Adhesive Hydrogels for Enhanced Interface Healing in Cartilage Repair
content:
An injectable OHA/QCS/SF hydrogel combines underwater super‐spreading, wet adhesion, and dynamic network self‐healing to improve contact with hydrated cartilage surfaces. Loaded with synovial membrane‐derived mesenchymal stem cells, the hydrogel promotes repair‐tissue integration and hyaline‐like cartilage regeneration in rabbit defects, offering a strategy for addressing the challenging tissue‐material interface in fluid‐rich joint environments.








ABSTRACT
Articular cartilage defects remain a major clinical challenge due to the tissue's limited self‐repair capacity. Although numerous biomaterial‐based strategies have been explored, achieving a stable and functional cartilage interface remains difficult. A critical barrier is the poor integration between grafts and native cartilage, leading to fibrocartilage formation, delamination, and repair failure. Current approaches show limited success due to inadequate wet adhesion, mechanical mismatch, and insufficient chemical bonding. Here, we report a dynamically adaptive wet‐adhesive hydrogel composed of oxidized hyaluronic acid, quaternized chitosan, and silk fibroin (OHA/QCS/SF) for enhanced cartilage interface healing. The precursor exhibited rapid underwater spreading on hydrated substrates and displaced interfacial fluid in a fluid‐covered assay. Fluorescence imaging further revealed wetting and infiltration into the PAAm hydrogel. Dynamic Schiff‐base bonding between aldehyde groups in the hydrogel and amine‐containing components at the cartilage interface further promoted wet adhesion, while the reversible network enabled self‐healing under mechanical disturbance. In a rabbit cartilage defect model, the hydrogel loaded with synovial membrane‐derived mesenchymal stem cells (SMSCs) improved defect filling, host–graft integration, and cartilage‐like regeneration. This study provides a dynamic wet‐adhesive hydrogel strategy for improving biomaterial–cartilage interface healing in fluid‐rich joint environments.

title: A Closed‐Loop‐Recyclable Liquid‐Crystalline Dynamic Covalent Network Soft Actuator Derived From Nonliquid‐Crystalline Monomers
content:
Reversible imine chemistry constructs mesogenic segments in situ and forms a dynamic liquid‐crystalline network from non‐mesogenic building blocks. The network supports thermal reprocessing, and aligned films exhibit 26% reversible thermomechanical actuation. Acid‐catalyzed hydrolysis enables recovery and reuse of the original building blocks for network reconstruction and function regeneration








ABSTRACT
Liquid‐crystalline networks constructed from nonliquid‐crystalline precursors offer an alternative to conventional routes based on liquid‐crystalline monomers, that is, mesogenic monomers. Here, we report a closed‐loop recyclable liquid crystal polymer network (CLLCP) synthesized from nonliquid‐crystalline aldehyde and amine building blocks through reversible imine chemistry. Imine formation constructs mesogenic segments and establishes network connectivity, linking liquid‐crystalline structural design with chemical recyclability. This approach avoids pre‐synthesis of liquid‐crystalline monomers and offers flexibility in the selection of network components. The combination of rigid imine‐linked segments and flexible spacers supports liquid‐crystalline order and segmental mobility, while dynamic imine bonds enable stress relaxation and thermal reprocessing. Aligned CLLCP films exhibit a reversible thermomechanical actuation strain of 26% with good cycling stability. Under acidic conditions, imine hydrolysis disassembles the network and enables recovery of the four original molecular building blocks. These components are reused to reconstruct networks with phase behavior, mechanical properties, and actuation performance comparable to those of the pristine materials. This molecular design couples in situ mesogenic‐segment construction with polymer‐to‐monomer closed‐loop recycling, providing a modular route to sustainable liquid‐crystalline soft actuators.

title: Coordination Number‐Tuned FeNx Single‐Atom Nanozymes for Sustained Peroxidase‐Like Catalysis in Tumor Therapy
content:
A series of FeNx (x = 4, 3, 2) single‐atom nanozymes reveals a volcano correlation between H2O2 adsorption and POD‐like activity. The optimized FeN3‐SAE achieves a favorable adsorption–turnover balance, combining high catalytic activity with sustained POD‐like catalysis under repeated H2O2 exposure and thereby enhancing tumor catalytic therapy.








ABSTRACT
Peroxidase (POD)‐like catalysis by single‐atom nanozymes (SAEs) under sustained H2O2 exposure requires both rapid substrate activation and durable catalytic turnover, both of which are closely linked to the coordination environment of metal sites. However, how the coordination number governs their balance remains unclear, especially when the interaction strength between SAEs and H2O2 is tuned. Herein, we construct three structurally comparable FeNx‐SAEs (x = 4, 3, and 2), revealing a volcano‐like relationship between POD‐like activity and H2O2 adsorption strength. The selected FeN3‐SAE exhibits the highest POD‐like activity (1.52 × 10−6 M s−1), which is 1.9‐ and 4.1‐fold greater than those of FeN2‐SAE and FeN4‐SAE, respectively. Moreover, the FeN3‐SAE sustains efficient H2O2 consumption and robust •OH generation during prolonged catalysis, whereas the FeN4‐SAE suffers from inadequate H2O2 activation, and the FeN2‐SAE undergoes rapid kinetic decay. Combined experiments and theoretical calculations attribute this performance to well‐balanced H2O2 adsorption at the FeN3 site, which facilitates substrate activation, intermediate desorption, and active‐site regeneration. Both cellular and animal experiments reveal that FeN3‐SAE enables continuous H2O2 conversion into cytotoxic •OH, depleting GSH and triggering tumor suppression accompanied by immune activation. This study provides mechanistic insights into sustained POD‐like catalysis from the perspective of coordination number‐regulated adsorption‒turnover balance.

title: cis–trans Isomerism Enables Visible Light‐Excited Room‐Temperature Phosphorescence and Dynamic Afterglow
content:
Two 9,10‐dihydrophenanthrene‐9,10‐dicarbonitrile derivatives, DPCN‐H and DPCN‐O, were developed. The trans‐isomers exhibit superior phosphorescence performance over their cis‐counterparts. Notably, trans‐DPCN‐O achieves a high afterglow quantum yield of ∼43% under visible‐light excitation, while trans‐DPCN‐H displays excitation power‐ and temperature‐dependent dynamic afterglow color switching, enabling applications in 4D anti‐counterfeiting and in vivo imaging.








ABSTRACT
Isomerism serves as a powerful strategy for modulating organic room‐temperature phosphorescence (RTP), which is crucial for developing novel RTP materials and elucidating structure‐property relationships. However, cis–trans isomerism that is widespread in organic compounds has not been deeply explored in terms of its influence on RTP properties. In this study, the cis–trans isomers of two 9,10‐dihydrophenanthrene‐9,10‐dicarbonitriles, DPCN‐H and DPCN‐O (with OMe group), are designed and synthesized. Significant differences in luminous behavior are observed between the cis‐ and trans‐isomers. The trans‐DPCNs exhibit notably superior RTP and afterglow performance compared to cis‐DPCNs for their better structural planarity and tighter packing. Among them, trans‐DPCN‐O achieves an afterglow quantum yield as high as 43% upon visible‐light excitation. Additionally, trans‐DPCN‐H displays excitation‐power‐dependent and temperature‐dependent afterglow color modulation, while the nanoparticles of trans‐DPCN‐O demonstrates efficient visible‐light‐excited afterglow in aqueous solution. The excellent RTP properties of the trans‐DPCNs enable their successful application in complex anti‐counterfeiting with four dimensions, and in vivo imaging in mice under white LED excitation with a signal‐to‐noise ratio of up to 228. This work presents the first investigation into how cis–trans isomerism affects organic RTP and provides new insights into designing high‐performance RTP materials.

title: Solid‐State Nanopores for High‐Accuracy Readout of Linear Biomolecules
content:
This review describes how solid‐state nanopores enable high‐accuracy readout of linear biomolecules. It examines physical limits imposed by fast translocation, stochastic translocation dynamics, molecular folding and device noise, and surveys translocation control, device optimization and ultrasmall nanopores. It outlines a scalable route toward precise single‐molecule DNA and protein sequencing.








ABSTRACT
Solid‐state nanopores offer a robust and highly integrable platform for single‐molecule analysis, with advantages over biological pores that include superior mechanical stability, tunable geometry, and compatibility with scalable device fabrication. High‐precision readout of linear biomolecules is fundamental to DNA sequencing, diagnostic strategies, and protein or peptide sequencing. Here we review recent progress in improving the detection of linear biomolecules, including DNA, proteins, and peptides, with emphasis on the physical limits of readout, translocation control, and device optimization. We discuss the major factors that constrain precision, including rapid transport, stochastic dynamics, molecular folding, and device‐dependent noise, and summarize engineering strategies that address these challenges through mechanical manipulation, gate‐controlled translocation, and electric field coupled nanopores. We also highlight recent advances in ultrasmall nanopores for high‐resolution molecular sensing and consider future opportunities for extending solid‐state nanopores toward accurate and scalable linear‐molecule analysis.

title: Quantitative Measurement of Li‐Ion Concentration in NCM811 Cathodes via Optimized Electrochemical Strain Microscopy
content:
Electrochemical strain microscopy is turned into a quantitative probe of lithium content in NCM811 cathodes. A stiff cantilever suppresses electrostatic artifacts and contact‐potential drift, and the shortened acquisition time makes multi‐particle sampling practical. The calibrated amplitude tracks bulk lithium concentration, resolving inter‐particle state‐of‐charge heterogeneity and classifying three charge states from only four images.








ABSTRACT
Inter‐particle state‐of‐charge (SOC) heterogeneity governs electrochemical degradation in Ni‐rich layered oxide cathodes, yet quantifying the underlying nanoscale lithium distribution remains inaccessible to bulk‐averaging characterization techniques and impractical for destructive nanoscale probes. Here, a practical process for nanoscale Li‐ion quantification in NCM811 cathodes is established by optimizing the measurement conditions of electrochemical strain microscopy (ESM). Through rational probe selection to suppress electrostatic artifacts and contact potential difference drift sensitivity combined with a markedly reduced acquisition time, a quantitative calibration framework directly correlating pixel‐averaged ESM amplitude with ICP‐MS‐derived bulk Li concentration is constructed. Classification among three SOCs exceeds 90% accuracy with as few as four images per sample. This work establishes multi‐particle ESM imaging as a statistically robust and non‐destructive platform for nanoscale Li‐ion quantification in NCM811 cathodes, with broad applicability across mixed ionic‐electronic conductors in which local Vegard strain arises from ion redistribution.

title: Faceted Photocatalytic Microswimmers for Adaptive Navigation and Cargo Transport via Structured Illumination
content:
Structured illumination provides both propulsion and guidance for faceted BiVO4 microswimmers. Non‐uniform photoactivation and facet‐dependent reactivity steer the particles along light–dark boundaries, where they autonomously follow curves and corners and adapt to changes in the pattern. This optical guidance enables independent particle manipulation and cargo transport along reconfigurable trajectories without externally applied magnetic or electric fields.








ABSTRACT
Precise navigation of photocatalytic microswimmers typically requires external fields, physical confinement, chemical gradients, or feedback control, limiting their operation in dynamically changing environments. Here, light‐programmable faceted BiVO4 microswimmers are introduced, where structured illumination provides both the energy for propulsion and the spatial information required for navigation. While uniform illumination activates self‐propulsion without directional guidance, patterned illumination defines light–dark interfaces that the microswimmers autonomously follow through continuous reorientation. Fluorescence mapping, EPR spectroscopy, tracer‐particle experiments, facet‐distribution controls, and numerical simulations support a mechanism in which partial illumination creates asymmetric photocatalytic activity, generating local chemical gradients and associated flow fields around the particle. These local imbalances allow microswimmers to remain coupled to projected boundaries, adapt to static and dynamically reconfigured geometries, and follow independently programmed trajectories within the same field of view. The same strategy enables light‐controlled cargo capture, transport, and release along confined and serpentine pathways. Overall, this work establishes an all‐optical strategy to activate, direct, and reprogram photocatalytic microswimmer motion, enabling adaptive navigation and cargo transport along complex pathways.
