title: A Breathable Nanomesh–Textile Electrode Interface for Integrated Multimodal Monitoring
content:
The duo‐electrode interface contains an electrospun nanomesh that serves as a conformal breathable tattoo electrode, and a conductive taffeta–foam fabric electrode that provides stable electrical coupling to textile‐routed electronics. Integrated into one bodysuit and eyemask, the system provides EOG, ECG, EMG, and body posture monitoring with long‐term comfort and reliability.








ABSTRACT
Long‐term wearable electrophysiology requires electrodes that are skin‐conformal, breathable, mechanically stable, and reliably connected to electronics. Existing dry electrodes address parts of this challenge, but the interface between soft electrodes and wearable electronics remains a major source of motion artifacts, open‐circuit failure, and poor long‐term usability. Here, we introduce a duo‐electrode interface that separates the functions of skin contact and electronic interconnection. An electrospun nanomesh serves as a tattoo electrode that conforms intimately to the skin, while a compressible conductive taffeta–foam fabric electrode embedded in a garment provides stable electrical coupling to textile‐routed electronics. This architecture preserves the advantages of skin‐conformal electrodes while avoiding fragile connections to electronics. We integrate the interface into a bodysuit and eyemask platform for multimodal monitoring of ECG, EMG, EOG, and body position using a centralized electronics module. The system maintains reliable signal acquisition under body motion and muscle activation, with performance comparable to or better than that of commercial hydrogel electrodes. By bridging breathable electrodes with textile‐based routing, the proposed duo‐electrode strategy establishes a practical method for scalable, comfortable, and long‐duration wearable bioelectronic monitoring. This approach may be broadly useful for remote healthcare, rehabilitation, sleep studies, human–machine interfaces, and personalized physiological sensing.

title:
Dynamic
Nonlinear Effects in the Asymmetric Kinetic
Resolution Polymerization of Racemic Diazoacetates to One-Handed Helical
Polycarbenes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The asymmetric kinetic resolution polymerization (AKRP) of racemic diazoacetates mediated by a [Rh(cod)Cl]2/chiral amine dual catalyst system exhibits dynamic nonlinear effects (DNLEs) in the relative rate constant (Krel). The overall Krel increases nonlinearly with the monomer conversion during polymer chain propagation and reaches a plateau at a medium conversion. These DNLEs originate from synergistic chirality amplification between the catalytic chain end and the evolving helical conformation of the growing polymer chain. Under optimized conditions, Krel increases from 15 at 3% monomer conversion to ∼ 138 at 33% conversion, and then reaches a plateau. The steric bulk of both the pendant groups of monomers and the chiral amine ligand critically regulates the magnitude and evolution of DNLEs, and reducing this bulk leads to a pronounced decrease in Krel. Chain extension experiments using the preformed helical macroinitiators exhibited a constant Krel, confirming that a well-formed helical conformation maintains stable enantioselectivity for AKRP. Computational studies further revealed that, during chain propagation, decameric species with well-developed helical conformations exhibit more pronounced energy differences between the R- and S-enantiomers than the corresponding initial monomer-inserted species. These results suggest that the one-handed helical conformation is associated with the enhanced enantiomer recognition at the catalytic center. This study reveals DNLEs in AKRP in which enantioselectivity evolves nonlinearly during polymer chain propagation, highlighting a dynamic chiral amplification mechanism that can surpass the intrinsic selectivity of a static catalyst through the cooperative action of chiral chain ends and helical conformation.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Electronic
Dynamics in Long Linear and Cyclic Polyynes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Carbyne─the one-dimensional sp-hybridized allotrope of carbon─has long been predicted to exhibit unique properties, yet its synthesis remains elusive. To probe its behavior, finite sp-carbon chains such as cumulenes and polyynes have been studied. While much has been established about the ground-state properties of cumulenes and polyynes, our understanding of their photophysical dynamics, which gives critical insight into how electronic relaxation, structural reorganization, and spin formation evolve, has focused almost exclusively on short, linear systems, with little consideration of topology. Here, we investigate long 48-carbon linear and cyclic polyynes in the liquid phase using steady-state and ultrafast, temperature- and polarization-resolved optical and vibrational spectroscopy. We find highly delocalized ground states in both topologies, with softened Peierls distortion and reduced bond-length alternation relative to shorter chains. In contrast, the excited state singlet dipole depolarization mechanism and subsequent intersystem crossing are strongly dependent on chain length and topology. As in shorter polyynes, transient infrared spectroscopy shows that photoexcitation of long linear polyynes induces a cumulene-like excited-state geometry; however, this structural rearrangement is weaker and shorter-lived than in shorter analogues. Comparison with shorter-chain trends and theoretical predictions shows that the Huang–Rhys factor remains far below the ideal infinite-chain value at 48 carbons, suggesting that vibronic coupling grows more slowly at long chain length than expected from simple extrapolation. Our results reveal how topology influences the largely backbone-dominated electronic dynamics of long polyynes and refine our understanding of finite sp-carbon systems at longer chain lengths than previously accessible with such time-resolved methods.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Effect of Water on
Elementary Reactions in Solid-Acid
Catalyzed Reactions: Thermodynamics of Acid–Base Interactions
in H-ZSM-5
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The influence of water on acid–base interactions in zeolites was quantified by measuring the enthalpy of pyridine adsorption on H-ZSM-5 with three Si/Al ratios (11.5, 40, and 140) in water using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). This calorimetric study reconciles the liquid- and gas-phase energetics of acid–base interactions in a solvated, pore-filled zeolite through a Born–Haber cycle analysis. In water, the apparent adsorption enthalpy is about 150 kJ/mol less exothermic than the gas-phase value and becomes more exothermic as the Si/Al ratio increases, whereas the gas-phase enthalpy is near −200 kJ/mol and independent of the Si/Al ratio. Since the intrinsic acid strength of the framework does not vary with Si/Al ratio, this increasing apparent adsorption energy trend with increasing Si/Al ratio reflects the influence of solvation rather than acidity. Water stabilizes both the acidic proton and the pyridinium ion, and a fraction of this stabilization is lost when adsorbed pyridine displaces water from the acid site. By combining ITC data with vapor-phase water adsorption isotherms and differential scanning calorimetry to construct a Born–Haber cycle for each zeolite, the aqueous-phase enthalpies are quantitatively reconciled with their gas-phase counterparts, and their dependence on Si/Al ratio is traced to the different extents to which the initial and final states are solvated.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Evolution of Interfacial
States Induced by Hydronium–Water
Ordering on Au(111)
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Structured interfacial water can substantially modify charge transfer at solid–liquid interfaces, yet direct spectroscopic evidence for how water ordering reshapes interfacial electronic states remains scarce. Herein, using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), we identify parabolic interfacial states (IFSs) arising with the ordered water structures on Au(111), in striking contrast to the insulating nature of disordered water multilayers. Light exposure induces partial dissociation of H2O, and the resulting hydrated protons combine with residual H2O molecules to form ordered Eigen/Zundel-type hexagonal hydronium-water monolayers on Au(111) at 120–140 K. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations based on Eigen/Zundel-type motifs reproduce the experimentally observed IFSs and indicate that the states derive from the renormalized Au(111) Shockley surface state with a reduced effective mass at the water/gold interface. Annealing-driven transition from the Eigen-type to Zundel-type monolayers is evidenced by the distinct changes in the dispersions of the IFSs. These results establish a band-structure perspective for ordered water/metal interfaces and show that hydrated-proton-introduced excess electrons, when confined at a two-dimensional interface, can reshape the interfacial electronic landscape and charge transport.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Mechanism-Guided Development
of Thioacetylene Probes
for Chemoproteomic Profiling of Cellular Protein Thiyl Radicals
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Protein thiyl radicals are transient reactive intermediates involved in oxidative stress and enzymatic catalysis. However, their proteome-wide, site-resolved profiling in living cells remains challenging due to the lack of suitable tools. Here, we report chemoproteomic probes enabling covalent capture and site-resolved identification of protein thiyl radicals in living cells. Designed to leverage sulfur-mediated stabilization of a vinyl radical intermediate, our thioacetylene-based probes selectively capture cysteine thiyl radicals while minimizing cross-reactivity with nucleophilic thiolates and nonradical amino acid residues. In vitro validation and live-cell chemoproteomic analysis established radical-dependent labeling and site-resolved detection of protein thiyl radicals. Notably, the probes enabled site-specific mapping of thiyl radical-associated cysteine residues in live E. coli, including Cys439 of ribonucleotide reductase A (NrdA), a canonical enzymatic thiyl radical site. Expanded residue profiling further confirmed cysteine-predominant labeling and detected probe modification at established and putative glycyl radical residues in PflB, NrdD, and YjjI, suggesting that the platform may extend beyond thiyl radicals to other protein-centered radicals. Application of the probe under oxidative and nitrosative stress revealed condition-dependent changes in cellular protein radical-associated labeling, including decreased labeling at established glycyl radical residues and bidirectional changes in cysteine radical-associated labeling. Together, these findings establish thioacetylene probes as a platform for site-resolved mapping and comparative monitoring of endogenous protein-centered radicals in living cells.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Enantioselective Three-Component
Reductive Coupling
of Aldehydes, Amines, and Alkynes via Ligand-Enabled Cobalt/Photoredox
Dual Catalysis for Modular Synthesis of Allylic Amines
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Here, we disclose a catalytic strategy that merges visible-light photoredox with cobalt catalysis to realize a previously elusive three-component enantioselective reductive coupling of readily available aldehydes, amines, and alkynes. This transformation provides a direct, step-economical route to high-value chiral allylic amines with broad substrate scope and high chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity, while overcoming long-standing challenges, including parasitic single-electron over-reduction, competitive aldehyde–alkyne coupling, and the inherent regioselectivity issues of unsymmetrical internal alkynes, and circumventing the moisture sensitivity and limited scope of pre-isolated imines. Central to this breakthrough is the rational design of a chiral phosphoramidite ligand featuring a tricyclic tetrahydrobenzoquinoline core, which avoids coordination saturation at cobalt and establishes a unique electronic “push–pull” synergy with a coordinated iodide anion. Mechanistic studies support an anion-promoted, single-ligand catalytic model wherein a high-spin cobaltacyclopentene intermediate serves as the key stereocontrol element. The monodentate, π-accepting phosphoramidite functions as a flexible electronic buffer, mitigating Pauli repulsion and dramatically lowering the oxidative cyclization barrier. The synthetic utility is demonstrated by late-stage functionalization of complex bioactive molecules and a concise synthesis of the antiplatelet drug prasugrel.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Magneto-Optical Studies
on the Orbital Angular Momenta
and Spin–Orbit Coupling in the Excited Triplet States of Octahedral
Mo6 Clusters: Magnetic Circular Dichroism and Magnetic
Circularly Polarized Luminescence
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The magneto-optical properties─magnetic circular dichroism (MCD) and magnetic circularly polarized luminescence (MCPL)─of octahedral hexanuclear [Mo6I8Y6]2– clusters (1, 2, and 3, possessing OPOPh2, N3, and CF3COO as the terminal Y ligands, respectively) were studied. In their MCD spectra, negative Faraday A terms corresponding to the S0 → Sn transitions were observed at ∼400 nm, reflecting the orbital angular momentum (OAM) and high symmetry of the molecular orbitals (MOs). In their highly concentrated solutions, positive Faraday A terms corresponding to the spin-forbidden S0 → Tn transitions were observed at ∼600 nm due to large spin–orbit coupling (SOC). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first direct observation of the spin-forbidden S0 → Tn transition in metal clusters by MCD. In their MCPL spectra, negative, strong phosphorescent MCPL signals (g ≈ 1.0 × 10–2 at 1.6 T) were observed at ∼690 nm, indicating that these Mo clusters are promising candidates for novel CPL materials. Time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) calculations performed for the model cluster [Mo6I8Cl6]2– could reproduce UV–vis absorption and MCD spectroscopic properties. Especially, the MCD signals were evaluated by analyzing the SOC and the Zeeman effects of the OAM and spin angular momentum in the excited triplet state. TD-DFT gradient calculations indicated the geometrical distortion and stabilization of the lowest excited triplet [Mo6I8Cl6]2– and the destabilization of its Franck–Condon ground state, which explain the large red shift of phosphorescence. These results open new possibilities for understanding and functionalizing metal clusters.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Solvent Cage Suppresses
Dynamically Induced Entropic
Pathways to Provide High Selectivity in Intramolecular Fe-Oxo Radical
Rebound Reactions
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>For homogeneous transition metal reactions, it is generally assumed that when intermediates are formed, they are sufficiently long-lived for the surrounding solvent cage to fully equilibrate prior to product formation. However, some transition metal reactions generate a highly reactive and transient intermediate for which product selectivity is not governed by subsequent competing transition states but rather by dynamic effects during descent from the transition state that forms the intermediate. In such reactions, solvent reorganization may be slow relative to product formation, which could significantly impact reaction pathway selectivity. Here, we demonstrate the important role of the solvent cage and explicit solute–solvent interactions in determining pathway selectivity for the ultrafast-evolving radical pair intermediate generated during (PDP)Fe-oxo-catalyzed intramolecular sp3 C–H functionalization. Quasiclassical reactive trajectories showed that with only a continuum solvent model a mixture of oxygen rebound/hydroxylation, desaturation, and direct carboxylate rebound products are formed due to dynamically driven, entropically favored wandering, which is inconsistent with experiments. In contrast, trajectories in explicit solvent reproduced the experimental product selectivity and demonstrated that solvent controls the nonstatistical, motion-driven selectivity by acting as a nonequilibrated solvent cage that restricts access to entropically favorable wandering configurations. The solvent effectively guides the radical pair intermediate toward one dominant product pathway. These results demonstrate the important role of the solvent cage in reactions involving highly transient intermediates where dynamic effects control selectivity.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Synergistic Interactions
Enable Superior Oxygen Evolution
Reaction Activity in Compositionally Complex Nanocrystal–Nanosheet
Hybrids
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Thiospinel nanoparticles are promising catalytic materials due to their compositional tunability, electronic conductivity, and structural stability. While significant gains in catalysis have been made through material engineering, one continuously developing route is through the use of support materials to enhance performance. Here, we report a simple, scalable, low-temperature method to coproduce colloidal multimetal nanocrystals (&lt;20 nm in diameter) and In2S3-based nanosheets (&lt;1 nm thick), forming compositionally complex hybrid nanocrystal–nanosheet heterostructures in situ. The in situ-formed heterostructures demonstrate enhanced catalytic activity in the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in alkaline conditions; peak performance was achieved in heterostructures formed between (Ni,Co,Fe)3S4 nanocrystals and (In,Fe,Mn)2S3 nanosheets with overpotentials as low as 283 mV at 10 mA/cm2. Heterostructures can also be produced ex situ by introducing nanosheets, postsynthetically, to the nanocrystals, reducing the overpotential of (Ni,Co,Fe)3S4 nanocrystals from 362 mV to 312 mV with only a 5 wt % addition. This improvement highlights synergistic interactions in the heterostructures. These results suggest that an optimum nanosheet loading that maximizes effective nanocrystal–nanosheet interfacial coupling while preserving access to the Ni/Co-rich catalytic domains is the relevant design parameter. Our findings provide a low-temperature, colloidal route for synthesizing compositionally complex and highly uniform (&lt;15% dispersity) sulfide nanocrystals, nanosheets, or heterostructures of the two with tunable structures and enhanced electrocatalytic performance. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a compositionally complex hybrid material that is able to enhance performance when formed both in situ or ex situ and the use of In2S3 as a scaffold for a support material for enhancing OER performance.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Unifying Polar and
Hydrophobic Models of Ice Recognition
by Antifreeze Glycoproteins
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Antifreeze glycoproteins (AFGPs) enable polar organisms to survive at subzero temperatures by inhibiting ice growth through selective association with specific crystallographic planes. However, the molecular basis of this interaction and its remarkable selectivity remain incompletely understood, and both polar and hydrophobic binding models have been proposed. Here, we combine the synthesis of AFGP variants with high-resolution NMR spectroscopy, antifreeze activity measurements, and molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the molecular determinants of ice recognition. Minimally perturbative chemical modifications, including site-specific deuteration and fluorination, were used to probe the contributions of nonpolar and polar interactions while preserving the characteristic AFGP conformation. The combined structure–activity relationships and computational analyses support an integrative binding model that provides a unified and parsimonious interpretation of the experimental observations. Within this framework, our experimental evidence is consistent with the view that dispersive interactions involving peptide and carbohydrate methyl groups favor productive association with the ice surface, whereas carbohydrate hydroxyl groups, together with sugar- and backbone-associated water molecules, contribute polar interactions that promote selective and persistent binding. This model reconciles key aspects of previously proposed polar and hydrophobic descriptions and provides a molecular rationale for the characteristic plane selectivity of AFGPs and the conservation of specific sequence motifs. More broadly, our results highlight minimally perturbative isotopic substitution and fluorinated molecular editing as useful chemical strategies for probing weak dispersive contributions to complex molecular recognition processes while preserving native molecular architecture.</jats:p>

title:
Optical Access to a
Molecular Nuclear-Spin Register
in Catalytically Relevant Palladium(I) Complexes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Paramagnetic metal complexes are powerful tools in chemical catalysis and, increasingly, quantum information science, positioning them as ideal tools for quantum sensing within reactions themselves. However, this application requires an interface between spins and light in chemically relevant platforms. Here, we demonstrate that circularly polarized light can generate electron spin coherence in low-symmetry, catalytically relevant Pd(I) complexes. By measuring ultrafast changes in optical polarization with time-resolved Faraday rotation, we optically detect coherent superhyperfine interaction between the Pd(I)-centered electron spin and adjacent 31P nuclei from the ligand at ambient temperature in solution. The electronic origins of this behavior are attributed to excited-state orbital angular momentum through combined spectroscopic and computational analysis, and the optically measured coherence is benchmarked against pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance. Spin polarization is coherently exchanged between the electron spin and initially incoherent nuclear spins, constituting a rare example of optical access to a nuclear spin register in an ambient-temperature, solution-phase molecular system. Both reactivity and quantum spin function are mediated by the bisphosphine ligand; taken together with in situ detection of coherent Pd(I) spin dynamics directly in reaction mixtures, this work moves molecular qubits toward quantum sensing in chemical reactions.</jats:p>

title:
Tailoring Three-Dimensional
Porphyrin Hosts to Control
Fullerene Recognition and Charge-Separation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Porphyrin–fullerene assemblies are widely regarded as model systems in artificial photosynthesis. However, attaining precise structural control over both fullerene binding and charge-separation behavior within a single, rigid three-dimensional porphyrin host continues to be a significant challenge in supramolecular design. Dihydroanthracene- and triptycene-functionalized tetraarylporphyrins are shown here to act as biconcave aromatic hosts for C60, forming 1:1 and 1:2 complexes with association constants up to 104 to 105 M–1, as evidenced by 1H NMR and fluorescence titrations, and electrospray ionization mass spectrometry. Key in the host design is the porphyrin β,β-substitution that generates a well-defined and encapsulating environment for C60. Triptycenoporphyrins exhibit more geometrically confined C60 binding than their dihydroanthracene analogues, highlighting the critical role of topological control in C60 recognition. Despite identical binding strengths in nonpolar toluene and polar benzonitrile, the corresponding C60@triptycenoporphyrins display pronounced solvent-dependent excited-state behavior. Charge-separated states are generated more rapidly in benzonitrile yet attain significantly longer lifetimes in toluene, as revealed by steady-state and time-resolved spectroscopic measurements. These results demonstrate that tailoring rigid three-dimensional porphyrin frameworks enables simultaneous enhancement of C60 binding and fine control over charge-separation and -recombination dynamics, establishing this scaffold as a versatile platform for artificial photosynthetic systems that require long-lived charge-separation.</jats:p>

title:
An Experimental MOF-Polymer
Latent Space for Composite
Design
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have tremendous promise for filtration, catalysis, and sequestration, but they are limited by the polymer matrices in which they must be embedded to form functional composites. Here, we find an experimental approach in which composite performance can be predicted using a single MOF particle. In particular, we attach single MOF particles to atomic force microscope (AFM) probes and find that the forces between the MOF-tipped probe and polymer films can be transformed into an instructive low-dimensional descriptor of MOF-polymer interactions. This two-dimensional latent space provides direct measures of chemical compatibility as well as the work of adhesion and can be used to understand interfacial phenomena in MOF-polymer composites. For example, polymer intercalation is observed via X-ray scattering for MOF-polymer combinations with high chemical-compatibility latent-space variables. Bulk composite performance can also be predicted using the latent space values for cases where the MOF is held constant. For example, a simple linear model was trained to predict CO2 absorption into composites of UiO-66-NH2 based solely on the latent space variables. In addition to providing a rapid way to screen polymer matrices to complement a MOF chosen for its bulk properties, these results suggest that composite performance may be a separable function of bulk properties and the interfacial latent space. In this way, this transfer-learning approach can vastly accelerate the design and understanding of functional composites.</jats:p>

title:
Decyanation, Dioxygenation,
and Oxidative Ring Contraction
Catalyzed by the DUF4243 Oxidase OzmD Rely on Ferric Oxygen Activation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Domain of unknown function 4243 (DUF4243) family proteins are an emerging class of nonheme mononuclear iron enzymes characterized by a distinctive iron-binding motif comprised of four histidine (His) and one Nε-carboxylysine (Kcx) residue. Although predominantly found in fungi, OzmD is the only characterized bacterial member. OzmD catalyzes oxidative rearrangement of an aminopyridone ring into a 1,3-oxazine moiety with concomitant cyanide elimination in the final step of oxazinomycin biosynthesis. Herein, the X-ray crystal structure of OzmD is solved, demonstrating the presence of a conserved 4-His-1-Kcx iron-binding motif similar to other DUF4243 family proteins. Biochemical characterization using a substrate analog carrying a hydroxypyridone ring reveals that OzmD also exhibits intrinsic dioxygenase activity, catalyzing a transformation analogous to those of fungal DUF4243 dioxygenases. Electron paramagnetic resonance and Mössbauer spectroscopic characterization of MinCC, a functionally equivalent homologue of OzmD, reveals that the as-isolated protein predominantly contains ferric iron, which can be reduced to the ferrous state upon binding with either the native substrate or the hydroxy analog under anaerobic conditions. These findings support a unified mechanism in which catalysis begins with single-electron transfer from the substrate to ferric iron, enabling molecular oxygen activation and formation of an alkylperoxide intermediate. Overall reaction mechanisms for substrates bearing aminopyridone and hydroxypyridone rings are proposed based on chemical precedents and computational analyses. These findings reveal that OzmD employs a distinctive FeIII-dependent path for oxygen activation in contrast to the classical FeII-dependent route used by most oxygenases and establish a functional connection between bacterial and fungal DUF4243 enzymes.</jats:p>

title:
All-Visible Wavelength-Gated
Multistate Photochromic
AIEgen: High-Efficiency Photocyclizations in a Single Luminogenic
System
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Synthetic photochromic molecules that enable noninvasive orthogonal control using distinct wavelengths of light are still in their infancy, yet ensuring the independence of photoreaction pathways and multiple addressable states in a single luminogenic system remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report an aggregation-induced emission (AIE) luminogen capable of undergoing wavelength-selective photocyclizations under visible-light irradiation, exhibiting a photorearrangement at 410 nm purple light and an oxidative photocyclization at 465 nm blue light to yield two stable yet distinct photochromic states. Experimental and theoretical results provide insight into the wavelength-dependent reaction pathways, as well as the corresponding synergistic mechanism of aromaticity, steric strain, and inductive effect in its photocyclizations. Eventually, a model information encryption system was developed to showcase its practical potential for all-visible-light-controlled multistate operations. This work thus offers both a viable strategy and a versatile structural motif for developing visible-light-controlled multistate luminogens and advanced multifunctional systems.</jats:p>

title:
A Molybdoenzyme Mediates
Carbon–Sulfur Bond
Making and Breaking in Ergothioneine Biosynthesis
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The molybdopterin-dependent ergothioneine synthase (MES) from Caldithrix abyssi is the first molybdoenzyme known to catalyze the formation of carbon–sulfur bonds. To complete its catalytic cycle, this bifunctional enzyme desulfurates l-cysteine at a pyridoxal 5′-phosphate binding site and transfers the harvested sulfur atom (S0) to the molybdenum center of a bis-molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide cofactor more than 50 Å away. Subsequently, the sulfurated Mo-center transfers the labile sulfur atom onto the imidazole ring of Nα-trimethyl histidine (TMH). Combining experimental observations from cryo-electron microscopy, X-ray crystallography, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, sequence-activity correlation, and substrate-specificity studies, we delineate the structural basis for long-distance sulfur transfer via a persulfide relay, the identity of the imidazole sulfurating species, and key sequence motifs that are indispensable for activity. Furthermore, the reversibility of MES-mediated sulfurization of TMH under physiological conditions suggests that ergothioneine may serve as a soluble reservoir of oxidizing equivalents, supporting anaerobic metabolism in deep-branching bacteria such as C. abyssi.</jats:p>

title: Decoding Symmetry-Breaking Band Structures in Nanocatalysts for Kinetically Favorable Li-S Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The conventional d-band center theory represents catalyst electronic structures using an averaged energy and may therefore overlook higher-order information contained in the complex and asymmetric density of states of alloy catalysts (ACs). Here, combining quantum chemistry with interpretable machine learning, we identify the transformed d-band peak position (Epp) as an alternative electronic descriptor for alloy–polysulfide interactions in lithium-sulfur batteries. Epp integrates information related to the d-band position, bandwidth, and band shape, and correlates with the electron occupation of S3p–Md (M = metal) antibonding states and the calculated polysulfide adsorption strength. A series of bimetallic ACs recovered from spent lithium-ion batteries was employed to experimentally evaluate the descriptor. Within this series, CoFe shows favorable electrochemical performance, enabling an ampere-hour-level pouch cell with an energy density of 426 Wh kg–1 under a sulfur loading of 12.5 mg cm–2 and an electrolyte-to-sulfur ratio of 3.6 mL g–1.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title:
Tunable Gaussian
Random Number Generator from a Nanoscopic
Domain-Wall-Based Spintronic Device
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Existing hardware implementations of Gaussian random number generators (RNGs) rely on large arrays of binary devices, resulting in substantial hardware footprints or sampling-time overheads. Here, we present a racetrack memory-based random number generator (RTM-RNG) that directly generates analog Gaussian random number streams from a single domain-wall-based nanoscale racetrack. A geometrically engineered racetrack tip creates a localized current-density gradient, enabling field-free stochastic domain-wall nucleation driven by nanosecond current pulses. The domain-wall nucleation probability is continuously tunable via an electrically generated Oersted field or an external magnetic field, providing direct control over the mean of the output distribution. We demonstrate more than 256 distinguishable states from a single nanoscopic RTM-RNG device, thus making a Gaussian RNG with more than 8-bit resolution possible. Compared with conventional binary random bitstreams, the RTM-RNG achieves high-quality Gaussian distributions up to 83 times faster.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Deciphering
Charge Delocalization across Mercaptobenzonitrile
Ligand Terminals and Inner Hydrides in Atomically Precise Cu14H10 Nanoclusters for Electrocatalytic CO2 Reduction
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cu hydride nanoclusters with atomic precision in composition and structure offer exciting catalytic activities and opportunities for rigorous structure–function correlations. Determination of their atomic structures, especially the hydride locations, hinges on the availability of high-quality single crystals and neutron beams, while their relatively weak UV–visible absorption and electrochemical instability challenge the analysis of their electronic properties. Herein, we synthesize a Cu14H10 nanocluster coordinated by three 4-mercaptobenzonitrile (MBN) and eight triphenylphosphine ligands. Two-dimensional NMR analyses combined with single crystal X-ray diffraction reveal unequivocally the locations of the ten hydrides in four groups (stoichiometry ratio of 1:3:3:3) with drastically different environments (chemical shifts 11–3 ppm): one H at the inversion center and three triangular layers along the C3 axial bridging together the Cu core. MBN serves two additional purposes besides stabilizing ligands: its electron-withdrawing nature and a highly sensitive vibrational reporter of its local charge density. The first property gives rise to a low-lying Cu-core-to-MBN metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) excited state, and the second property enables direct spectroscopic probing of both the charge transfer nature and dynamics of the MLCT excited state through the dynamic spectral shift of the MBN CN stretching mode. Through combined transient IR absorption spectroscopy and time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) calculations, we obtained the complete atomic and electronic structure, revealing core-to-ligand charge transfers in these nanoclusters. Computed under identical conditions using an iso-structure with a mildly electron-donating ligand, the Cu14H10 featuring charge delocalization toward the electron-withdrawing MBN has a smaller HOMO–LUMO gap, which is deemed favorable for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. The preferential formation of complex multielectron-hydrogenation products (8–12 e–, C1 hydrocarbons, and C2+ products) over two-electron pathways such as CO formation or the competing hydrogen evolution reaction highlights their promise as atomically precise catalysts for deep CO2 reduction.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Full-Length Protein
Classification through Sequence
Reading by Solid-State Subnanopores
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nanopore sequencing for full-length proteins is daunting due to inaccuracy of fingerprinting amino acids with ionic current and lack of theoretical models. Here, we demonstrate that nanopores drilled in 5 nm-thick membranes with constriction diameter &lt;1 nm, i.e., subnanopores, can site-specifically read the primary structure of amyloid-β (Aβ) isoforms after 50-fold coverage. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that charged side chains near the constriction swing and modulate the volume exclusion of neighboring residues, resulting in a sequence context-dependent signal altered between translocation orientations. Orientation of individual label-free molecules is inferred by clustering, which yields high-fidelity empirical consensus that strongly correlates with computational trajectories (PCC = 0.78 ± 0.03). A homemade self-supervised learning method categorizes Aβ42 and Aβ40 at the single-molecule level (AUC = 0.88 ± 0.02) and predicts the mole fraction in agreement with actual ratios. Solid-state subnanopores offer a straightforward strategy for proteoform single-molecule classification and sequence extraction in mixtures.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Defect-Tolerant
Frenkel Exciton Delocalization in
Supramolecular Nanotubes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Preserving exciton delocalization in the presence of structural and environmental disorder is a central challenge for nanoscale photonic and optoelectronic materials. Here we show that Frenkel excitons in two-dimensional supramolecular nanostructures retain extensive delocalization even in the presence of intentionally incorporated deep-energy traps. Fluorescent trap molecules introduced during the self-assembly of double-walled molecular nanotubes provide a controlled model system in which strong local energetic perturbations are created without significant distortion of the host structure. Increasing the trap concentration shortens the host-exciton PL lifetime from ∼190 ps to ∼15 ps, while polarization-resolved microscopy of individual nanotubes shows that the collective excitonic polarization remains essentially unchanged. Frenkel-exciton calculations based on experimentally established molecular structures reproduce this robustness and reveal that delocalization decreases only weakly because the excitonic wave functions redistribute around the trap sites while remaining extended over large molecular domains. These results demonstrate an intrinsic defect tolerance of delocalized Frenkel excitons in a two-dimensional supramolecular architecture and identify dimensionality as an important design principle for preserving collective excitonic states in structurally imperfect nanomaterials.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
ZnO–Te Anti-Ambipolar
Switch Integration with
Complementary Field-Effect Transistors Enabling a Pull-Middle Architecture
for Standard Ternary Inverters
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We demonstrate a pull-middle architecture for standard ternary inverters (STIs) operating at 77 K, enabled by the cointegration of a ZnO–Te antiambipolar switch (AAS) and vertically stacked ZnO/Te complementary field-effect transistors (CFETs) using a BEOL-compatible low-temperature process (≤150 °C). Operation at 77 K not only isolates the intrinsic pull-middle switching mechanism by suppressing thermally activated off-currents but also establishes the architecture’s immediate viability for extreme-environment computing, such as radiation-hardened space data centers and cryogenic aerospace systems. In this architecture, the ZnO–Te AAS acts as an independent pull-middle device connected to an explicit Vdd/2 node, while the ZnO and Te FETs in the CFET serve as the pull-down and pull-up devices, respectively. Unlike conventional ternary logic schemes governed by precise pull-up/pull-down current matching, by explicitly clamping the intermediate state, this architecture structurally prevents variation-induced voltage shifts and suppresses static power dissipation. Consequently, the proposed STI exhibits a narrow middle-state voltage distribution across 25 cells and achieves an I/O swing ratio of 1, with cascaded operation without level-restoring circuitry supported by measurement-calibrated circuit simulations. Ultimately, this vertically integrated ZnO/Te STI offers a compact and variation-tolerant platform for cryogenic logic, while presenting a material-optimization pathway toward room-temperature multivalued systems.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Engineered
Peptide Nanoparticle Targeting Both Bacterial
Load Reduction and Bone Repair for the Treatment of Bone Infections
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Bone infection is a common and serious complication in orthopedic surgery. Conventional antibiotic strategies frequently induce antibiotic resistance, leading to the persistence of bone infections. In this study, an engineered peptide nanoparticle named C8-IK21 was designed based on the coiled-coil motif. Specifically, C8-IK21 effectively targeted bacterial cell membranes, further exacerbating bacterial death through lipid peroxidation. At safe doses, local administration of C8-IK21 demonstrated high efficacy in treating S. aureus-infected cortical bone defects in mice. No detectable resistance emerged under the tested experimental conditions. Additionally, C8-IK21 exhibited anti-inflammatory activity. Furthermore, C8-IK21 could enter cells by binding to ADAM9, activating the ERK signaling pathway to regulate osteoblast differentiation. Meanwhile, C8-IK21 reduced the expression of ITGB1 via ADAM9, thereby inhibiting osteoclast differentiation and function. Moreover, the pro-osteogenic effect of C8-IK21 was validated in organoids. In conclusion, C8-IK21 represents a promising therapeutic approach for the treatment of refractory bacterial infections and bone homeostasis disorders.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Decoupling
Conductivity and Interfacial State in Pristine-Like
Carbon Nanotube Coatings Reveals Their Distinct Contributions to Neuronal
Function
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) combine high electrical conductivity, mechanical robustness, and nanoscale architecture, making them promising materials for neural interfaces. However, the strong coupling between CNT morphology, electrical transport, and surface chemistry has limited identification of the material properties that directly regulate neuronal function. Here, we establish an experimental strategy to disentangle morphology-dependent network transport from interfacial wettability using pristine-like CNT coatings. Multiwalled CNTs with comparable diameters but distinct lengths were reversibly functionalized, spray-coated, and thermally defunctionalized to produce homogeneous conductive networks while recovering pristine-like electrical transport and surface chemistry. Subsequent conditioning in phosphate-buffered saline substantially reduced surface hydrophobicity without detectable alteration of the graphitic CNT framework, generating coatings with comparable interfacial wettability but distinct network morphologies. Primary spinal cord neuron-glia cultures grown on these substrates were characterized by immunocytochemistry, electrophysiology, and calcium imaging. All CNT coatings supported comparable neuroglial density and network formation, whereas PBS-conditioned coatings, characterized by a more wettable interface, consistently exhibited enhanced spontaneous bursting and calcium activity compared with their untreated coatings. Across all conditions, neuronal network activity was more consistently associated with the initial interfacial state of CNT coatings, as experimentally reflected by their wetting behavior, than with CNT length or morphology-dependent electrical transport. These findings identify the initial CNT interfacial state, with wettability serving as an experimentally accessible descriptor, as a key design parameter for CNT-based neural interfaces. Furthermore, they suggest that the initial interfacial state may influence the subsequent evolution of the biomolecular layer at the cell-facing interface, thereby contributing to the modulation of neuronal function.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
MXene-PS-Based Soft
Actuator with Deformation Reversal
Capability through Time-Sequence Difference of Asymmetric Water Absorption
Kinetics
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Many soft actuators have been developed to achieve bending deformation under external stimuli through asymmetric structures or nonuniform material distributions. However, most existing actuators can only produce bending in a single direction, and developing soft actuators with deformation reversal capability remains a challenge. To address this issue, this study proposes an MXene-PS/MXene bilayer soft actuator, which is fabricated by sequential vacuum-assisted filtration, resulting in a loose MXene-PS top layer and a dense MXene bottom layer. The MXene-PS layer features a high water absorption/desorption rate but low capacity, while the MXene layer exhibits a low rate but high capacity. This complementary kinetic-capacity coupling mechanism, termed the time-sequence difference of asymmetric water absorption kinetics, enables the actuator to achieve reversible deformation reversal under NIR light and humidity stimuli. Furthermore, simply by changing the placement orientation of the actuator, two distinct self-sustained oscillation behaviors can be obtained in a humidity gradient environment, namely, periodic motion toward or away from the water surface. Leveraging this deformation reversal capability, we demonstrate two proof-of-concept applications: a biomimetic flower and a self-sustained motion sailboat. This work introduces a deformation mode and actuation principle for MXene-based soft actuators and further broadens their application prospects in biomimetic devices and soft robotics.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Ferroelectric-Empowered
van der Waals Spectrometer
with Record-High Sensitivity and Ultralow Noise
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Miniaturized spectrometers are essential for portable and consumer-oriented applications, yet their reduced physical footprint inherently limits the detector’s active area, leading to compromised sensitivity. Conventional strategies to enhance sensitivity, such as cryogenic cooling or photomultiplier tubes, are incompatible with miniaturization due to their bulk, cost, and power demands. Here, we present a miniaturized spectrometer based on a van der Waals heterojunction integrated on a ferroelectric thin film. Spectral discrimination is enabled by engineering both interlayer and intralayer photoresponses within the heterojunction, which can be dynamically tuned solely via the source-drain bias, eliminating the need for a gate electrode and enabling a two-terminal architecture. This design is inherently compatible with simple two-pad readout integrated circuits, facilitating scalable array integration for compact spectroscopic systems. Critically, the built-in electric field generated by the ferroelectric polarization promotes efficient dissociation of interlayer excitons, yielding an ultralow noise floor of below 5 × 10–16 A Hz–1/2, more than 2 orders of magnitude lower than existing miniaturized spectrometers and surpassing the performance of most benchtop instruments. This work in sensitivity without sacrificing size or complexity present a strategy for deploying high-performance spectroscopy in real-world applications.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title: Cucurbit[ n ]uril-Programmed Chlorogenic Acid Release for Collagen Mineralization and Pulp–Dentin Repair in Near-Pulp Bonding
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Long-term failure of resin–dentin bonding arises from persistent hydration and enzymatic degradation of exposed collagen in the deep hybrid layer, whereas diffusion of bioactive components through dentinal tubules toward the pulp may cause pulpal irritation. An ideal pretreatment should therefore promote collagen remineralization and interfacial stabilization while reducing pulp-adjacent cellular irritation and supporting pulp–dentin repair. Herein, supramolecular complexes of chlorogenic acid (CGA) and cucurbit[n]uril (Q[n], n = 6, 7, and 8), denoted CGA@Q[n], were constructed to regulate CGA loading, release, and interfacial exposure. CGA@Q[6] showed limited loading, release, and mineralization capacity. CGA@Q[7] exhibited faster early release and achieved complete collagen mineralization within 24 h, whereas CGA@Q[8] showed the highest encapsulation efficiency, sustained CGA supply, complete mineralization at 36 h, and a continuous, dense, integrated intrafibrillar mineral phase. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that CGA released from Q[8] reanchored to collagen and recruited Ca2+, promoting mineral formation within confined intrafibrillar spaces. These advantages extended to three-dimensional collagen networks and demineralized dentin, yielding higher HAp content, enhanced mineral–collagen integration, tubule occlusion, mechanical recovery, and MMP-9 inhibition. As a bonding pretreatment, CGA@Q[8] reduced nanoleakage, endogenous gelatinolytic activity, and aging-induced bond-strength loss. It also improved cytocompatibility relative to free CGA and promoted mineralization and odontogenic differentiation of human dental pulp stem cells (hDPSCs). In vivo, CGA@Q[8] promoted dentin remineralization, maintained near-pulp interfacial stability, alleviated pulpal irritation, and enhanced odontogenic repair. Together, these findings identify CGA@Q[8] as the most effective formulation and show that homologue selection can tune CGA exposure kinetics for coordinated dentin interface repair.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Receptor-Modular
Nanocaptors for Programmable Cytokine
Sequestration
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Pathological cytokine networks underlie inflammatory injury and tumor-associated immunosuppression, yet most cytokine-targeted therapies rely on molecularly fixed, pathway-specific antagonists. We present a receptor-modular nanomaterial strategy for constructing modular cytokine nanocaptors (MCNs) whose sequestration profiles can be reconfigured by exchanging receptor modules. Cytokine receptor ectodomains are engineered as independently producible serum albumin fusion proteins and coassembled with poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) into compositionally defined nanoparticles. This architecture decouples cytokine-binding specificity from nanoparticle structure, enabling high-density codisplay of multiple receptor modules on single particles. Representative MCNs simultaneously sequester IL-6, TNF-α, and IFN-γ and suppress cytokine-driven inflammatory signaling more effectively than matched soluble receptor mixtures. By altering module composition while preserving the same assembly framework, MCNs can be redirected from sequestering pro-inflammatory cytokines in sepsis, acute lung injury, and fulminant hepatitis to depleting immunosuppressive mediators in tumors. These results establish receptor-modular nanocaptors as programmable materials for disease-tailored cytokine sequestration and immune-microenvironment reconfiguration.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Nontrivial Edge
Superconductivity in Dirac Superconductor
PdTe2
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Superconducting topological materials with coexisted superconductivities and topological boundary states are promising platforms for realizing intrinsic topological superconductivity. In this work, the superconducting type-II Dirac semimetal PdTe2 is shown to exhibit clear periodic critical current oscillations in perpendicular magnetic fields due to the fluxoid quantization, indicating the existence of edge superconductivity in PdTe2. Furthermore, a comparative study of the different superconducting properties of the bulk and edge of PdTe2 provides direct evidence for this edge superconductivity. More importantly, by a careful analysis of the flux penetration area, the nontrivial character of the edge superconductivity is revealed, i.e., the edge superconductivity appears not only at the physical boundary of the flake, but also at the interior interface between superconducting and normal regions of PdTe2. The emergence of nontrivial edge superconductivity, indicative of the putative bulk topological superconductivity, not only reveals the great potential of PdTe2 but also provides an experimental avenue for exploring intrinsic topological superconductivity by leveraging bulk-boundary correspondence.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Janus Biofuel Cells
for Electrosynergistic Enhancement
of Microenvironment-Adaptive Cascade Catalysis in Infected Diabetic
Wound Healing
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The treatment of infectious diabetic wound is greatly hampered by hyperglycemia, inflammation, and microcirculatory dysfunction. Bioelectric stimulation and nanozyme catalysis provide a potential strategy for chronic wound repair but suffer from limitations including external electric power, low activity, and competitive multienzyme reactions. Given this, we developed microenvironment-responsive Janus GOx-Au@PCH–Pt nanoparticles (NPs) as biofuel cells, integrating cascade enzymatic catalysis and self-powered electrical stimulation. The biofuel cell features hydroxylated polyaniline (PCH) NPs as conductive bridges, Pt nanoclusters as the cathode, and glucose oxidase (GOx)-grafted Au (GOx-Au) as the anode. Under infection (acidic pH), conductive PCH shuttles electrons to generate microcurrent that accelerates enzyme catalysis on both the Au anode (GOx) and Pt cathode (peroxidase, POD). The enhanced GOx-POD cascade strengthens ·OH generation, and the self-powered electric field enhances ·OH diffusion across phospholipid bilayers, achieving significant bacterial killing and biofilm dispersion. During tissue repair, neutral/alkaline conditions switch Pt nanozyme from POD to catalase (CAT) and transform PCH into a benzoquinone structure as the electron acceptor. Reversed electron flow boosts the GOx-CAT cascade catalysis on the electrodes, accelerating glucose consumption, suppressing advanced glycation end product formation, and alleviating oxidative stress, while electrical stimulation reduces hypoxia-inducible factor-1α expressions. This synergistic effect promotes collagen deposition and orderly arrangement and normalizes microenvironment with oxygen-generating, hypoglycemic, anti-inflammatory, and macrophage phenotype-shifted features, thereby accelerating wound healing. This designed nanoscale biofuel cells realize adaptive microcurrent modulation and spatiotemporal cascade catalysis, offering a minimally invasive paradigm for infected diabetic wound therapy.</jats:p>

title: Competitive Solvation Structure in a Deep Eutectic Electrolyte Enables High‐Voltage LiCoO2‐Based Pouch Cells With 5000‐Cycle Stability
content:
A competitive solvation strategy, enabled by the comparable Li+ coordination ability of dimethyl sulfone (MSM) and succinonitrile (SN), reconstructs the Li+ solvation structure and enhances lithium metal compatibility, while synergistic TFSI−/DFOB− anion chemistry builds a robust interphase for stable high‐voltage lithium metal batteries.








ABSTRACT
Anion‐rich solvation structures improve interfacial stability but often impede Li+ desolvation, limiting fast‐charging and low‐temperature performance in high‐voltage lithium metal batteries. Unlike conventional high‐concentration or weakly solvating electrolytes, we propose a deep eutectic electrolyte (DEE) using succinonitrile (SN) and dimethyl sulfone (MSM) with competitive coordination capability. This design shifts the Li+ solvation from aggregate clusters (AGGs) to a balanced AGGs/contact ion pairs (CIPs) distribution, which lowers the Li+ desolvation energy barrier, enhances the transport kinetics, and endows the DEE with an ionic conductivity of 3.87 mS cm−1 and a Li+ transference number of 0.81. MSM moderates excessive SN coordination, suppressing parasitic reactions on the anode, thereby enabling stable Li plating/stripping for 6800 h. A lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI)/lithium difluoro(oxalato)borate (LiDFOB) dual‐salt system further optimizes interfacial chemistry, yielding a bilayer solid electrolyte interphase comprising an inorganic‐rich inner layer and a flexible organic outer layer. LiCoO2||Li cells retain 97.1% capacity after 1000 cycles at 5C (3.0–4.5 V) and operate stably at −10°C. A 3.0 Ah LiCoO2||Li pouch cell further delivers a high energy density of 417 Wh kg−1, and LiCoO2||graphite pouch cells sustain long‐term durability over 5000 cycles. This competitive solvation strategy effectively harmonizes kinetics and interfacial robustness for high‐voltage, fast‐charging DEEs.

title: Synergistic Surface‐Bulk Induction of Uniform Out‐of‐Plane (100) Orientation for High‐Efficiency Perovskite Solar Cells
content:
A surface‐bulk synergistic induction strategy coordinates ESAI interactions with the perovskite framework during crystallization. Combining precursor‐solution engineering with wet‐film intermediate treatment improves both the degree and through‐thickness uniformity of the out‐of‐plane (100) texture, achieving an orientation factor of 88.7% and a champion efficiency of 26.98% (certified 26.41%), together with enhanced operational stability.








ABSTRACT
Perovskite thin films featuring out‐of‐plane oriented (100) crystallographic facets are pivotal for advancing the efficiency and stability of perovskite solar cells, owing to their superior charge transport properties and reduced deep‐level defect density. However, conventional single‐strategy modification approaches are typically constrained by limited control over crystal orientation and spatially heterogeneous orientation distribution, hindering the full exploitation of such beneficial facets. Herein, we present a surface‐bulk synergistic induction strategy that overcomes the limitations of single modification approaches, effectively promoting directional grain alignment and cooperatively guiding ordered out‐of‐plane growth during thermal annealing. Benefiting from the successful fabrication of a perovskite film with a uniform and predominant preferred orientation, the inverted perovskite solar cells achieve a champion power conversion efficiency of 26.98% (certified 26.41%). Furthermore, the homogeneous texture and high intrinsic stability of the (100) facets enable the devices to retain 93.5% of their initial PCE after 1000 h of operational stability testing. This strategy effectively tackles the technical constraints of precursor solution regulation and solid‐state surface treatment, offering a novel research model for the precise modulation of perovskite thin film crystal facets and the secondary growth of polycrystalline thin films.

title: Characterizing Fill Factor Limitations in Perovskite‐Silicon Tandem Solar Cells
content:
The fill factor of monolithic perovskite‐Si tandem solar cells is limited by the photoshunt behavior of the perovskite top cells, which is the result of the competition between slow charge extraction through the transport layers and recombination in the absorber. If this photoshunt is suppressed, the FF of tandem devices could reach over 85% according to the simulation results.








ABSTRACT
Monolithic perovskite‐silicon tandem solar cells have achieved power conversion efficiencies approaching 35%. However, a significant gap remains to their thermodynamic limit, primarily due to fill factor (FF) losses. This work presents a methodology to identify the underlying mechanisms of the losses. Electroluminescence characterization reveals the potential FF without series resistance losses but cannot fully explain the observed FF limitations. An additional loss mechanism is the photoshunt, a phenomenon which the parallel shunt resistance apparently reduces under illumination in perovskite solar cells. Using an analytical model, we show that the photoshunt originates from competition between charge extraction, governed by transport‐layer properties and electric field, and recombination in the absorber and at interfaces. An equivalent circuit model quantifies its impact on subcell and tandem FF. Additionally, the two‐diode property of the Si subcell can also influence the tandem FF losses. Measurements on tandem devices under spectrally independent LED illumination show that photoshunt losses can be hidden under bottom‐cell‐limited conditions, explaining the preference for slightly bottom‐cell‐limited tandem designs. Reducing the photoshunt through improved charge transport and reduced recombination could enable operation closer to current matching while minimizing FF and efficiency losses.

title: Lumped Circuits Modeling of Dynamic Energy Transfer in Triboelectric Nanogenerators with Nonlinear Electromechanical Coupling
content:
This work presents a lumped electromechanical model that identifies resonance, impedance matching, and structural dynamics as key determinants of energy transfer in triboelectric nanogenerators. Experimentally validated across mechanically distinct devices, the framework also shows that excitation‐dependent responses enable simultaneous energy harvesting and information extraction, coupling enhanced electrical energy storage with self‐powered environmental sensing.








ABSTRACT
Powering autonomous electronics, sensors, and wearable systems using small‐scale daily mechanical energy is becoming increasingly important. Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) offer a lightweight, flexible, and adaptable route for such applications, particularly when movements are involved. Here, we present a first‐of‐its‐kind unified dynamic energy‐transfer framework for TENGs, coupling their mechanical and electrical domains through a lumped element‐based equivalent circuit (LEEC) model. The framework captures time‐varying electrostatic behavior and key mechanical parameters, mass, damping, and stiffness, within a single predictive platform, enabling system‐level analysis of dynamic efficiency, impedance, resonance, and power transfer under different excitation conditions. The Thévenin equivalent model reveals that TENG performance is dynamically governed by excitation frequency, resonance, load matching, and surface charge density, approaching a time‐averaged theoretical efficiency of ∼54%. Experimental validation across devices with varied mechanical parameters shows close agreement with theory in electrical response and frequency‐dependent behavior. Furthermore, four borophene‐modified TENGs with different charge‐generation characteristics exhibit a systematic increase in electrical output and an estimated efficiency of up to 14.2% for the examined parameter space, supporting the model‐predicted dependence of energy‐conversion performance on surface charge density. The LEEC‐guided platform enables coupled energy and information harvesting through resonance‐enhanced capacitor charging and self‐powered road‐state sensing.

title: Nonlinear Kinetic Optimization via Strong–Weak Cosolvent Synergy in Aqueous Zinc Batteries
content:
Pairing strong and weak cosolvents unlocks a nonlinear kinetic advantage in aqueous zinc batteries. Complementary roles within and beyond the primary solvation shell regulate Zn2+ coordination and interphase formation, lowering the charge‐transfer barrier by approximately 40% relative to single‐cosolvent electrolytes. This synergy preserves electrolyte stability while enabling optimized kinetics and durable cell operation.








ABSTRACT
Cosolvent engineering for aqueous Zn metal batteries has traditionally emphasized thermodynamic stabilization, whereas the kinetic dimension of Zn2+ charge transfer—particularly in multi‐cosolvent systems—remains far less understood. Here we conduct a systematic study on a dual‐cosolvent electrolyte pairing a strong cosolvent (DMSO) with a weak cosolvent (DMC). Through spatial decoupling, the strong cosolvent directly coordinates to stabilize the primary solvation shell, while the weak cosolvent forms a dynamic outer‐shell buffer. This unique context modulates Zn–ligand binding, facilitates desolvation, and guides the formation of a regulated SEI. Consequently, this architecture preserves comparably high thermodynamic stability while unlocking a nonlinear kinetic optimization exclusive to the dual‐cosolvent regime. Using a multi‐descriptor framework, we demonstrate a ∼40% reduction in the charge‐transfer barrier relative to single‐cosolvent systems. This kinetic enhancement translates into robust practical performance, establishing strong–weak cosolvent synergy as a versatile design principle for next‐generation aqueous batteries.

title: Dual Metal Dopants Advance Near‐Room‐Temperature PbS‐based Thermoelectrics
content:
A synergistic strategy combining homologous Se/Te alloying with dual‐metal Zn/Ge co‐doping advances the performance of PbS‐based thermoelectrics, demonstrating its potential for near‐room‐temperature solid‐state cooling and low‐grade heat recovery.








ABSTRACT
Low‐cost lead sulfide (PbS) exhibits poor near‐room‐temperature (300–573 K) thermoelectric performance, limiting its practical applications. Here, Se/Te alloying coupled with dual‐metal Zn/Ge co‐doping is employed to enhance the near‐room‐temperature thermoelectric performance of n‐type PbS. Se/Te alloying forms a single‐phase PbS0.5Se0.35Te0.15 solid solution (PbS(Se/Te)), where alloy‐induced mass and strain fluctuations enhance phonon scattering, reducing the lattice thermal conductivity from ∼2.09 W m−1 K−1 for PbS to ∼0.75 W m−1 K−1 at 300 K without compromising electrical transport. Zn/Ge co‐doping further optimizes carrier transport by regulating lattice defects and tuning carrier density, achieving a high carrier mobility of ∼522 cm2 V−1 s−1 and an optimized carrier density of ∼1.03 × 1019 cm−3. The optimized PbS(Se/Te)+0.6‰Zn+5‰Ge sample exhibits an enhanced power factor of ∼20.23 µW cm−1 K−2 at 300 K, yielding a ZT of ∼0.54 at 300 K and an average ZT of ∼0.80 over 300–573 K. A seven‐pair thermoelectric module achieves a maximum temperature difference (ΔTmax) of ∼33.4 K at Th = 343 K, and a single‐leg device reaches a peak conversion efficiency of ∼7.2% under a temperature difference of 300 K. These results highlight the potential of Zn/Ge co‐doping for advancing n‐type PbS‐based materials toward near‐room‐temperature cooling and low‐grade heat recovery.

title: Efficient H2O2 Photosynthesis With Valorization by X‐Packing NDI Cocrystal Catalyst
content:
DPNDI‐Py, an X‐packed charge‐transfer (CT) cocrystal with strong intermolecular CT interactions, enables coexisting electron‐ and energy‐transfer pathways for H2O2 production coupled with ascorbic acid oxidation (AA) to dehydroascorbic acid (DHA).








ABSTRACT
Solar‐driven photocatalytic H2O2 synthesis offers a sustainable and green alternative to the energy‐intensive anthraquinone process. However, coordinated regulation of electron‐transfer (ET) and energy‐transfer (EnT) pathways for efficient H2O2 production remains challenging. Organic charge‐transfer (CT) cocrystals, which reconfigure the energy‐level structure through new intermolecular electronic states, provide a promising avenue to overcome this limitation. Herein, we report a CT cocrystal photocatalyst, DPNDI‐Py, prepared by liquid‐assisted grinding (LAG) of N, N′‐bis(4‐pyridyl)‐1,4,5,8‐naphthalenediimide (DPNDI) and pyrene (Py). The cocrystal harbors an X‐packed donor‐acceptor arrangement, with a crossing angle of 52° between the long axes of DPNDI and Py. Spectroscopic measurements confirm strong intermolecular CT, and transient spectroscopy supports CT‐related excited‐state dynamics and the formation of long‐lived triplet states, while theoretical calculations indicate electronic structure favorable for intersystem crossing (ISC). Mechanistic studies indicate that both EnT and ET pathways are utilized in photocatalysis. Under LED irradiation in air, DPNDI‐Py delivers an average H2O2 production rate of 18.47 ± 0.57 mmol g−1 h−1 coupled with an 83.7 ± 2.26% dehydroascorbic acid (DHA) yield from ascorbic acid (AA) oxidation. This work provides mechanistic insight into CT‐mediated photocatalysis, offering a design principle for organic photocatalysts.

title: Synergistic Dual‐Site Regulation in a Tailored Imine‐COF for Enhanced Hydrogen Peroxide Photosynthesis
content:
Nitrogen‐site engineering in isostructural imine‑linked COFs is established to reveal the crucial role of pyridine‐imine units in steering the oxygen reduction pathway. Synergistic coordination of main‑group metals at the pyridine‐imine sites further promotes charge separation and 2e− selectivity, achieving a superior H2O2 production rate of 15.3 mmol g−1 h−1 in O2‑saturated isopropanol aqueous solution, surpassing most reported COF‑based photocatalysts. This work unlocks a dual‑site regulation strategy for efficient photosynthesis of hydrogen peroxide.








ABSTRACT
Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) emerge as promising candidates for the photocatalytic production of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). However, precise modulation of the chemical environment of active sites in COFs remains a significant challenge. Based on a molecular engineering strategy, this study focuses on hierarchical regulation of nitrogen coordination environments for efficient photocatalytic H2O2 production through the 2e− ORR. Intrinsic nitrogen configurations (triazine vs. pyridine) are first tailored to construct two types of COFs. The pyridyl‐imine TAPT‐BTPA (4) optimizes charge carrier separation and extends visible‐light absorption, leading to an enhanced H2O2 production rate of 8.12 mmol g−1 h−1 in aqueous solution containing isopropanol as a sacrificial agent under an O2 atmosphere. Main‐group metals (In, Sn, and Sb) are then anchored at the pyridine‐imine sites to modulate local electron density further and steer reaction pathways. Structural characterization and activity tests reveal that Sb‐coordinated TAPT‐BTPA‐Sb (10) induces a unique synergistic effect, redirecting the ORR toward a more favorable stepwise 1e− route. This significant pathway regulation ultimately boosts the H2O2 production rate to 15.3 mmol g−1 h−1 under the same conditions. This work clarifies the decisive role of coordination environment engineering and establishes a molecular‐level design paradigm for advanced H2O2 synthesis photocatalysts.

title: Bridge‐Level Electronic Compensation in Prussian White Cathodes: Charge‐Transfer Kinetic Regimes and Design Principles
content:
Prussian White cathodes can exhibit bridge‐level electronic‐compensation constraints beyond Na+ diffusion. This Perspective introduces descriptor‐based kinetic regimes for Fe–C≡N–TM bridges using Marcus‐type descriptors and translates this framework into descriptor‐guided strategies for tuning redox‐level alignment, cyanide‐mediated coupling, bridge connectivity, and structural reorganization toward low‐polarization, kinetically robust sodium‐ion cathodes.








ABSTRACT
Prussian White (PW) cathodes are promising sodium–ion battery materials because of their open framework, low cost, and high structural reversibility. However, polarization and capacity loss under high‐rate or low‐temperature operation arise from coupled ionic, structural, interfacial, and electronic processes that are not fully captured by Na+ diffusion or average structural evolution alone. This perspective introduces a bridge‐level electronic‐compensation framework in which the Fe─C≡N─TM bridge is treated as a local unit for describing local charge redistribution. Using Marcus‐type descriptors together with concepts of metal‐to‐metal charge transfer, intervalence charge transfer, and metal–ligand interactions, three physical contributions are emphasized: the local charge‐state free‐energy difference (ΔG°), cyanide‐mediated electronic coupling (Hab), and structure‐coupled reorganization energy (λ). Local bridge states are organized into descriptor‐based kinetic regimes based on the balance among energetic mismatch, electronic coupling, and structural reorganization, with transition‐metal chemistries serving as representative mechanistic cases. These descriptors are further translated into design principles involving redox‐level alignment, cyanide‐mediated coupling and network connectivity, and control of local structural reorganization. This perspective provides a physical basis for interpreting bridge‐level electronic compensation and considering how local energetic alignment, coupling, and structural reorganization can be regulated in PW cathodes.

title: Intranasal Pathogenesis‐Adaptive Nanotherapeutics Reinstate Regenerative Competence for Post‐Stroke Neural Repair
content:
Single‐cell transcriptomics reveals disrupted neuron‐microglia‐neural stem cell communication after stroke, inspiring an intranasal biomimetic strategy that leverages commensal bacterium‐derived extracellular vesicles for efficient nose‐to‐brain delivery and coordinated regulation of oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and nitric oxide signaling to protect injured neural tissue and promote endogenous neural repair. This figure was created with Adobe Illustrator 2021.








ABSTRACT
Poststroke neurorehabilitation is limited by the poor regenerative capacity of adult neurons. Although neural stem cells (NSCs) can generate new neurons, their reparative potential is constrained by inefficient delivery to cerebral lesions and a hostile regenerative niche. Here, analysis of a single‐nucleus transcriptomic dataset revealed pronounced dysfunction and intercellular crosstalk among neurons, microglia, and NSCs, highlighting redox imbalance and impaired nitric oxide (NO) signaling as potential therapeutic targets. Guided by these findings, we develop FCeO2@GLp, a pathogenesis‐adaptive nanotherapeutic integrating reactive oxygen species scavenging, NO replenishment and immune modulation within cerebral ischemic microenvironment. Following intranasal administration, FCeO2@GLp actively adheres to the olfactory epithelium (OE), reaches infarcted brain regions, releases cerium oxide (CeO2) nanozyme, fingolimod, and a NO donor in response to local acidity. This coordinated strategy alleviates oxidative stress, reprograms microglia, protects neurons, and enhances NSC proliferation and neuronal differentiation. Consequently, FCeO2@GLp effectively reduces infarct volume and cerebral edema during the acute phase, and improves long‐term neurological function and survival, establishing a lesion‐responsive strategy for poststroke neural repair.
