title: Structural and Mechanistic Basis of Dual Substrate Promiscuity in the Acyltransferase AntB Enables Late‐Stage Diversification of Natural Products
content:
The bacterial acyltransferase AntB exhibits striking dual promiscuity toward both acyl donors and acceptors. Structural and biochemical analyses elucidated the molecular basis of its spacious active‐site architecture, which accommodates 43 donors and 8 structurally diverse natural product acceptors. Harnessing this versatility in a one‐pot cascade enabled the late‐stage diversification of an agrochemical precursor into potent antifungal analogues.








ABSTRACT
Biocatalytic regioselective acylation is a powerful strategy for diversifying natural products and optimizing their pharmacological properties. Compared with plant acyltransferases (ATs), bacterial tailoring ATs remain poorly understood. AntB from the antimycin pathway was previously reported to possess acyl‐donor promiscuity toward limited acyl‐CoA thioesters, yet its acyl‐acceptor promiscuity, structural basis, and catalytic mechanism had not been elucidated. Here, we systematically characterize AntB and uncover its remarkable dual substrate promiscuity. The enzyme accepts eight structurally diverse natural product acceptors—including terpenoids, alkaloids, polyketides, and aromatics—and supports iterative acylation, while also processing 43 chemically distinct acyl donors, including 22 previously unreported. Structural analysis revealed the molecular basis of its dual substrate promiscuity and catalysis. Engineering afforded the S17A/M265L variant with a 4.45‐fold increase in activity toward SPN‐J acylation. To harness this catalytic flexibility, we developed a one‐pot biocatalytic platform by combining AntB with engineered acyl‐CoA synthetases UkaQFAV and AliA100 for in situ acyl‐CoA regeneration. Application of this system to the late‐stage modification of the agrochemical precursor deacyl‐UK‐2A generated a panel of acylated analogues, including three novel derivatives with enhanced antifungal activity. This study advances understanding of bacterial tailoring ATs and establishes AntB as a versatile biocatalyst for late‐stage natural product diversification.

title: Conformation‐Selective Binding Domains of Intramolecular Chemically Induced Protein Dimerisation Systems
content:
Intramolecular chemically induced dimerisation transforms FK506‐ and cyclosporine A‐responsive protein pairs into high‐affinity pseudo‐allosteric switches. Holo‐selective binders isolated by mRNA display convert these switches into gain‐of‐signal biosensors and ultrasensitive ELISAs, enabling direct quantification of both immunosuppressants in unprocessed patient blood with accuracy comparable to LC–MS/MS and revealing a general route to small‐molecule detection.








ABSTRACT
Chemically induced protein dimerisation (CID) is a widely used approach for detecting and actuating small‐molecule‐protein interactions. Here, we demonstrate that CID systems can be used as building blocks for higher‐order ligand‐controlled protein systems. To this end, we converted classical FK506‐ and cyclosporine A‐controlled CIDs into single‐chain pseudo‐allosteric proteins. These systems displayed 15‐ and 50‐fold gains in ligand affinity compared with the parental components operating in trans. Using these fusion proteins as baits in mRNA display, we identified FN3con binding domains that recognise the holo state of each bait with subnanomolar affinity and >100‐fold selectivity over the apo form. Integration of the binding domains and intramolecular CIDs into two‐component enzymatic protein biosensors enabled quantification of the cognate ligands with low‐nanomolar limits of detection (LODs). ELISA assays based on the developed systems displayed mid‐picomolar LODs and accurately quantified FK506 and cyclosporine A in unprocessed blood samples from transplant patients with accuracy comparable to that of LC‐MS/MS. This work establishes a generalisable strategy for harnessing the affinity gains of intramolecular CID systems to create gain‐of‐signal assays for small molecules and ions.

title: Intermolecular Carbon–Carbon Naphthalene Coupling Involves a Radical Mechanism Driven by Cytochrome P450 in Alternaria alternata
content:
1,8‐DHN is an important intermediate to form complex aromatic ring systems. Phenol‐coupling reactions are important for the dimerization of two molecules. Here, we show that a fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme catalyzes specific C─C bonds.








ABSTRACT
Dihydroxynaphthalene (DHN) derivatives are precursors of biologically important molecules, including melanin and perylenequinones (PQs). Biosynthesis of DHN‐derived metabolites requires precise spatial control of radical reactions to form specific C─C or C─O─C bonds. Investigating fungal PQ biosynthesis in Alternaria alternata, we identified a cytochrome P450 enzyme that catalyzes a highly regio‐ and stereospecific C─C radical coupling reaction. Conversely, a DHN‐converting P450 from Berkleasmium sp. utilizes a diradical mechanism yielding a C─O─C bridge. Comparing these enzymes revealed five sequence motifs that, with structural modeling, allowed the identification of a novel A. alternata enzyme converting 1,8‐DHN to a 2‐2' DHN dimer. We demonstrate that P450‐dependent PQ biosynthesis in A. alternata is fundamentally distinct from the laccase‐fasciclin‐mediated pathway in Cercospora beticola, indicating that PQ biosynthesis evolved via distinct, lineage‐specific pathways through convergent evolution. Finally, PQs contribute to microbial niche shaping on tomato fruits. Understanding these pathways provides a foundation for producing PQs for medical applications.

title: The Nature of Cell‐Penetrating Poly(disulfide)s
content:
The mode of action of cell‐penetrating poly(disulfide)s (CPDs) is elucidated to understand thiol‐mediated uptake (TMU) in general and guide future efforts to control cellular entry for chemicals delivery and pathogen defense.








ABSTRACT
Cell‐penetrating poly(disulfide)s (CPDs) are the most popular thiol‐mediated uptake (TMU) tools for delivering attached substrates of interest (SOIs) into the cytosol. Despite their widespread use, their mode of action remains unknown. Herein, we elucidate how CPDs work using combined data from protein knockdown, µMap proteomics, coacervate assembly, mechanosensitive fluorescent membrane probes, CPD inhibitors, activators, and depolymerization. Their guanidinium sidechains first ion‐pair with anionic clusters on cell surfaces. By enhancing effective CPD concentration, these non‐covalent interactions enable, accelerate, and direct dynamic covalent disulfide exchange cascades with cellular thiols and disulfides. CPD bioconjugation rates match their uptake activity, exceeding those of disulfide monomers by 3000 times. Exchange with proteins capable of membrane remodeling allows CPDs to exploit these proteins' primary functions to mobilize anionic lipids (scramblases, ANO6), form toroidal elastic pores and related membrane deformations, and repair all after CPD‐SOI conjugates have passed through (tetraspanins, TSPAN8, flippases, etc.). Within cells, CPDs form coacervates and integrate into biological condensates, particularly nucleoli, until they depolymerize and release the SOIs. This understanding of the nature of CPDs also clarifies TMU in general and will guide future efforts to control cellular entry for drug delivery and pathogen defense.

title: Recognition Mechanism of Serotonin by a G‐Quadruplex–Duplex Hybrid Aptamer
content:
High‐resolution NMR structures reveal an unexpected G‐quadruplex–duplex hybrid architecture for the widely used serotonin aptamer—a key neurotransmitter sensor. Serotonin binds specifically at the junction between the G‐quadruplex and duplex, stacking directly onto the G‐quadruplex plane without contacting with the duplex, providing a structural basis for high‐affinity recognition and biosensing application.








ABSTRACT
Serotonin is a key neurotransmitter, and aptamer‐based tools using the 44‐nt Apt44 have been successfully developed for its in vitro and in vivo detection. Nevertheless, the structural basis of recognition by this aptamer remains unclear. Here, we report high‐resolution NMR structures of Apt38, a 6‐nt truncated variant in the third loop of Apt44, in free and serotonin‐bound states. Both structures reveal a two‐layered antiparallel chair‐type G‐quadruplex core with three edgewise loops and a terminal duplex, forming a G‐quadruplex–duplex hybrid structure. Serotonin binds at the G‐quadruplex–duplex junction by stacking directly onto the G‐tetrad plane without contacting the duplex, representing a newly identified binding mode at this hotspot junction. This binding is stabilized by stacking, electrostatic attraction, hydrogen bonding, and hydrophobic contacts. Apt38 is preorganized for binding, whereas the longer third loop of Apt44 introduces conformational dynamics into the G‐quadruplex scaffold, which enables a pronounced binding‐triggered conformational switch in PBS buffer, explaining its sensing mechanism. Our work reveals the recognition and sensing mechanism of the serotonin aptamer and provides a framework for aptamer design in serotonin biosensing.

title: Molecular Engineering at Electrode Interface Enables Efficient Catalytic Nitrogen Reduction
content:
Overcoming the limitations of homogeneous catalysis and the challenges of molecular skeleton modification, a pyrene‐functionalized molybdenum complex was synthesized and efficiently assembled at the electrode interface for the first time. The molecularly engineered electrochemical and photoelectrochemical nitrogen fixation devices significantly enhanced catalyst utilization and turnover frequency for nitrogen reduction, while reducing the required applied bias and producing value‐added oxidation products. 








ABSTRACT
Molecular catalysts are promising for nitrogen (N2) fixation due to their well‐defined sites and tunable coordination, yet most molecules in homogeneous systems reside in the bulk solution, leading to poor catalyst utilization. Here, we introduced a molecular engineering strategy by assembling a functionalized molecular molybdenum complex (PyMoBr3PNP) on graphdiyne (GDY) through π–π interactions. The resulting interface‐assembled molecular electrode, PyMoBr3PNP/GDY/carbon paper (CP), catalyzed N2 conversion to ammonia (NH3) using 2,4,6‐trimethylpyridinium triflate ([ColH][OTf]) as the proton source. Rigorous isotopic labeling and continuous time‐dependent controls confirmed the genuine nature of catalytic N2 to NH3 turnover. Encouraged by the intrinsic N2 reduction activity, the PyMoBr3PNP/GDY/CP cathode was further coupled with a molecular hybrid photoanode (ZnTCPP/Al2O3/BiVO4) for photoelectrocatalytic N2 reduction. The integrated system decreased the applied bias, achieved a turnover frequency (TOF) of 47.52 h−1 and a turnover number (TON) of 157.54 over 4 h for NH3 production, representing the highest performance reported to date for molecular‐based electrochemical and photoelectrochemical N2 reduction. All of these results highlight the potential of molecular engineering platforms to enhance catalyst utilization, improve reaction efficiency, and lower energy consumption for N2 fixation.

title: Rigid Bis‐Amidinium Anchoring Engineering Enables Synergistic Defect Suppression and Ion Stabilization for High‐Performance Flexible Perovskite X‐Ray Detectors and TFT‐Array Imaging
content:
Rigid bis‐amidinium p‐BDAm regulates the local Pb–I‐containing environment through favorable multisite interactions, suppressing defect‐related recombination and improving charge transport and electrical stability. The same molecular regulation strategy enhances flexible MAPbI3 nylon composite membrane detectors and blade‐coated MAPbI3 TFT‐array devices, enabling both single‐pixel scanning and TFT‐array parallel X‐ray imaging.








ABSTRACT
Flexible direct‐conversion X‐ray detectors based on halide perovskites hold great promise for mechanically compliant and array‐integrated imaging, yet their performance is limited by grain‐boundary defects and electrical instability in polycrystalline thick films. Here, we introduce 1,4‐benzenedicarboximidamide dihydrochloride (p‐BDAm) as an additive for regulating polycrystalline methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3) detector layers. Spectroscopic measurements and density functional theory (DFT) calculations support multisite interactions between the bis‐amidinium framework and Pb–I‐containing species as a plausible contribution to the p‐BDAm‐mediated regulation of the local grain‐boundary environment and crystallization behavior. Overall, p‐BDAm incorporation suppresses nonradiative recombination, increases the resistivity and mobility–lifetime product, raises the apparent activation energy extracted from temperature‐dependent conductivity from 0.17 to 0.49 eV, and substantially improves dark‐current stability. The optimized flexible perovskite composite membrane detector achieves a sensitivity of 2165.5 µC Gyair−1 cm−2 at 10 V and an estimated detection limit of 15.0 nGyair s−1. Moreover, the p‐BDAm‐regulated MAPbI3 layer is compatible with thin‐film transistor (TFT)‐array integration, enabling parallel X‐ray imaging. A representative TFT image was obtained at an X‐ray dose rate of 12.3 µGyair s−1 with an exposure time of 0.5 s. These results demonstrate a transferable molecular‐regulation strategy for stabilizing polycrystalline perovskite X‐ray detectors across flexible and array‐integrated architectures.

title: Pre‐Strain‐Activated Strain‐Sensing Ink for Facile Printing of Highly Sensitive and Stable Electronic Textiles
content:
Pre‐strain‐activated printable strain‐sensing ink constructs robust percolated conductive networks within elastomeric and textile substrates, enabling highly sensitive, stable, and breathable wearable electronic textiles. The system delivers reliable real‐time monitoring of human motion and physiological signals, while maintaining excellent electromechanical stability, fast response, and durability under complex and repetitive mechanical deformations.








ABSTRACT
Printable strain‐sensing electronic textiles (e‐textiles) are promising for wearable health monitoring and human–machine interfaces, yet achieving simultaneous high sensitivity, mechanical stability, and comfort remains challenging due to unstable conductive networks and weak interfacial integration with textile substrates. Here, we report a printable strain‐sensing ink based on a styrene–isoprene–styrene elastomer integrated with carbon nanotubes and graphene oxide. Guided by percolation theory and interfacial interaction engineering, we introduce a pre‐strain‐activated conductive‐network strategy to reconstruct and regulate conductive pathways within the printed sensing layer, enabling efficient strain‐to‐resistance conversion while maintaining structural robustness under repeated deformation. The resulting e‐textile exhibits a low strain detection limit of 0.05%, a high gauge factor of 160.5, a fast response time of 45.4 ms, a sensing range of 36.7%, and durability over 1000 cycles at 15% strain. Thanks to strong interfacial adhesion between the infiltrated sensing layer and porous textile scaffold, the device maintains stable electromechanical performance under complex deformations while preserving intrinsic softness and breathability. It further enables reliable real‐time monitoring of respiration and human motion. This work provides a simple and scalable conductive‐network engineering strategy for high‐performance strain‐sensing e‐textiles, offering a generalizable route toward next‐generation wearable electronics.

title: Spatially Convergent Encoding of Linked Data Through Assembled DNA Nanostructures
content:
DNA‐based data storage provides a platform for information archiving, yet DNA molecules encoding related sequences can lose association during amplification‐based retrieval. Here, we introduce a Y‐shaped DNA nanostructure that consolidates correlated sequences into a single scaffold, preserving linkage before microdroplet partitioning. This architecture enables coordinated amplification and accurate reconstruction through microdroplet PCR, enhancing the fidelity of DNA‐encoded data recovery.








ABSTRACT
DNA‐based storage is a promising candidate for next‐generation data media, providing a powerful strategy for preserving digital information in molecular formats. As information complexity increases, multiple DNA molecules are often used to encode related data elements, but their independent distribution can compromise information linkage during amplification‐based readout. Although microdroplet PCR reduces amplification bias through spatial compartmentalization, stochastic partitioning of individual DNA molecules may hinder the recovery of associated information. Here, we present a Y‐shaped DNA nanostructure system that integrates multiple related DNA sequences into a single molecular scaffold, enabling physical co‐localization of linked information before compartmentalization. The Y‐shaped architecture serves as a unified input unit for microdroplet PCR, allowing coordinated amplification and accurate recovery of associated data within individual droplets. By maintaining molecular linkage during processing, this strategy improves the uniformity of DNA‐encoded linked information recovery. Overall, this system provides a programmable framework for DNA data organization and droplet‐based retrieval of linked information.

title: Modulated Laser‐Assisted Nanopore Fabrication With Ammonium Sulfate for Single‐Molecule Sensing
content:
In summary, we developed a temporally modulated CW laser‐assisted method for reliable solid‐state nanopore fabrication with reduced bubble formation and contamination, even in viscous electrolytes. Ammonium sulfate further enhanced DNA–pore interactions through interfacial ion adsorption, enabling prolonged translocation and discrimination of poly(dA) and poly(dC), while aptamer‐mediated Scp1 detection demonstrated broader molecular sensing capability.








ABSTRACT
Nanopore sensing provides a label‐free platform for single‐molecule analysis. To achieve reliable solid‐state nanopore sensing, however, it is essential to optimize appropriate nanopore fabrication methods, as variations in pore diameter, geometry, surface state, and fabrication residues can affect molecular discrimination capability. Here, we report a temporally modulated CW laser‐assisted dielectric breakdown method for facilitating in‐situ fabrication of nanopores in silicon nitride membranes, coupled with ammonium sulfate electrolytes to improve sensing performance. Systematic characterization revealed that temporally modulated CW laser minimizes contamination/debris formation during pore fabrication and yields improved nanopore sensing. Streaming‐potential measurements and interfacial ion‐transport simulations suggest that ammonium‐containing electrolytes modify the SiN nanopore interface by promoting NH4+ adsorption on the inner pore surface as well as SO42− ions, thereby enhancing DNA–pore interactions. This effect slowed a subset of DNA translocation events, enabling longer dwell‐time observations and differentiation between poly(dA) and poly(dC) blockade populations. Furthermore, aptamer‐assisted detection enabled detection of Scp1‐bound aptamer complexes under conditions where the protein alone tended to clog the pore. The Scp1–aptamer complex showed prolonged dwell times compared with those of free aptamers, even under 0.14 M KCl. Together, these results demonstrate that integrating our approach provides an improved approach for high‐performance single‐molecule nanopore detection.

title: Crystallographic Design of Electrodeposited Copper for Ultra‐Low‐Temperature Cu‐Cu Direct Bonding
content:
Crystallographic orientation controls energy dissipation in low‐temperature Cu–Cu direct bonding. Unlike (100) and (111) Cu, (101) Cu converts grain‐boundary energy into cross‐interface grain growth, removing the original interface and suppressing void formation.








ABSTRACT
Low‐temperature Cu‐Cu direct bonding (<150°C) for 3D integration faces a severe bottleneck from interfacial voids caused by limited atomic diffusion. While nanocrystalline Cu (NC‐Cu) has emerged as a promising bonding material owing to its high stored energy, the thermodynamic influence of initial crystallographic orientation remains unclear. Here, we systematically investigate the orientation‐dependent bonding thermodynamics of NC‐Cu thin films with (100), (111), and (101) orientations. Despite high internal energy, (100) and (111) Cu consume significant energy for internal defect curing (dislocation glide and twin annihilation), inducing void aggregation. Conversely, (101) Cu, despite not possessing the largest absolute total driving force, directs the largest fraction of its available positive driving force toward macroscopic grain‐boundary migration, thereby achieving extensive interfacial‐crossing growth and enhanced overall mechanical reliability. We demonstrate that reliable bonding requires targeted allocation of grain boundary energy, establishing a novel crystallographic design principle for advanced heterogeneous integration and solid‐state joining technologies.

title: Uniform Radial Compression Enabling Densification of High‐Curvature Fiber Electrodes for High‐Rate Ah‐Level Energy Textiles
content:
Uniform radial compression enabled by a flexible elastomer‐wrapped steel roller allows damage‐free densification of high‐curvature fiber electrodes by converting point contact into conformal surface contact. The resulting microstructure exhibits improved particle packing and ion‐transport pathways, enabling high‐rate, high‐loading FLIBs through a scalable and manufacturing‐compatible calendering strategy.








ABSTRACT
Fiber lithium‐ion batteries (FLIBs), which can be woven into flexible energy textiles, are promising power sources for wearable electronics. However, increasing their cell‐level energy density requires high‐loading fiber electrodes that are limited by the porous, loosely packed structures formed during dip‐coating, since conventional calendering cannot be applied to highly curved fibers without fracturing the coating. Here, we address this limitation by applying uniform radial compression around fiber electrodes through a flexible‐roller calendering approach that uses an elastomer‐wrapped steel roller, enabling efficient densification with substantially reduced structural disruption. X‐ray computed tomography (CT) shows that calendering reduces porosity to 27.36% and removes large voids, along with improved particle packing and coating‐collector contact. These microstructural optimizations effectively enhance transport kinetics, enabling calendered FLIBs to deliver a 72.70% increase in 4C capacity and improved cycling stability (300 cycles with retention over 87.41%). Their strengthened structural integrity affords reliable operation upon repeated deformations like bending and knotting, supports integration into Ah‐level energy textiles, and allows conformal mounting on drone arms for high‐power use. This work presents an effective, damage‐free densification route for high‐curvature fiber electrodes and provides a scalable microstructure‐engineering approach for advancing wearable energy textiles and other deformable energy systems.
